schema_notes.level: Original level label from source (PK/K, 1-5, MS, HS)
schema_notes.boundary_includes: What students are expected to do (Boundary Statement 1)
schema_notes.boundary_excludes: What students are NOT expected to do (Boundary Statement 2)
schema_notes.ai_related: Whether the standard is flagged as AI-related
schema_notes.keywords: Curated search keywords for matching curriculum content. Includes core terms from the standard, common curriculum synonyms, and concept-specific vocabulary.

standards.statement: Carry out algorithms in daily activities.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should demonstrate simple, step-by-step activities in the correct sequence for familiar classroom or home tasks. Following classroom routines (e.g., cleaning up or lining up) or completing personal tasks (e.g., eating snacks or washing hands) are appropriate. Teachers should explicitly teach the word algorithm in context.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to carry out algorithms that include conditionals or iteration. Students are not required to write algorithms or use a programming language.

implementation_examples.description: The teacher introduces an algorithm for packing up at the end of the day using picture cards showing the steps posted near the cubbies. Students work individually to execute the algorithm by following the specific sequence demonstrating their understanding by successfully completing the routine in the correct order, showing they can translate a visual list of instructions into a physical sequence of actions.

Students participate in a class movement activity, like "Head, Shoulders, Knees, and Toes." The teacher models and uses visual cues for each action. Students perform the sequence repeatedly, then demonstrate understanding by leading peers or reordering pictures of the steps.

math.standard: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).
math.description: Students practice sequence and the algorithm of counting up by practicing counting forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence.

math.standard: Model shapes in the world by building shapes from components (e.g., sticks and clay balls) and drawing shapes.
math.description: Students work individually to build a house using pattern blocks following a shape algorithm (e.g., "Step 1: Place a square. Step 2: Place a triangle on top."). Students show understanding by producing the correct shape, proving they followed the "algorithm" of the blueprint.

ela.standard: Follow words from left to right, top to bottom, and page by page.
ela.description: Students explicitly discuss and practice the algorithm of how to read from left to right, top to bottom, and page by page.

ela.standard: With prompting and support, retell familiar stories, including key details.
ela.description: After reading a story, students work in pairs to place story events in order using picture cards identifying that the story is like an algorithm. Students produce a reordered physical timeline of the book that they physically act out.

science.standard: Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth’s surface.
science.description: Students describe the algorithms followed by natural systems (e.g., the sun comes up, it gets light and warmer, the sun goes down, it gets dark and cooler) to connect events with causes that generate observable patterns.

other.standard: Child follows classroom rules and routines with increasing independence.
other.description: Students execute multistep algorithms posted as a sequence of pictures illustrating the classroom rule (e.g., hang backpack → put folder in bin → choose lunch → sit on dot) with increasing independence.

other.standard: Make still and moving body shapes that show lines (for example, straight, bent, and curved), changes levels, and vary in size (large/small). Join with others to make a circle formation and work with others to change its dimensions.
other.description: Students learn and perform choreography (an algorithm) to common songs that make use of body shapes, like "Y.M.C.A.," or levels, like "Head, Shoulders, Knees, and Toes."

standards.statement: Decompose a problem or task into individual parts to develop an algorithm.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to break down familiar, multistep tasks into smaller, ordered steps, focusing on sequencing and logical thinking. For example, decompose classroom routines, a game in physical education, or instrument maintenance in music into distinct, sequenced steps.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to work with abstract problems or create algorithms involving conditional logic (if/then). Students are not required to use a programming language.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs where one student acts as the "robot" and another as the "programmer." The teacher sets a simple task or problem, such as having the robot walk from their desk to the classroom door. Students must decompose this task into a sequence of simple, one-step commands ( e.g., "step forward," "turn left," "step forward," "step forward"). The programmer gives the commands one by one, and the robot follows them exactly.

The teacher has the class work together to decompose cleaning up the classroom after an activity into distinct parts and then has them put the parts in the proper order to create a clean-up algorithm. Students are then asked to follow their steps to clean up the room. The teacher then facilitates a discussion on how breaking the big job into these parts created a successful Cleanup Algorithm that was easier for everyone to follow.

math.standard: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 – 4 = 13 – 3 – 1 = 10 – 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 – 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
math.description: Students create an algorithm to solve an addition problem using the "making 10" strategy using a 10 frame and recording a sequence of steps.

math.standard: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.
math.description: Students focus on the specific task of what to do when they have too many ones in the ones column after adding. They decompose the problem of regrouping the ones by creating a "trading algorithm" to explicitly show the procedure of "composing a 10" in clear, repeatable steps.

ela.standard: Write narratives in which they recount two or more appropriately sequenced events, include some details regarding what happened, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide some sense of closure.
ela.description: Connect learning to write a narrative story to learning to write an algorithm. Students decompose their story into a sequence of steps representing a beginning, a middle, and an end using temporal "code" words like first, next, and last to signal the order of the events.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they name a topic, supply some facts about the topic, and provide some sense of closure.
ela.description: Students practice "how to" writing by creating a real world algorithm (e.g., "How to Wash Your Hands") that decomposes the task into a sequence of small, clear steps. The final written algorithm can be tested and debugged by having a partner try to follow the written algorithm to see if it works.

science.standard: Use tools and materials to design and build a device that uses light or sound to solve the problem of communicating over a distance.
science.description: Connect solving a scientific communication problem with algorithms. Students solve a problem like "How can you send a secret message to your friend across the room using a flashlight?" by decomposing the task into smaller, individual parts.

science.standard: Use materials to design a solution to a human problem by mimicking how plants and/or animals use their external parts to help them survive, grow, and meet their needs.
science.description: As a whole class, students decompose a bird's survival strategy for staying warm in the winter into individual parts (e.g., growing thick feathers, fluffing them up to trap air, finding shelter). Students then work individually to develop a Stay Warm Algorithm for a human (e.g., 1. Put on a base layer. 2. Add a puffy coat. 3. Put on a hat.) and demonstrate understanding by drawing the steps of their design and describe how each part mimics the bird's survival parts to solve the human problem of staying warm.

other.standard: Demonstrates problem solving strategies in a variety of games/activities.
other.description: Students act as game designers, working with their teacher, to develop the rules for a new or existing class game by decomposing the game into its essential parts (e.g., how to win, how players can move, rules for taking turns) and then arranging these parts into a clear sequence to create the game's official algorithm/protocols.

other.standard: Makes safe choices with physical education equipment.
other.description: Students decompose the directions from the teacher to create a poster illustrating the step-by-step algorithm for safe and proper use of equipment. This could be expanded to have students create an algorithm for safety drills (fire drill, tornado, etc.).

standards.statement: Create an algorithm that includes sequence, events, and iteration to solve a problem or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create simple algorithms using a sequence of steps that respond to events (e.g., "Ready, set, go!" or tapping on a character) and include iteration (e.g., loops) to accomplish a task or express an idea. Appropriate activities include creating a storyboard for a story to be coded later, developing an algorithm to solve a math story problem, or designing an algorithm of the steps to complete a science experiment. Students may complete this work individually or with peers.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use complex or nested loops. Students are not required to create algorithms with conditional branches or variables.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to create a storyboard for a narrative story they later code in a block-based programming platform. The storyboard illustrates the events, sequence, and looping actions in the story using symbols, drawings, and simple sentences. Teachers may provide a storyboard template on paper or in an appropriate digital platform.

Students collaborate in pairs or small groups to create an algorithm for a simple dance. Each pair or group uses large index cards or printed coding blocks to create their algorithm, which includes an event to start the dance, a sequence of basic movements, and a portion of the dance that repeats multiple times. Each pair or group trades their algorithms with another pair or group to see if the instructions are clear and complete.

math.standard: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
math.description: Students create algorithms to solve multistep math problems by breaking them into ordered sequences (e.g., Step 1. Identify information. Step 2. Solve the first part. Step 3. Use that answer to solve the second part.) to connect the steps needed to solve multistep math problems to algorithms.

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: As a class, students develop algorithms that they use for collecting, organizing, and displaying data through sequential steps.

ela.standard: Write narratives in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.
ela.description: Students create algorithms for stories with clear beginning, middle, and end sequences, including events that trigger actions.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 2 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: Students work collaboratively to create and refine algorithms, explaining their reasoning and listening to peers' ideas.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students create algorithms to solve problems about situations people want to change through systematic step-by-step approaches to connect the scientific processes of asking questions, gathering information, and observing to algorithms.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.
science.description: Students create and test multiple algorithms for the same problem, comparing effectiveness through iteration and debugging to connect analyzing results of multiple tests in science to the iterative process of developing algorithms.

other.standard: Describe the skills and knowledge required to produce certain goods and services.
other.description: Students create an algorithm for an "assembly line" to produce classroom goods (e.g., a bookmark). Each student is assigned one specific step of the algorithm where iteration occurs. Each student repeats their single task on every bookmark that comes to them, solving the problem of producing many goods efficiently.

standards.statement: Create algorithms that include sequence, events, iteration, and selection to solve a problem or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on solving problems or expressing ideas that include sequences, responses to events, iteration (e.g., loops), and/or selection (e.g., conditionals, if/then statements). An appropriate activity is writing instructions for a game. Students may complete this work individually or with peers.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to learn formal conditional logic. Students are not required to create one single algorithm that includes all control structures (i.e., sequencing, events, iteration, and selection). However, all control structures should be included throughout multiple algorithms.

implementation_examples.description: As a class, students create a step-by-step algorithm for starting the school day: hang up backpack, if homework is complete → then turn it in, else → keep it in the folder, then sharpen pencil. The teacher documents the student-created algorithm, which is displayed in the classroom and followed each day.

Students, individually or with a partner, write an algorithm on paper or in a word processing document to draw a square (e.g., move forward, turn right, repeat four times) and then add a choice (e.g., "Do you want to draw a triangle?" which would then repeat three times with an appropriate turn). Students explain how the program's condition (drawing a triangle) changes what happens next.

math.standard: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.
math.description: Working in pairs or small groups, students design a rounding algorithm that a peer could follow to round any two-digit number to the nearest 10. Pairs swap and test each other's algorithms.

math.standard: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
math.description: Students create an algorithm that repeatedly adds five and checks whether the result ends in zero or five, showing the same pattern through steps and choices.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: Students work collaboratively to create an algorithm for a game that includes how the game is played and any decisions that need to be made. For example, in "Rock, Paper, Scissors," you would need to include if/then statements in your algorithm like "IF the first player shows rock and the other player shows scissors, THEN the first player wins."

science.standard: Define a simple design problem that can be solved by applying scientific ideas about magnets.
science.description: Students design an algorithm with steps to test different objects by repeating "place magnet near object, check if it sticks," and then recording whether the object is magnetic or not.

science.standard: Use evidence to construct an explanation for how the variations in characteristics among individuals of the same species may provide advantages in surviving, finding mates, and reproducing.
science.description: As a class, students create and follow an algorithm that uses selection for a simulated survival game (e.g., "IF your card is green, THEN you are camouflaged and safe, ELSE you are caught."). The game uses colored cards representing an animal's camouflage with a variety of events they need to survive (e.g., "A predator is hunting in the green forest!", "A predator is hunting in a muddy field."). After the game, the teacher facilitates a class discussion about the effectiveness of their algorithm and how traits provide advantages in different situations.

other.standard: Explain how rules and laws change society and how people change rules and laws.
other.description: Students create an algorithm that models how a bill becomes a law, including the initial sequence of steps and key selection points, such as, "The bill goes to a committee. IF the committee approves it, THEN it goes to a full vote, ELSE the bill does not continue."

standards.statement: Create written representations of algorithms that incorporate a combination of sequence, events, iteration, and selection to solve a problem or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should write step-by-step representations of an algorithm using grade-appropriate, everyday language that includes sequences, responses to events, iteration (e.g., loops), or selection (e.g., conditionals, if/then statements). Outlining a Choose Your Own Adventure story where readers make decisions that alter the path is appropriate. Students may complete this work individually or with peers.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create visual representations, flowcharts, or formal pseudocode. Students are not required to create a single representation that includes every program control structure (i.e., sequencing, events, iterations, and selection). However, all control structures should be included in multiple written representations..

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs or small groups and use age-appropriate, common language to write the directions for a Rock, Paper, Scissors game that includes: (a) a countdown to start the game; (b) choosing rock, paper, or scissors; (c) selecting a winner; and (d) repeating the game until a winner is determined. The teacher could supply a template for writing the algorithm on paper or in a digital format. Students exchange algorithms with another group to test whether the directions are clear and complete.

Students work individually and use age-appropriate, common language to write the steps to draw different quadrilaterals. The teacher could supply a template for writing the algorithm on paper or in a digital format. They could share their directions with a classmate to review their algorithm correctness and determine which shapes include repeated patterns.

math.standard: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
math.description: Students work with a partner or in small groups to create a clear, written step-by-step algorithm for solving long division problems. Their final algorithm would need to include the core sequence of steps (e.g., Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring Down) and iteration (e.g., Repeat these steps until there are no more numbers to bring down.)

math.standard: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
math.description: Students write an algorithm (e.g., Repeat adding the numerators until all parts are combined. If the numerator is larger than the denominator, then convert it to a whole number.) for a peer on how to solve a mixed-number addition problem that their peer tests.

ela.standard: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
ela.description: Students work with a partner or in small groups to write the step-by-step directions for the algorithm used to complete a long division problem or a science experiment.

ela.standard: Introduce a topic clearly and group related information in paragraphs and sections; include formatting (e.g., headings), illustrations, and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
ela.description: When writing their algorithms, students should use clear formatting (e.g., numbered lists, bullet points) to separate their sequence from their selection logic. This helps them understand that technical writing requires a specific structure to be "readable" by others.

science.standard: Use a model to describe that animals receive different types of information through their senses, process the information in their brain, and respond to the information in different ways.
science.description: Students write an algorithm that mimics an animal's behavior to help students connect that biological responses are effectively natural algorithms. For example, a Squirrel Survival Algorithm might use an event (See a predator.), a selection (If the tree is close, climb it, else hide in the bushes.), and iteration (Repeat gathering nuts until the winter hole is full.).

science.standard: Make observations and/or measurements to provide evidence of the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation.
science.description: Students write an algorithm that describes the process of erosion breaking down the scientific process into discrete, logical steps.

other.standard: Identify positive and negative incentives that influence the decisions people make.
other.description: Students write a Grocery Shopping Algorithm based on a budget that includes sequence (walking each aisle), selection (if/else based on price or other condition), and iteration (repeatedly checking prices until the cart is full or the money is gone and navigating all the aisles) to connect to the fact that economic decisions are often based on if/then logic.

standards.statement: Create visual representations of algorithms that include variables and incorporate a combination of sequence, events, iteration, and selection to solve a problem or express an idea.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create visual representations (e.g., physical coding blocks, mind maps, annotated diagrams) showing algorithms that use variables and combinations of the following control structures: sequence, events, iteration, and selection. Illustrating an algorithm as a drawing on index cards showing the sequence of events from start to finish on a horizontal line with branches for selection is appropriate. Students may complete this work individually or with peers.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to include complex data structures (e.g., arrays, lists), procedures, or more than one level of nested iteration or selection. Students are not required to use formal flowchart notation or a single comprehensive diagram showing all control structures in a single representation.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to draw algorithms to address conflicts caused when playground rules are not followed. Each group can focus on a unique rule and draw the sequence of steps starting with events and including conditionals and repeated actions, where appropriate. Students display their drawings and explain each step.

Students work with a partner to design the rules and structure for a simple digital game (e.g., a simple maze, a trivia game). They will use classroom-defined symbols for program control structures and a teacher-provided document (on paper or digital) to construct a detailed visual representation of the game's logic. Their document should clearly show where a variable tracks the score, where iteration is used to repeat moves, and where events or selections trigger new actions (e.g., "IF player answers incorrectly, THEN subtract 1 from score.").

math.standard: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.
math.description: Students create a step-by-step diagram that visually represents the steps for the order of operations (i.e., parentheses, exponents, multiplication/division, and addition/subtraction) as an algorithm. Students then use the algorithm to solve a complex multistep expression.

math.standard: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.
math.description: Students construct a flowchart to classify shapes using a variable (e.g., Side_Count) where the algorithm asks, "How many sides?" which is saved to the variable and then uses Selection to branch (e.g., If Side_Count is 3, it's a triangle. If Side_Count is 4, it's a quadrilateral.)

ela.standard: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., how characters interact).
ela.description: Students construct a story map using index cards as a visual representation of an algorithm for a story with multiple outcomes. The story map should show a main sequence of events that leads to a critical selection point, with two branching paths illustrating how a character's choice leads to two contrasting plot developments.

science.standard: Develop a model using an example to describe ways the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and/or atmosphere interact.
science.description: Students construct a visual representation of ways the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and/or atmosphere interact. For example, if modeling the water cycle, their diagram could show the main sequence as a circular loop to represent iteration and include selection points, such as "IF the temperature is below freezing, THEN precipitation is snow. ELSE, it is rain." which could be shown with words and illustrations.

science.standard: Develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment.
science.description: Students construct a visual representation of a food web using arrows to show the sequence of energy transfer and branching paths to represent selection (e.g., a rabbit can be eaten by a fox OR a hawk).

other.standard: Explain how cultural and environmental characteristics affect the distribution and movement of people, goods, and ideas.
other.description: Students create a map-based flowchart to show the decision points that lead people to settle in specific areas based on environmental resources.

standards.statement: Design an algorithm that includes variables of multiple data types to solve a problem or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should design and explain an algorithm that uses multiple variables with different data types (e.g., integers, string, Boolean) to solve a problem or express an idea. The algorithm should show how variables are created, updated, and used (e.g., tracking a score, storing a name, checking a true/false condition, responding to user input, calculating a result). Representations may be verbal, visual, physical, pseudocode, or block-based and should emphasize the logic and data changes rather than producing executable code.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write executable programs, manage memory, use or implement data structures (e.g., lists/arrays, dictionaries/maps, objects), or analyze efficiency.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a branching decision-making routine such as a morning schedule, a choose-your-own-path story, or a classroom task workflow and model the logic using a flowchart. Their diagram includes clear steps, if/then/else decisions, repeated actions, and simple variables like time remaining or points earned.

Students use a digital diagramming tool  to outline the logic for a number-guessing game or other interactive scenario. Their flowchart or pseudocode shows the sequence of steps, an event that starts the process, a loop for repeated guesses or actions, a conditional check, and a variable that tracks attempts or stored values.

math.standard: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.
math.description: Students create an algorithm that uses variables to represent quantities, stores multiple data values, and applies a multistep mathematical procedure to calculate and output a result.

math.standard: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.
math.description: Students design an algorithm that uses variables to represent quantities in a real-world problem (e.g., calculating total cost with tax and discounts, determining a final score with bonus points). They explain how each variable represents a specific value, how expressions are formed within the algorithm, and how changing variable values affects the output.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students design an algorithm that includes variables and conditional logic to solve a computational problem (e.g., calculating grades with bonus points or determining eligibility based on criteria). They then write an explanatory text describing how the algorithm works, defining each variable, explaining decision points, and clarifying how changes to inputs affect the output.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students work in small groups to design an algorithm that includes variables and control structures to solve a shared problem. During structured discussion, students explain their design choices, ask clarifying questions about peers' logic, and suggest revisions to improve clarity or efficiency. Groups refine their algorithm based on feedback and present their final design to the class.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students design an algorithm that includes variables and control structures to model a proposed engineering solution. They compare multiple algorithm designs and evaluate how effectively each meets the criteria and constraints of a given problem.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students test their designed algorithms using sample inputs and analyze how changes to variables or control structures affect outcomes. They use this analysis to refine their algorithm to better meet performance goals.

other.standard: Demonstrate openness in trying new ideas, materials, methods, and approaches in making works of art and design.
other.description: Students design a step-by-step process that includes adjustable variables (e.g., color, size, repetition) to generate a visual pattern or digital artwork. They explain how modifying variables changes the outcome of the design.

standards.statement: Model a given algorithm with a flowchart or pseudocode that includes a combination of control structures and procedures.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should model a teacher- or peer-provided algorithm using either a flowchart or clearly structured pseudocode that shows how the algorithm runs. The model should include a combination of control structures (i.e., sequence, iteration, and selection) and should represent at least one procedure (a named, reusable set of steps) being used within the algorithm. Models may include variables and other supporting details only as needed to accurately represent the algorithm's logic. Teacher-provided templates or agreed-upon formats are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or optimize the algorithm, justify efficiency, refactor for readability, or apply formal software engineering practices. Students are also not expected to use professional programming syntax or convert pseudocode into executable code.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a short written algorithm (teacher- or peer-provided) for a branching routine (e.g., a morning routine, classroom workflow, choose-your-own-path scene). The algorithm includes at least one repeated section and a named procedure (e.g., CheckBackpack, DoMorningTasks) that is used more than once. Students translate the provided algorithm into a flowchart that clearly shows sequence, if/then/else decisions, a loop for repeated actions, and any simple variables included in the given algorithm (e.g., timeRemaining, points).

Students are given pseudocode (or a step list) for an interactive scenario such as a number-guessing game. Using a digital diagramming tool (or typed pseudocode template), students model the given algorithm so it clearly shows the starting event (e.g., "when game starts"), the sequence of steps, a loop for repeated guesses/actions, a conditional check (e.g., too high, too low, correct), at least one procedure (e.g., GiveHint, UpdateAttempts), and a variable that tracks attempts or a stored value. Students submit the diagram or pseudocode plus a brief note identifying where the loop, conditional, variable, and procedure appear.

math.standard: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.
math.description: Students design structured, multistep procedures that use repeated reasoning and conditional logic to model and solve problems.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students read a description of a multistep process (e.g., how a bill becomes a law, how a scientific investigation is conducted) and create a flowchart or pseudocode model representing the sequence of actions and decision points. They then write a brief explanatory paragraph describing how their model captures the key steps and clarifies the process.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students are given a design problem (e.g., create a water filtration system within cost and material constraints). Before proposing solutions, they develop a flowchart or pseudocode model outlining the decision-making process for selecting materials and testing prototypes. The model explicitly represents criteria (e.g., water clarity level) and constraints (e.g., budget, available materials), helping clarify how design decisions will be made.

other.standard: Structure and critique ideas, plans, prototypes, and production processes for media arts productions, considering intent, resources, and the presentation context.
other.description: Students create a flowchart or storyboard to model the sequence of actions in a stop-motion animation project. They use pseudocode or structured steps to represent how scenes transition and how timing or repetition is controlled.

standards.statement: Verify the accuracy of an algorithm for given inputs.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should test whether a given algorithm produces expected outputs for specific inputs by tracing steps or running the algorithm. For example, students could check whether a sorting algorithm correctly orders numbers or whether a set of instructions builds a shape as intended.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform formal proofs of correctness, analyze efficiency, or optimize algorithms. Students are not required to use mathematical notation or comparison of multiple algorithms for performance.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs to test a provided step-by-step algorithm using a small set of given inputs, such as instructions for ordering numbers or drawing a shape on grid paper. Each pair traces the algorithm's steps by hand or runs it using manipulatives, recording the output for each input. Students compare the actual output to the expected result and identify whether the algorithm behaves as intended. To demonstrate understanding, students explain their conclusion using a brief written note, an annotated trace, or an oral explanation, with options to use diagrams, symbols, or color-coding to support clarity and accessibility.

Students work in pairs to test a provided algorithm in a block-based programming environment by entering a set of teacher-given inputs (including edge cases like repeated values or an empty list) and recording the program's outputs. Students use built-in features (e.g., step/run controls, variable watchers, or print statements) to trace the algorithm's steps and compare the actual outputs to an expected-results table. When outputs do not match, students pinpoint the step where the behavior diverges and note what the algorithm did instead. To demonstrate understanding, each pair submits a short test log showing inputs, expected outputs, actual outputs, and a brief explanation of whether the algorithm is correct for the tested cases.

math.standard: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.
math.description: Students trace a step-by-step algorithm that represents a numeric rule and verify whether it produces the correct output for given inputs by comparing results to an input-output table.

ela.standard: Follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks.
ela.description: Students read a written algorithm as a technical procedure, follow its steps with given inputs, and explain whether the procedure produces the intended result, citing specific steps that led to success or error.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students work in pairs to run a provided algorithm on a set of test cases and record results in a simple test table (inputs, expected outputs, actual outputs, pass/fail). Students analyze their test data to identify patterns in failures (e.g., errors only with repeated values, negative numbers, or empty inputs) and infer which condition the algorithm is not handling correctly. To demonstrate understanding, students submit a brief "test report" that summarizes which cases the algorithm handles correctly, which cases it fails, and what the failure pattern suggests about the algorithm's behavior.

standards.statement: Justify whether a problem is best solved using procedural instructions, rule-based logic, data-driven methods, or a combination of these approaches.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should justify whether a problem is best solved using explicit step-by-step instructions, pattern-based rules, data-driven approaches, or a combination of these. Examples may include explaining why a procedural approach fits a fixed and predictable task (e.g., calculating a total score), why rule-based logic supports responsive or conditional behavior (e.g., enforcing game rules), or why a data-driven approach is appropriate when patterns are identified from collected data (e.g., recommending a song based on listening history). Students may also justify combining approaches when a solution requires both defined procedures and conditional or data-based decision-making. The emphasis is on evaluating and explaining the reasoning behind the chosen approach.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use formal logic notation, compare imperative and declarative paradigms, or design/implement machine learning models.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to examine short problem scenarios, such as detecting spam messages, recommending music, calculating a score, or controlling a simple game character. For each scenario, students decide whether the problem is best solved using explicit step-by-step instructions, pattern-based rules, data-driven approaches, or a combination of these. Examples may include explaining why a procedural approach fits a predictable task (e.g., calculating a score), why pattern-based rules support responsive behavior (e.g., game interactions), or why a data-driven approach is useful when decisions rely on patterns identified from collected data (e.g., filtering spam). Students focus on evaluating and justifying the approach rather than implementing advanced systems and record their reasoning in a comparison chart or discussion notes. Groups share their decisions with the class, highlighting what information is known in advance versus what depends on patterns in data. To demonstrate understanding, students produce a brief justification in a format of their choice explaining why the selected approach fits the problem.

Students use a simple, teacher-provided interactive that enables them to compare procedural instructions, pattern-based rules, data-driven methods, and a hybrid approach to solve a task such as recommending music genres or sorting images. They experiment by running multiple inputs through each approach, documenting when each method succeeds or fails. Students compile a brief comparison report with screenshots and identify the context in which they would choose each approach, demonstrating understanding of trade-offs such as predictability, flexibility, and reliance on data.

math.standard: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers. For example, “How old am I?” is not a statistical question, but “How old are the students in my school?” is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students’ ages.
math.description: Students analyze problem scenarios and decide whether a solution should use explicit step-by-step instructions, pattern-based rules, or a data-driven approach by determining whether the situation involves predictable procedures or variability that depends on patterns in data.

math.standard: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.
math.description: Students translate pattern-based conditions into mathematical expressions (e.g., if temperature > 80°, classify as "hot") and test edge cases to see where fixed rules succeed or break down. They compare this to a data-driven method that uses collected examples to make classifications and justify which approach is more appropriate for the situation.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write a short argument explaining which problem-solving approach (i.e., explicit step-by-step instructions, pattern-based rules, data-driven methods, or a hybrid) best fits a given scenario, supporting their claim with clear reasoning and relevant evidence from the problem description.

ela.standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
ela.description: Students read two short explanations (e.g., one advocating for a procedural or rule-based approach, one for a data-driven approach) and identify the strengths and limitations of each argument. They evaluate which reasoning is more convincing for a specific problem scenario and justify their conclusion.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare three prototype solutions (e.g., one procedural, one pattern-based, one data-driven or hybrid) using the same set of test cases. They evaluate how well each meets criteria such as accuracy, adaptability, and consistency and justify which approach best fits the problem constraints.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students run test inputs through different solution approaches and record the results in a table. They analyze similarities and differences in performance to determine which method performs best overall and explain the conditions that cause one approach to outperform another.

other.standard: Analyze the role of innovation and entrepreneurship in a market economy.
other.description: Students examine how online stores use procedural filters (e.g., sorting by price), pattern-based rules (e.g., category tags), and data-driven recommendations (e.g., purchase history patterns) to influence shopping behavior. They explain which approach, or combinations, they believe most effectively supports consumer decision making and why.

other.standard: Select programs of music (such as a CD mix or live performances) and demonstrate the connections to an interest or experience for a specific purpose.
other.description: Students explore how music apps organize or recommend songs using procedural sorting (e.g., alphabetical, by release date), pattern-based tags (genre, tempo), and data-driven analysis (listening patterns). They compare these approaches using sample tracks and justify which method, or combination of methods, better supports creative discovery and user experience.

standards.statement: Use AI tools to generate outputs that assist in solving a computational problem.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use age-appropriate AI tools or prebuilt models to generate outputs that support solving a computational problem. Examples include generating text to brainstorm ideas, using image recognition to classify objects, or asking a chatbot for troubleshooting help. Students should focus on interpreting and assessing AI outputs, not building or programming AI systems. Students can validate teacher generated output without generating outputs themselves if students are prohibited from using generative AI.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to train AI models or explain underlying algorithms.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to use a prebuilt AI system to generate outputs that support a computational task, such as brainstorming steps for a program, classifying images into categories, or suggesting fixes for a logic error. Students review the AI-generated output and decide which parts are useful, unclear, or incorrect for their specific problem. They then apply or revise the output to improve their solution, noting any changes they made and why. To demonstrate understanding, students share an annotated list, revised plan, or brief explanation in a format of their choice.

Students work in small groups with a teacher-facilitated "simulated AI" activity. The teacher provides a computational task (e.g., debugging a short program, categorizing images, generating steps for a solution) along with multiple pre-generated AI responses created from slightly different prompts or inputs. Students compare the outputs to identify patterns in how the AI responds, noting differences in accuracy, relevance, detail, or bias. They discuss which version best supports solving the task and explain why, considering how changes in the input may have influenced the results. Students then revise or combine elements from the outputs to create an improved solution and provide a brief explanation of the decisions they made and how the AI-assisted results supported their work.

math.standard: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.
math.description: Students evaluate AI-generated suggestions for solving a multistep math problem, identify which steps are mathematically sound, and revise the solution to ensure the final answer is reasonable.

ela.standard: Distinguish among facts, reasoned judgment based on research findings, and speculation in a text.
ela.description: Students analyze AI-generated output related to a computational task and identify which parts are factual, speculative, or based on assumptions, explaining how this evaluation affects their final solution.

standards.statement: Design an algorithm using appropriate data structures to solve a problem or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should create a logical plan for a program that selects a specific way to organize data (e.g., using a list to store a collection of items, using an object to represent a single complex entity) to effectively solve a specific challenge. For example, a student might design a leaderboard system for a game by choosing a list to store player scores and designing a sorting algorithm to arrange them from highest to lowest.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement complex data structures (e.g., manual memory management for linked lists). The focus is on the selection and application of existing high-level structures available in modern programming languages to support the algorithm's goal.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a set of building instructions that repeat the same 10 steps for four different "towers." They must optimize the instructions by creating a "Tower Procedure." They write the 10 steps once and then give a single command: "Build Tower" four times. They discuss how this makes the "algorithm" for building easier to follow.

Students are tasked with designing a "Contact Manager" application. They must decide whether to store the contacts in a simple list of strings or an array of objects where each object contains a name, phone number, and email. They then design the algorithm (in pseudocode or a flowchart) for searching through that structure to find a specific person by their last name.

math.standard: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).
math.description: Students are provided a complex word problem regarding compound interest or population growth. Students will create the formula/function to represent the growth. Students will then design an algorithm that uses a list to store the population/balance at the end of each year for 20 years. Because the values occur in sequence over time, students should select a data structure that allows them to store and access multiple ordered values.

ela.standard: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
ela.description: Students write a design document justifying why their chosen data structure (e.g., a dictionary vs. a list) is the most "coherent" and effective choice for their specific algorithm.

standards.statement: Optimize the design of an algorithm using procedural abstraction and control structures.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate existing algorithms to identify redundancies, inefficiencies, or unclear logic, and then refine them using procedural abstraction (e.g., defining functions or methods that encapsulate repeated steps). They should also apply control structures, including iteration and selection, to streamline processes and improve the algorithm's clarity, efficiency, and reusability. For example, a long, repetitive script for calculating student grades could be optimized by creating a "calculateGPA" procedure and using a loop to process a list of scores.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform formal Big-O complexity analysis or optimize at the assembly/hardware level. This standard does not require the use of advanced dynamic programming or complex recursive optimizations, as the focus is on the structural improvement of the logic using fundamental programming constructs.

implementation_examples.description: Students begin with a basic thermostat algorithm that continuously checks the temperature every minute and turns the heater or air conditioner on or off based on the current reading. This initial version may repeatedly toggle the system on and off or continue checking even when the temperature is stable. Students optimize the algorithm by creating a procedure called regulateTemp that groups temperature monitoring and adjustment into a reusable abstraction. They add conditional logic that includes a tolerance range (e.g., ±1 degree) to prevent unnecessary system toggling. They also redesign the loop so that it reduces how often the system checks the temperature once the target range is reached or exits the adjustment loop once the temperature is stable. Through these changes, students see how procedural abstraction and improved control structures make the algorithm more efficient, reduce unnecessary operations, and create clearer, more maintainable code.

Students start with a basic, inefficient algorithm that checks every number in a list. To improve it, they create a SearchPattern function that groups the pattern-finding steps into one reusable procedure (procedural abstraction). They also add a While loop with a break, so the algorithm stops as soon as it finds what it is looking for instead of checking every remaining number. This helps students see how organizing code into functions and using control structures can make an algorithm clearer and faster.

math.standard: Look for and make use of structure.
math.description: Students apply the mathematical practice of identifying patterns and structures to refactor a complex algebraic calculation into a series of reusable procedural steps in code.

ela.standard: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
ela.description: Students complete a "modular argument essay" in which each major section of the paper (introduction, evidence 1, evidence 2, counter-argument, conclusion) is treated as a separate procedure. Control structures include logical transitions between these areas, such as "however," to control the flow of the argument. After the first draft, students optimize their writing by finding and removing repetitive phrases as well as checking that the logical flow makes sense.

science.standard: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.
science.description: In this activity, students move from a simple observation of a biological system to a well-structured and optimized computational model. To start, students are given a basic "food web" model in a program. The code is inefficient. For example, perhaps every "rabbit" has its own individual lines of code for its behavior (e.g., eat, move, reproduce). As the number of rabbits increases, the simulation crashes or slows. Students put the behavior logic into distinct procedures (e.g., a checkSurvival() function). Instead of checking each rabbit one by one in a long list, students use iteration to apply the procedures to the whole population in an efficient way. This optimization enables them to run this simulation for much larger populations.

standards.statement: Evaluate algorithms for efficiency, correctness, and clarity, using metrics or test cases.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze algorithms for efficiency (time or memory use), correctness of outputs, and clarity (human readability), using simple metrics or test cases. For example, they could compare two algorithms for finding the largest number in a list by testing runtime when using different sized lists. Metrics may be qualitative or comparative (not formal analysis).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to apply formal mathematical proofs or Big O notation. Students are not required to analyze all possible inputs.

implementation_examples.description: Students find a name in a physical phone book. One student flips page by page (linear search), while another opens to the middle and eliminates halves (binary search). Students evaluate both for efficiency (number of flips) and clarity (which set of instructions is easier to follow?).

Students are given two versions of a program that calculates a Fibonacci sequence. One is short, but highly inefficient (recursive). The other is longer, but much faster (iterative). Students run both with large inputs to see which one "hangs" (efficiency), check the math (correctness), and rate the readability of the comments (clarity).

math.standard: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
math.description: Students "audit" different methods to solve a mathematical problem such as finding the sum of all integers from 1 to n. They are given a program that solves the problem in two different ways. Algorithm 1 solves the problem by iteratively adding each number one by one. Algorithm 2 uses Gauss's formula (n(n+1))/2. Students first create a test case (e.g., n=100) to verify that both algorithms work correctly. Students then count the steps for each algorithm. Algorithm 1 takes n steps, whereas Algorithm 2 takes a constant number of steps (1 multiplication, 1 addition, 1 division) no matter how large n is. Students then need to write an argument for why Algorithm 2 is the better design for a computer processing a value of n = 1,000,000.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students form a hypothesis about an algorithm's performance, design an experiment (test cases), collect and analyze data, and draw conclusions. This reinforces the scientific practice of analyzing and interpreting data to evaluate a solution.

standards.statement: Describe the differences between deterministic and probabilistic algorithms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to explain that deterministic algorithms always produce the same output from a specific input and follow the same sequence of states, whereas probabilistic (randomized) algorithms use a source of randomness as part of their logic, which may result in different outputs or runtimes across different executions. For example, students could describe how a deterministic search algorithm always checks a list in a fixed order, whereas a probabilistic approach might pick elements at random to find a target more quickly in certain datasets.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to calculate formal probability distributions or perform complex mathematical proofs.

implementation_examples.description: To demonstrate deterministic logic, students follow a rigid set of instructions to get from the classroom to the cafeteria: "Turn right, walk 50 feet, turn left." Every student who follows this precisely ends up at the same door. To demonstrate probabilistic logic, students are told: "Walk to the hallway, then flip a coin. If heads, turn left, and if tails, turn right. If you hit a wall, flip again." Students arrive at different destinations or take different amounts of time to reach the cafeteria, illustrating how randomness affects the process.

Students compare two programs. Program A (deterministic) calculates the area of a circle using the fixed formula A = $\pi$*r^2. Program B (probabilistic) uses a Monte Carlo method where the computer "throws" 1,000 random digital darts at a square and counts how many land inside a circle to estimate the value of $\pi$. Students run Program B multiple times to observe how the estimated value of $\pi$ changes slightly with each run due to the randomness.

math.standard: (+) Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.
math.description: Students can calculate the "expected" number of steps a probabilistic algorithm takes to find a target and compare it to the fixed number of steps in a deterministic version.

science.standard: Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions to a complex real-world problem with numerous criteria and constraints on interactions within and between systems relevant to the problem.
science.description: Students can use a probabilistic simulation (like a Monte Carlo simulation) to model weather patterns or population growth, describing why a deterministic model might be less effective for predicting outcomes in systems with many variables.

standards.statement: Evaluate AI-generated output to assess bias, accuracy, and potential harms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze and critique AI-generated content (e.g., text, images, code) for accuracy, bias, and potential harms. For example, they might examine how an image-generation tool underrepresents certain groups or produces inaccurate results due to biased training data. Students should focus on critical evaluation of outputs rather than technical implementation.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build or debug AI models or understand their internal mathematical algorithms.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given "draft articles" supposedly written by an AI about a local school event. They are also given the actual fact sheet from the event. Students must use a red pen to mark up the draft for accuracy (finding names or dates the AI got wrong) and identify any slanted language or bias (e.g., if the AI only interviewed one specific group of students). Finally, they discuss the potential harm if the unedited article were published in the school newspaper.

Students use an AI image generator to create pictures for various professions (e.g., CEO, housekeeper, software engineer). They run the prompt 10 times and create a tally of the demographics represented. Students then evaluate the data to see if it matches real-world statistics or if it reflects historical biases and stereotypes. They conclude by writing a model report detailing the risks of using these images in an official marketing campaign.

math.standard: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).
math.description: Students use statistical reasoning to detect unexpected patterns or biases in AI results.

ela.standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
ela.description: Students analyze AI-generated essays, summaries, or articles as they would any other text. They need to identify the claims made and evaluate the quality of the reasoning and evidence, recognizing that an AI's output is not a human's output and thus lacks genuine understanding or intent. This activity directly connects media literacy and source evaluation to a new form of digital content.

science.standard: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.
science.description: Students evaluate an AI-generated explanation of how DNA structure determines protein structure and function, checking for scientific accuracy, completeness, and potential misconceptions (e.g., oversimplified relationships between genes and traits or missing steps in transcription and translation). They compare the AI-generated explanation to accepted biological models and evidence, identify any biases or inaccuracies in the representation, and revise or annotate the explanation to improve its scientific validity.

science.standard: Analyze geoscience data and the results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of the current rate of global or regional climate change and associated future impacts to Earth systems.
science.description: Students evaluate AI-generated climate forecasts (e.g., summaries or visualizations produced from global climate models), comparing them to authentic geoscience datasets and established model outputs. They assess the accuracy of the predictions, identify potential biases or misleading representations (e.g., cherry-picked data, exaggerated trends, or omission of uncertainty ranges), and evaluate the potential consequences of relying on flawed interpretations when making evidence-based climate predictions.

other.standard: Evaluate how historical events and developments were shaped by unique circumstances of time and place as well as broader historical contexts.
other.description: Students use AI to generate summaries of historical events from different perspectives (e.g., a summary of a war from the perspective of each warring nation). They then critique the outputs, identifying biases and omissions, and discuss how the AI's "understanding" of history is a reflection of its training data rather than a neutral, objective truth. This helps them understand the subjective nature of historical narratives.

standards.statement: Recognize attributes of objects to notice patterns and make decisions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should notice and identify that objects (e.g., people, animals, plants, other items) have specific characteristics (e.g., color, size, shape, texture) that can be used to classify them. For example, students might notice that a square and a triangle have different shapes, but recognize that they share the attribute of being red so they can be grouped together based on color.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to recognize hidden attributes that cannot be seen or felt. Students are not required to work with more than one or two clear, observable attributes at a time to make a decision.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine real or pictures of classroom waste items and sort them into two labeled bins (i.e., trash and recycling). The teacher guides observation: "What do you notice about items in the recycling bin? They're clean paper or plastic that can become new things!" Students identify observable features that help them categorize. Students practice with new items, predicting which bin each belongs in and discussing how finding patterns helps people make environmental decisions based on characteristics.

Students sort animal picture cards or digital images in an app into categories based on observable features. Students begin by sorting animals into "has fur" and "does not have fur." They then repeat the process with new criteria, such as "has feathers" versus "does not have feathers." As the activity progresses, the teacher guides discussion, highlighting how a single animal can belong to different groups.

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Students sort a bin of multicolored blocks by an attribute (e.g., number of sides, color, size). They then describe to a partner, the teacher, or the class how recognizing the attribute helped them decide which bucket each block belonged in before counting the totals for each group.

ela.standard: Sort common objects into categories (e.g., shapes, foods) to gain a sense of the concepts the categories represent.
ela.description: Students sort a bin of plastic foods or pictures of foods into two categories using hoops or containers labeled Everyday Foods and Sometimes Foods. Students verbally identify a specific attribute of the food (e.g., this is a vegetable and I can eat it any time, this is candy and has too much sugar to eat all the time) to justify their decision.

ela.standard: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
ela.description: After a nature walk, the class works together to recognize attributes of leaves they collected (e.g., pointy vs. round). They use these attributes to answer the question "Which trees in our playground are the same?" by grouping the leaves or photos of the leaves together.

science.standard: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of pushes and pulls on the motion of an object.
science.description: Students observe patterns in cause and effect, using repeated observations to predict how objects will move based on force patterns.

science.standard: Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth’s surface.
science.description: Students collect observational data, recognize patterns (e.g., sunny areas are warmer), and use those patterns to make predictions (e.g., dark clouds mean rain might come soon).

other.standard: Child understands simple patterns.
other.description: Students recognize a pattern (e.g., color, shape, size) used to sort objects into categories and use the pattern to sort additional objects.

other.standard: Child compares and categorizes observable phenomena.
other.description: Students examine different types of weather-related clothing (e.g., mittens, sunglasses, raincoats) and recognize attributes (e.g., waterproof, fuzzy) of the clothing. Students work in pairs to decide which "weather bucket" a new item belongs in, demonstrating how recognizing an object's properties helps to make a decision about its use.

standards.statement: Recognize that AI systems are a technology that uses patterns in data to make decisions or generate new things.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to identify that AI systems are a technology created by people that looks for repeating patterns in information to make a choice or create something new. For example, students recognize and verbally express that an app knows which book they may want to read next because it has seen a pattern of the books they have read before.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the different types of machine learning (e.g., supervised, unsupervised).

implementation_examples.description: Students act as human designers for a new AI Snack Bot. One student acts as the AI and is given a rule created by the group (e.g., "If the pattern is a fruit, put it in the lunchbox. If the pattern is a vegetable, put it in the bowl."). The other students provide pictures of various foods as training data for the AI. The group watches the AI make decisions based on their human-created rule and discusses how AI is a tool they built to help sort things quickly using patterns.

Students use a simple AI-powered music generator or doodle-recognition game. In pairs, they experiment with different inputs and explain to each other that the computer isn't "thinking" on its own, but is using patterns in data that humans gave it to decide which note to play or what the drawing might be.

math.standard: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.
math.description: Students sort shapes by their defining attributes (patterns) and discuss how they are acting like an AI tool by using those patterns to decide which category a new shape belongs to.

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
ela.description: After reading a picture book about AI, the class discusses where they can find AI in their lives. Students will then use AI to draw a picture of themselves or a family member.

other.standard: Explain why and how people, goods, and ideas move from place to place.
other.description: Students discuss how a GPS or map app is a tool that uses traffic patterns to decide the fastest way home. They act out a scenario where a student volunteer is the AI helping a driver (also a student volunteer) navigate a classroom obstacle course using data about traffic (other students).

standards.statement: Examine how data is used to train machine learning models.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore simple examples of how a trained machine learning model identifies patterns in data and makes predictions or recommendations based on those patterns. Students should notice that models can make more mistakes for some kinds of examples than others, especially when the training examples were mostly of one kind. Students should focus on observing that machine learning models use patterns in data to make predictions or choices and that limited or unbalanced examples can lead to unfair or uneven results. For example, they might label images for a teacher-trained model and observe how well it classifies new pictures or use a drawing app that predicts what object they are sketching before they finish.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to independently train machine learning models.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: The teacher has the class sort data (e.g., pictures of food) into two to three labeled categories (e.g., fruits and vegetables, treats). The teacher then demonstrates how to train a machine learning model on the labeled data. The students predict and examine the output from the model when new items are shown to the model, and they reflect (e.g., write, dictate, draw, discuss) on what patterns the machine has learned from the training data.

Students play a Pictionary-type game in pairs and then participate in a class discussion about how they knew what was being drawn. The teacher asks if a computer could recognize what we draw and what a computer would need in order to do that. After students talk to a partner about this and share with the class, the teacher demonstrates or has students use a website that has an AI guess what they are drawing. Students examine the data that the website uses to guess what people are drawing and then write, dictate, or draw a brief explanation of how the program learned to identify what people draw.

math.standard: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
math.description: In a whole-class activity, students provide "training data" to a "computer" by sorting numbers into Even and Odd categories based on whether they can be divided into two equal groups of cubes. Students then examine the resulting pattern and explain, verbally or in writing, how a computer could use this pattern of numerical properties to predict the category of a new, larger number, like 20.
