math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students collect data on the favorite colors of their classmates and create a bar graph. They examine the graph to see if they can find a pattern (e.g., "Most students like blue."), and the teacher facilitates a discussion on how a computer could use this "data" to predict which color of balloon to buy for a class party.

ela.standard: Recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
ela.description: After examining how data is used to train machine learning models, students write, draw, or record observations about their experiences, recalling specific examples from class activities and explaining what they noticed about how the machine learned.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 2 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: Following an activity during which the class labeled data that was used to train and test a machine learning model, students discuss the patterns in the outputs of the model and reflect on the performance of the machine learning model.

science.standard: Plan and conduct an investigation to describe and classify different kinds of materials by their observable properties.
science.description: After conducting investigations to classify materials by properties (texture, color, hardness), students articulate how they could train a machine learning model to classify these same or similar materials.

standards.statement: Investigate how machine learning models can change when new data is added to a training set.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should observe and describe what happens when a machine learning model receives additional training data. They should notice when adding missing or underrepresented examples helps the model make more accurate predictions. For example, students could use an image-recognition tool to identify animals, then add more pictures to see how the model's predictions change or improve. Students should focus on observing how new data affects outcomes.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to train their own machine learning models or understand the technical or mathematical processes behind them. The term bias may be introduced informally, but students are not expected to use it. Students are not expected to analyze complex datasets or create models from scratch.

implementation_examples.description: The teacher acts as a machine learning model that has been trained to identify writing tools. Initially, the "training data" only contains two items: a yellow colored pencil and a small wood golf pencil. Students work in small groups to test the model by presenting a blue pen. Because the model hasn't seen a pen or the color blue, it might "fail." Students then investigate how the model can be improved by adding a blue pen to the training data. They continue the experiment by adding new data like a marker, a crayon, and a mechanical pencil. Students demonstrate understanding by documenting how the model's accuracy in identifying a writing tool changed from "something made of wood" or "something yellow" to including broader characteristics based on the new data provided.

Students explore a simple image classifier for what does and does not belong in the ocean (e.g., fish, tires, starfish, garbage). They start with sorting items into fish or not fish categories, test the model, then add more pictures of each type and observe how the model's accuracy or confidence changes when identifying new photos. Students demonstrate understanding by comparing the model's predictions before and after adding new data, explaining how additional examples improved or hindered the model's ability to classify images correctly.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students investigate how a model (picture graph) of their class's preferences evolves based on the amount of data. For example, they poll a small "training set" of five students about their favorite season and create a bar graph. Based on this, they make a prediction about the class's favorite. Then, they add new data by polling the rest of the class. They investigate how the bar graph (their visual model) evolves and describe how their prediction for the favorite season changed once the model was trained on more data.

math.standard: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
math.description: Students act as a machine learning model initially using a small data set (e.g., 1, 3, ?) and hypothesize a simple "add 2" rule. The teacher reveals the next number is 6, and students, acting as a machine learning model, refine their logic to discover a more complex pattern (add the next counting number) based on the increased data and new pattern.

ela.standard: Report on a topic or text, tell a story, or recount an experience with appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace.
ela.description: Students present their findings about how their machine learning model changed when new data was added, using descriptive language to explain what they observed and what they learned from their investigation.

science.standard: Construct an argument with evidence that in a particular habitat some organisms can survive well, some survive less well, and some cannot survive at all.
science.description: Students look at a model of an animal (e.g., a polar bear) in a snowy habitat. They investigate what happens to the survival model when new data about the environment is added (e.g., the ice is melting). Students explain how the animal's chances of survival evolve, or change, based on the new environmental data provided.

other.standard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions and their environmental characteristics.
other.description: Students look at a model of their neighborhood using a single old photograph and then investigate how their understanding of the area evolves when new data such as a modern satellite map and a physical walking tour are added. Students explain how adding more data (different types of maps) enabled their mental model of the neighborhood to become more accurate and detailed.

standards.statement: Analyze relationships between the properties of training data and a machine learning model's output.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should examine how characteristics of training data (e.g., amount, accuracy, labeling quality, representativeness) affect a machine learning model's performance. Students should connect unbalanced or poorly labeled data to inaccurate outputs and may learn the term bias to describe this pattern. Students should focus on making qualitative observations (e.g., "More data improves accuracy." "Labeling mistakes lead to incorrect predictions."). For example, students might observe that when too few images are used to train a classifier, the model often mislabels new images, leading them to conclude that data quantity and quality influence accuracy.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use statistical formulas, understand machine learning works mathematically, or define or correct specific bias types.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs using a visual machine learning platform to train a model that classifies two types of objects (e.g., apples and oranges). They begin with an imbalanced dataset (20 apple images, five orange images) and test how accurately the model classifies new, unlabeled images. Students then add more orange images to balance the dataset, retrain the model, and observe how its accuracy and fairness improve. Students demonstrate understanding by presenting before-and-after results, explaining how balancing the dataset affected the model's performance and why diverse data improves reliability.

Students work in small groups to simulate how mislabeled data affects a machine learning model that classifies cats and dogs. They are given 30 image cards, five of which are intentionally mislabeled (e.g., a cat labeled "dog"). Acting as the trained model, groups predict how those errors may lead to misclassifications when new pictures are introduced and identify patterns in how bias enters training data. Students then write a reflection detailing the mislabeled cards and explaining how flawed data can cause a machine learning model to make an inaccurate classification for a specific test image.

math.standard: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
math.description: Students examine how changing the examples in a simple classification activity affects the results. For example, they compare how a model trained on mostly large animals versus mostly small animals classifies new animals. Students identify patterns in the outputs and explain how differences in the training examples influence the model's decisions.

ela.standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
ela.description: Students read a brief explanation of a model trained with different sets of examples and then describe how changes in the training data affected the model's results. In their explanation, students identify what happened and why, using details from the scenario.

standards.statement: Train a machine learning model to make a classification or prediction.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should upload a labeled dataset (e.g., text, numbers, images, sounds, poses) to train a machine learning model that classifies, predicts, or recommends. Students should reflect on results that do not match expectations (e.g., who is missing from the training data, how adding more diverse examples might make results more accurate). Students should focus on recognizing that training data influences model accuracy. For example, students might create a labeled dataset of animal sounds to train a machine learning model, test its accuracy on new examples, and reflect on outputs that differ from their expectations.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the mathematical processes behind training a machine learning model to make predictions. Students are not required to use specific tools or specialized hardware.

implementation_examples.description: Students use the camera on their device to train a machine learning model on images of their hands making rock, paper, and scissors. After their models are trained, students trade and test the accuracy of one another's models. Students then participate in a class discussion about the successes and failures of the class's machine learning models and what could be done to improve the accuracy. Students then try to improve their model and test it again.

As a class, students collaborate to design an "automated librarian" that recommends book genres. The teacher divides students into small groups, each focusing on one genre (e.g., realistic fiction, mystery, fantasy, nonfiction). Groups brainstorm reasons someone might like their assigned genre (e.g., "I like solving puzzles." "I enjoy learning about real people.") and contribute data for model training. After the model is trained by the teacher, the class tests its recommendations and discusses how the training data influences outcomes and fairness. Students present examples of accurate and inaccurate recommendations, explaining how the machine learning model used patterns in the data to make suggestions and proposing ways to reduce bias or improve the model's performance.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students work in pairs to create a line plot for data on real-world mathematical problems that is given to them on paper or on an electronic device. Students then use the graph to make predictions. Students learn how this method compares to machine learning models in making predictions based upon the available data.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students work in pairs or small groups on solutions to a problem such as predicting the amount of trash generated. They then compare the different solutions and predict future trends on trash generation. Students learn how this method compares to machine learning models in making predictions based upon the available data.

standards.statement: Hypothesize how a machine learning model generates classifications or predictions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop a hypothesis about how a machine learning model might be processing information based on the observed inputs and outputs of the model. Students should focus on forming credible, evidence-based inferences from experimentation and observation. For example, students might test an image classification tool by submitting several pictures of animals and, after noticing that it consistently labels striped animals as "tiger," hypothesize that the model is prioritizing visible patterns like stripes over other features such as size or habitat.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explain exactly how machine learning models work internally.

implementation_examples.description: Working in small groups, students read a summary of the intended purpose of a machine learning model and design a series of experiments to reveal how the technology is producing its outputs. After carrying out their experiments they should deliver a summary of their results, including which experiments were run, the data they suspect was accessed by the machine learning model, and how varying the inputs in specific ways appeared to affect the outputs.

Working in small groups, students evaluate printouts of multiple runs of a machine learning model that classifies emails as "spam" or "not spam." After reviewing which messages are labeled correctly or incorrectly, students make predictions about which words or patterns the model appears to prioritize when assigning classifications.

math.standard: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.
math.description: Student pairs analyze a scatter plot that shows the relationship between two variables used in a machine learning classification task (e.g., email length and number of flagged keywords for messages labeled "spam" or "not spam"). Students identify patterns such as clustering, outliers, and positive associations and make predictions about how these patterns might influence the model's classifications.

math.standard: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.
math.description: Students examine the results of a machine learning model that classifies songs into genres such as "rock," "pop," or "jazz." From a test set of 100 songs, they observe how many songs were labeled as each genre. Students calculate the probability that a randomly selected song from the set will be classified as "rock" and interpret whether that outcome is unlikely, about equally likely, or likely.

ela.standard: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
ela.description: Students are given a short story and several excerpts labeled by a machine learning model as "suspenseful" or "not suspenseful." Working with a partner, students cite specific textual evidence (e.g., word choice, tone, imagery) to determine whether they agree with the model's classifications. Students then hypothesize which features of the text the model may be using to assign its labels.

ela.standard: Analyze how particular elements of a story or drama interact (e.g., how setting shapes the characters or plot).
ela.description: Students read excerpts from short stories that a machine learning model has classified by setting (e.g., "urban," "rural," "fantasy"). Students analyze how the setting shapes the characters' actions, motivations, or conflicts, citing specific textual evidence. After discussing how these elements interact, students hypothesize which interactions or textual patterns the model may have relied on when assigning its classification.

science.standard: Construct an explanation that predicts patterns of interactions among organisms across multiple ecosystems.
science.description: Students examine data about organisms in different ecosystems and review classifications made by a machine learning model (e.g., predator-prey, competition, mutualism). Students construct explanations predicting patterns of interaction across ecosystems, using evidence about traits and environmental conditions. They then hypothesize which organism characteristics the model may have used to assign its classifications.

science.standard: Use argument based on empirical evidence and scientific reasoning to support an explanation for how characteristic animal behaviors and specialized plant structures affect the probability of successful reproduction of animals and plants respectively.
science.description: Students analyze examples of animal behaviors and plant structures and use evidence to argue which traits most increase the probability of successful reproduction. In teams, they identify which of those traits would be most important for a machine learning model that predicts reproductive success and justify their reasoning.

standards.statement: Investigate ways to improve the accuracy of a machine learning model and reduce bias by refining the quality of examples and nonexamples in the training data.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should test a machine learning model to evaluate the outputs, identify overrepresented or missing examples in the training data, and suggest improvements to increase accuracy or reduce bias. Students should focus on testing, interpreting results, and suggesting refinements based on evidence. For example, students might notice that a model misidentifies certain objects and propose adding more diverse examples, then retest to see if performance improves.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create machine learning models or understand the technical mechanics of training. Students are not expected to make changes to machine learning models; this can be a conceptual discussion.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs to test a machine learning model and evaluate its outputs, identify overrepresented or missing examples in the training data, and suggest improvements to increase accuracy or reduce bias. For example, students might notice that a model misidentifies certain objects and propose adding more diverse examples, then retest to see if performance improves.

Students are given sample pictures of homes generated by an AI image generator. Students examine the images to identify objects that do not belong and features that are overrepresented, then propose adding more diverse examples to the training data to produce a broader range of homes that represent a wider variety of living spaces.

math.standard: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.
math.description: Students work in pairs to critique a machine learning model trained on biased training sets such as a model trained only on one demographic (e.g., an image recognizer that only recognizes tropical fish) to see how lack of diversity may lead to problematic generalizations. Students recommend additional training data to improve results, add it to the model, and retest to see if it is improved.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students train a simple image classifier to identify native wildlife and plants then test for accuracy. Students investigate improvements by systematically refining training data and then analyze test results to determine which data curation strategy best reduces bias and improves accuracy.

other.standard: Select, organize, and design images and words to make visually clear and compelling presentations.
other.description: Students curate a training dataset for a machine learning tool that identifies artistic movements based on technique, medium, and imagery. They select, organize, and design a clear and balanced visual portfolio of example and nonexample images for each movement included, investigating how the composition, variety, and labeling of their curated set reduces bias and improves its accuracy.

standards.statement: Evaluate the features and limitations of a machine learning model.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should examine machine learning model documentation, including model cards, to determine the model's features and limitations. Students should review information about the machine model, including (a) datasets used for training, including potential sources of bias; (b) the contexts or scenarios in which the model should or should not be used; (c) the computing power or time required for operation; and (d) potential risks, ethical concerns, privacy considerations, and recommendations for fair and responsible use. Students should evaluate the observable inputs and outputs of a machine learning model for utility and reliability. Students should focus on reviewing documentation and analysis, not implementation or debugging.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build a machine learning model or access proprietary training data.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students test a publicly available machine learning system (e.g., an image classifier) by submitting a variety of inputs designed to explore how the system responds. Students document cases where the system performs well and where it produces inaccurate, biased, or unexpected outputs. Based on these observations and available documentation, students create a short model card summarizing the model's purpose, typical use cases, limitations, and recommendations for responsible use.

Students design paper "trading cards" for two or more different machine learning tools (like a chatbot or image generator). Students will list key features including datasets used for training, limitations, and ethical considerations in addition to the model name, version, and typical use cases. The trading cards can incorporate an image of the AI's output, either a screenshot of an example or an illustration.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students train an image classifier to identify two common objects, such as cats and dogs, and test the model with a set of new images. Students record the model's accuracy in a table, calculate the mean accuracy and the range of its confidence scores, and note any patterns in its errors. Students then use this numerical data summary as key evidence in the "Limitations" and "Performance" sections of their model card.

ela.standard: Introduce a topic clearly, previewing what is to follow; organize ideas, concepts, and information into broader categories; include formatting (e.g., headings), graphics (e.g., charts, tables), and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
ela.description: Students research and test a machine learning model (e.g., chatbot, translation tool) and then apply their informative writing skills by drafting a model card. Students should include the model's purpose clearly and organize its features and limitations into distinct, labeled categories, such as training data, ethical concerns, and use cases. Students will incorporate a simple table or chart summarizing the model's test performance as well as examples of input and output of the model.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students test two different machine learning models designed for the same purpose (e.g., translating text or classifying plant species from images). Students analyze the performance data to identify each model's strengths and weaknesses (e.g., misidentification or mistranslation, bias, including details about an identified plant species). Students then synthesize this analysis by creating a model card for each model, using the "Features and Limitations" sections to clearly report which design characteristics best meet specific success criteria.

other.standard: Apply relevant criteria to examine, reflect on, and plan revisions for a work of art or design in progress.
other.description: Students use an AI-based image generator to create artworks based on specific prompts, then participate in a structured peer critique of the outputs. Students should analyze how well the system's outputs met the artistic vision, noting consistent failures and successes. Students then create a model card for the AI tool, where the "Limitations" section is informed by their critique and the "Features" section reflects the refined understanding of its capabilities gained through the revision process.

standards.statement: Justify the selection of a type of AI algorithm to accomplish a task.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should support the selection of an AI algorithm for a specific task by evaluating its strengths and limitations relative to the problem requirements. This justification may consider data size and type, human interpretability, and desired outcomes. Students should focus on evaluating appropriateness, not technical construction. For example, students might explain that a Decision Tree is suitable for classifying spam emails because its logic is transparent and easy to explain, even if less accurate than other models.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand or implement the underlying mathematics or statistics of these algorithms.

implementation_examples.description: Students are presented with two scenarios: (1) Identifying who is eligible for the "Honor Roll" based on GPA and attendance, and (2) Detecting "suspicious" login activity on school computers. Students must write a Selection Memo justifying which AI algorithm or approach to use for each. They might argue that the Honor Roll needs a rule-based system for fairness and interpretability (it must be clear why someone was or wasn't chosen). For login detection, they might justify a data-driven approach because suspicious patterns change constantly and are too complex for static rules.

Students are given a dataset of mythical creatures and asked to build a classifier. They first try a simple Decision Tree (rule-based) and then a K-Nearest Neighbor model (data-driven) using a visual, block-based machine learning platform. After testing both, students must create a short presentation justifying their final selection based on which model was more accurate and which was easier for a user to understand in terms of interpretability.

math.standard: Evaluate reports based on data.
math.description: Students review reported performance data for two AI algorithms and evaluate whether the conclusions about each model's effectiveness are supported by the evidence. They justify their selection of an algorithm based on analysis of accuracy and other relevant metrics.

ela.standard: Develop claim(s) and counterclaims fairly, supplying evidence for each while pointing out the strengths and limitations of both in a manner that anticipates the audience’s knowledge level and concerns.
ela.description: Students compose an argument recommending an AI algorithm for a given task, supporting their claim with evidence from model performance data and addressing counterclaims by analyzing the strengths and limitations of alternative approaches.

science.standard: Develop and use models to illustrate that energy at the macroscopic scale can be accounted for as a combination of energy associated with the motions of particles (objects) and energy associated with the relative position of particles (objects).
science.description: Students must present a reasoned argument for their chosen algorithm, citing evidence from their evaluation (e.g., performance on test cases, interpretability).

standards.statement: Evaluate training data by examining its source, quality, representativeness, potential biases, and privacy implications.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should critically evaluate datasets before use by examining their origin, purpose, accuracy, completeness, representativeness, and privacy implications. For example, when using crime statistics, students might check where the data originated (e.g., police reports, surveys), assess its quality, ensure all communities are represented, and identify potential biases or privacy concerns.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct advanced statistical analyses to prove representativeness or to apply formal bias correction techniques.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a printed Dataset Summary for a new AI system that predicts which students should get college scholarships. The summary shows the data comes from a single wealthy school district (source/representativeness) and includes student names and home addresses (privacy). Students must write an Evaluation Report explaining why this data is unfit to use for a national scholarship program, citing specific biases toward high-income families and privacy risks for the students involved.

Students visit a public data repository to find data for a Heart Disease Prediction model. They must use a checklist to evaluate the data: Does it include multiple genders and ethnicities (representativeness)? Are there many null or 0 values in important columns (quality)? Is there a clear license for use (source)? Students then decide whether to Keep, Clean, or Discard the dataset based on their findings.

math.standard: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion; develop a margin of error through the use of simulation models for random sampling.
math.description: Students evaluate whether a sample is representative and free from bias when estimating population values. In CS, this connects to evaluating training data by checking its source, quality, representativeness, potential biases, and privacy issues before using it to train a model.

ela.standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning (e.g., in U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents) and the premises, purposes, and arguments in works of public advocacy (e.g., The Federalist, presidential addresses).
ela.description: Students examine documentation accompanying a dataset (e.g., source description, collection methods, stated purpose) and evaluate the reasoning and assumptions behind how the data was gathered. They identify potential limitations, sources of bias, and gaps in representation and assess whether the dataset provides sufficient and appropriate evidence for the intended application.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students examine a dataset intended for training a machine learning model and evaluate its quality before drawing conclusions, similar to how scientists assess experimental data. They consider factors such as sample size, representativeness, measurement accuracy, and potential sources of bias, and determine whether the data is sufficient and reliable to support claims made by the model.

other.standard: Critique the appropriateness of the historical sources used in a secondary interpretation.
other.description: Students examine the source and context of a dataset used to train a machine learning model, similar to how historians evaluate primary and secondary sources. They analyze who collected the data, for what purpose, whose perspectives may be overrepresented or missing, and how those factors could influence conclusions drawn from the model's output.

standards.statement: Develop a machine learning model for a chosen task using appropriate data and tools.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should develop a machine learning model for a defined task by selecting suitable tools and data, training the model, and testing its performance against task requirements. Students should focus on applying available tools to create and evaluate functional models, not on mastering the mathematics that underlie them. For example, a student could use a block-based platform or a simple Python library to create a model that recognizes handwritten digits or classifies objects.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write algorithms from scratch or use advanced programming languages.

implementation_examples.description: Using an image recognition tool, students develop a model that recognizes their own hand gestures or facial expressions to trigger specific emojis on the screen. Students must collect at least 30 images for each gesture (data), use the tool's interface to train the model, and then refine the model if it confuses a "peace sign" with a "high five."

Students develop a manual classification model to identify a mystery object. One group of students acts as the Data Source, providing feature cards (e.g., "Has fur," "Barks"). Another group acts as the Model, creating a logic flow on a poster board to categorize the inputs. They iterate on their design when they realize their current logic can't distinguish between a dog and a wolf, adding more specific data points to improve their model.

math.standard: Decide if a specified model is consistent with results from a given data-generating process, e.g., using simulation. For example, a model says a spinning coin falls heads up with probability 0.5. Would a result of 5 tails in a row cause you to question the model?
math.description: Students can use probability and statistical reasoning to evaluate their model's predictions and performance.

science.standard: Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions to a complex real-world problem with numerous criteria and constraints on interactions within and between systems relevant to the problem.
science.description: Students develop a machine learning model to predict outcomes (e.g., classifying plant species based on environmental conditions, predicting equipment failure from sensor data). They use the model to explore relationships among input variables and outputs, refining the model based on performance results, similar to how scientists build and revise models to represent and test relationships within a system.

other.standard: Gather relevant information from multiple sources representing a wide range of views while using the origin, authority, structure, context, and corroborative value of the sources to guide the selection.
other.description: Before training a machine learning model, students gather datasets from multiple sources and evaluate their credibility, accuracy, and relevance to the chosen task. They compare the origin, completeness, and potential biases of each dataset, justify which sources to include or exclude, and explain how their selections may influence the model's performance.

standards.statement: Describe how people create algorithms to solve problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should recognize that computers function according to algorithms created by people. They should describe, in simple terms, the human process of developing an algorithm (i.e., identifying a task, breaking it into smaller parts, and ordering steps to reach a goal). For example, students might describe how people design instructions for making a sandwich or sorting classroom supplies.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe all aspects of computational thinking. Students are not required to understand how algorithms are translated into computer code.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: The teacher leads a whole-class discussion using a familiar daily routine, such as getting ready for school. Students identify the problem (e.g., being ready for school on time) and describe how people break it into smaller steps (e.g., waking up, getting dressed, eating breakfast, brushing teeth). The class discusses how the order of steps matters and explores different logical sequences (e.g., brushing teeth before or after eating). Students demonstrate understanding by retelling or illustrating the routine in order and explaining why some steps must come before others, showing that people create algorithms by organizing actions to reach a goal.

Students work in small groups or pairs to arrange picture cards showing steps in a simple task such as planting a seed or lining up for recess. Each group discusses the goal of the task and arranges the cards in the correct order. The teacher guides reflection with questions like "What did you have to think about to put these in order?" and "Why does a person need to do this thinking?" Students share their ordered cards with another group and describe their reasoning, explaining that people make algorithms by deciding the goal, identifying all steps, and checking that the order makes sense.

math.standard: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes. For example, “Can you join these two triangles with full sides touching to make a rectangle?”
math.description: Connect how combining simple shapes to make larger shapes is similar to creating an algorithm to solve a problem by having students use simple shapes (e.g., triangle, square, circle) and describing an algorithm to build a larger shape (e.g., "First, take a square. Then, place a triangle on top. Then, add two circles for eyes."). Students then test their algorithm and revise, if needed, describing the changes needed.

ela.standard: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.
ela.description: Students describe a simple familiar task (e.g., brushing their teeth) through writing, drawing, or saying the steps involved in the event, ensuring they add the detail that the steps must be in the correct order.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students identify a problem in their classroom (e.g., a classroom plant that is wilting) and brainstorm how a robot could help. Students work together to describe what a human would need to do to create that robot, including a simple algorithm that would be needed (e.g., "Check the dirt. When it is dry, add water."), connecting the scientific process with how humans use algorithms to solve problems.

other.standard: Child shows interest in and curiosity about the world around them.
other.description: Connect student curiosity about the world to understanding that people create the instructions that make things (including computers) work. Students explore how things work by investigating how people create algorithms for games or classroom tools by asking questions like "Who decided these steps?" and "How did they know what order to use?"

other.standard: Child holds information in mind and manipulates it to perform tasks.
other.description: Students describe how people think ahead about what steps are needed and what order makes sense, reinforcing that creating algorithms requires thoughtful planning and that this is something humans do.

standards.statement: Explain how changes to algorithms lead to different outcomes.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should express, through everyday activities or drawings, that changing the order of steps can produce different results. For example, when following two sets of instructions to build a block tower, one set might create a tall, stable tower, whereas another creates a shorter or weaker one.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write or modify computer code. Students are not required to understand complex algorithms used in digital tools.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs using picture cards or printed coding blocks to create an algorithm for sorting school lunch options. They begin by sorting items using one rule (e.g., by temperature: hot or cold) and then modify one step in their algorithm to use a new rule (e.g., by student preference). Students observe how the new algorithm changes the final organization and the results for different students. Students share their results with the class, explaining how a small change in the sorting rule affected who received their preferred lunch first or how efficiently meals were served.

As a class, students simulate algorithms that determine the order of tablet use, applying different rules such as "first come, first served" or "alphabetical order." Students act out each version, keeping track of who gets the tablet and when. They compare outcomes and discuss how each algorithm affects fairness, waiting times, and students' experiences. Students record or draw their observations, explaining which algorithm felt fairest or most efficient and describing how changing the steps led to different outcomes for people involved.

math.standard: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
math.description: Students experiment with completing the steps in a word problem (the algorithm) in different orders to see what happens. Students draw, write, or verbally describe how changing the order of the steps affected the answer.

math.standard: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.
math.description: Students create a Daily Schedule algorithm (e.g., 8:00 School Starts, 12:00 Lunch). They would describe the consequences of swapping the times or when things happen in the schedule (e.g., students would be hungry, school day would be shorter), connecting the sequence of time to the outcome of their day.

ela.standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
ela.description: Students read a simple how-to book and describe the connection between the order of the steps and the successful outcome of the project.

ela.standard: Describe people, places, things, and events with relevant details, expressing ideas and feelings clearly.
ela.description: The teacher tells the class that they are going to make a change to a classroom game's rules (algorithm) and has the students play the game with the new rules. Students describe how that change made them feel and express why the new outcome was "fair" or "confusing," demonstrating an understanding of how modifying a sequence directly impacts the people involved.

science.standard: Use tools and materials to design and build a device that uses light or sound to solve the problem of communicating over a distance.
science.description: Students develop a simple algorithm to send a message using light (e.g., 1 Flash = Hello, 2 Flashes = Help). They demonstrate and describe how changing the algorithm to 1 Flash = Help could lead to a misunderstanding in an emergency.

science.standard: Use observations of the sun, moon, and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted.
science.description: The teacher guides the class to develop a simple algorithm for the sun (e.g., 1. Rise in East. 2. Move across sky. 3. Set in West). Students describe how a change to this pattern (e.g, the sun staying up for 24 hours) would change the outcomes for people, such as when they sleep or how they know when to eat dinner.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: As a class, the students and teachers develop a Lunchroom Rule Algorithm: 1. Use a quiet voice. 2. Stay in your seat. 3. Raise your hand to be excused. Students then draw or write what would happen to the school community if Step 2 was changed to "Run around the room."

other.standard: Explore uses of materials and tools to create works of art or design.
other.description: Students create art projects by following a sequence of steps and testing how changing the order of steps produces different artistic effects. To show understanding, students describe how changing the sequence changed the outcome.

standards.statement: Describe how algorithms might impact peers in varied situations.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate how algorithms affect peers by determining if outcomes are fair or unfair and explaining their reasoning using simple criteria. Students should recognize that the same algorithm can affect different people in different ways depending on the situation. For instance, when a teacher draws names from a bucket to choose a line leader, students might evaluate whether this is fair by considering if everyone has an equal chance, if anyone is left out, or if the same person might be chosen multiple times while others never get a turn.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to analyze technical details of how algorithms work, understand complex concepts like bias or discrimination, design solutions to fix unfair algorithms, or evaluate algorithms beyond determining basic fairness in concrete, familiar situations.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Hand-Raising Algorithm: The teacher leads a whole-class activity using a simple two-step algorithm for calling on students: 1. Ask a question. 2. Call on the first person to raise their hand. After a few rounds, the class pauses to evaluate how this algorithm affects different peers. Students consider: Is it fair that fast hand-raisers always get picked? Is it unfair that students who think carefully before raising their hands never get a turn? Does everyone have an equal chance to participate? The teacher guides students to evaluate whether this algorithm works fairly for all classmates, recognizing that it might impact quick thinkers differently than careful thinkers.

Drawing Names for Classroom Jobs: The teacher uses a bucket with all students' names to assign the weekly "pencil sharpening" job. Each Monday, one name is drawn, and that student has the job all week. The class evaluates this algorithm by considering: Is it fair that everyone's name stays in the bucket each week, so the same person could be picked multiple times? Is it unfair if some students get picked twice before others get picked once? How does it affect a student who really wants the job but hasn't been picked in three months? How does it affect a student who got picked two weeks in a row? Students evaluate whether this algorithm is fair or unfair for different peers in different situations (someone never picked vs. someone picked repeatedly).

math.standard: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
math.description: Students solve the same addition problem (e.g., 35 + 17) using their own favorite strategy and share their unique step-by-step method with a partner. Students evaluate the impact of each algorithm, discussing which strategy felt faster, which was easier to understand, and which made them feel most confident in their answer.

math.standard: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
math.description: Students use two different mathematical algorithms (e.g., pairing objects, counting by 2s) for determining if a number is odd or even. The teacher facilitates a class discussion about the impact each algorithm has on different types of learners in the classroom. The visual "pairing" algorithm could have a positive impact on a student who likes to see and touch the numbers, while the faster "counting by 2s" algorithm might have a better impact on a peer who is quick with mental math.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or book they are writing about, state an opinion, supply reasons that support the opinion, use linking words (e.g., because, and, also) to connect opinion and reasons, and provide a concluding statement or section.
ela.description: Students write an opinion piece evaluating whether a classroom algorithm is fair or unfair. They state their evaluation (e.g., "I think the alphabetical lineup algorithm is unfair") and support it with reasons based on impact ("because my name starts with a Y and I am always last in line, which makes me feel left out" or "because students with names starting with A always get first choice"). Students evaluate how the algorithm affects different peers in different situations.

ela.standard: Recount stories, including fables and folktales from diverse cultures, and determine their central message, lesson, or moral.
ela.description: After reading a book about fairness, students identify the algorithm used to deal with a lack of fairness and discuss the impact the algorithm had on the different characters in the story.

science.standard: Compare multiple solutions designed to slow or prevent wind or water from changing the shape of the land.
science.description: Students use the same set of materials (e.g., rocks, pebbles, sticks) to design their own unique, step-by-step algorithm (their plan) to solve an erosion problem. After building and testing their solutions, students evaluate the impact of different algorithms by considering: Is it fair that some groups' plans worked better than others even with the same materials? How did each team's unique algorithm affect their results differently? Students evaluate how different algorithms can cause very different impacts, even when starting with the same materials and goals.

science.standard: Develop a simple model that mimics the function of an animal in dispersing seeds or pollinating plants.
science.description: Students discuss the "algorithm" a bee follows when it visits only bright, colorful flowers and evaluate the impact this behavior has on different flowers in the garden. Students consider: Is it fair that bright flowers always get pollinated while plain flowers don't? How does this affect the plain flowers' ability to grow seeds? Students evaluate how the bee's natural algorithm creates varied impacts for different types of flowers.

other.standard: Use listening, consensus-building, and voting procedures to decide on and take action in their classrooms.
other.description: After identifying an unfair classroom algorithm, students describe its impact on their peers. Then, as a class, they brainstorm a list of feelings or problems due to the rule or procedure to help them practice their listening and consensus-building skills to agree on why the rule is a problem for their community, keeping the focus solely on describing the impact.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: Students compare a classroom situation without and with clear rules to understand their importance through activities without any rules or algorithm (e.g., simulate getting art supplies in a free-for-all with no algorithm and describe the chaotic impact this has on their peers, use a simple, step-by-step algorithm [rules] for the same task [e.g., "Table 1 goes first."]). Students compare the feelings and outcomes of both scenarios, describing the importance of having fair algorithms (step-by-step rules) to create a safe and orderly classroom community where everyone gets a turn.

standards.statement: Compare how different algorithms may affect outcomes, situations, and people with a wide range of needs.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate examples of algorithms that produce different outcomes and discuss how those differences may help or harm people with diverse needs or perspectives. Students should focus on comparing impacts, not on programming or implementation. For example, students might consider how a navigation app choosing the fastest route differs from one choosing the safest route.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to analyze algorithms at a technical level or evaluate efficiency or performance trade-offs.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: As a class, students compare two algorithms for assigning classmates to teams, one that uses a random shuffle and one that groups students by height. Students simulate each approach and observe how the teams change. They discuss how each algorithm might feel to different people (e.g., those who are tall or short or prefer to work with certain peers) and consider whether either method seems fairer or inclusive. Students share their observations through a class discussion or short reflection, explaining how different team-assignment rules (algorithms) can create different experiences and outcomes for the people involved.

As a class, students examine two navigation routes generated for the same destination, one optimized for the fastest travel time and another for safety. Working in pairs or small groups, students discuss which route would be better for different users, such as someone bicycling or a family walking. They analyze how the algorithm's goal (speed vs. safety) changes what is considered the "best" route. Students present their conclusions through a short discussion, drawing, or written explanation comparing how algorithmic choices can affect people's experiences differently depending on their needs or situations.

math.standard: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
math.description: A teacher uses skip counting patterns (e.g., counting by 2s, 3s, 4s) as an algorithm to form groups and observe how different patterns change how evenly groups are formed. They explain how the chosen arithmetic pattern affects fairness, efficiency, and the experience of classmates, connecting mathematical structure to impact.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students compare two different classroom scenarios and data tables in which different algorithms are used to distribute supplies and interpret a table and bar graph to compare outcomes. They explain how each algorithm changes who receives more or less, highlighting how algorithmic choices can affect fairness and people's experiences.

ela.standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
ela.description: Students read an article or watch a short video about two different GPS algorithms, one that prioritizes the shortest distance (causing traffic on small neighborhood streets) and one that prioritizes using main roads. Students then work in pairs to create a cause and effect chart illustrating how the different algorithms lead to different outcomes for people who may live in neighborhoods to which traffic gets directed.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students examine simplified city maps that follow different decision rules (e.g., fastest route, safest route, most accessible route) and compare how each route affects people with different needs. They discuss how changing the algorithm changes the outcome and consider how some routes may help or harm certain individuals, emphasizing the human impact of algorithmic choices rather than how the routes are created.

standards.statement: Evaluate how different algorithms for solving the same problem produce outcomes that may benefit or disadvantage different groups of people.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should compare two or more algorithms that solve the same problem and explain how each affects people differently. Examples include different ways to sort items, plan routes, or schedule activities, noting who benefits or is disadvantaged.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design new algorithms or evaluate effectiveness. Students are not required to analyze algorithmic bias.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to compare two different algorithms for lining up for recess, one based on birthdays and another based on clothing color. After following each procedure, students observe and discuss which method feels fair and which gets the class outside faster, noting how different rules may help or disadvantage friends with varying needs (e.g., those who walk more slowly or need extra time to transition). Students record their reflections in a shared class chart or drawing, explaining how each algorithm affects people differently. To demonstrate understanding, groups share their conclusions about which algorithm is most inclusive and why.

Students work in small groups to organize a small collection of classroom or library books using two different algorithms, such as by color and by topic. After sorting the books, each group invites classmates to find a specific book and observes which organization method makes searching easier or more confusing. The class then discusses how each method affects different people—for instance, sorting by color may help those who recognize book covers visually, while sorting by topic supports those who remember what the book is about. To demonstrate understanding, groups create a simple chart or drawing showing which sorting method helped the most classmates and explain why that method might be fairer or more useful for everyone.

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: A teacher divides students into equal teams for a game and compares this to making teams of different sizes. Students then create an equation that represents how the different arrangements might produce different outcomes for different groups.

math.standard: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
math.description: Students compare two different algorithms for forming classroom groups (sorting by birthday month vs. alphabetically by name) and identify patterns in the outcomes (e.g., noticing that the birthday-based method creates groups in which some months have many students while others have few, potentially benefiting students who prefer larger or smaller groups in different ways).

ela.standard: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
ela.description: Students refer to specific details from algorithm descriptions or examples to explain how different approaches to solving the same problem affect different people.

ela.standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
ela.description: Students identify reasons and examples that support explanations of why certain algorithms benefit some groups while inconveniencing others.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information.
science.description: Students compare two different algorithms for organizing classroom announcements (chronological order vs. priority-based sorting), analyzing how each pattern of information transfer benefits different groups (e.g., how chronological ordering helps students who need complete context, whereas priority-based sorting benefits those who need urgent information first).

standards.statement: Articulate how human-centered design principles are incorporated into the development of computing technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify familiar examples of computing technologies (e.g., websites, voice assistants, video games, recommendation systems) and explain how human-centered design considerations (e.g., empathy, user needs, requirements, accessibility, fairness, sustainability, accountability) can be incorporated into their development. Students should consider the impact of their values (e.g., personal, community, larger values) on the design. They should also recognize that computing technologies are created by people, which may sometimes lead to unfair or inaccurate outcomes.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the technical details of computing technologies.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: In groups, students brainstorm ideas for a "Homework Helper" app on paper or digitally. Each group presents their idea to the class, clearly explaining how they would use human-centered design in creating their app (e.g., interviewing students who find a subject difficult, defining specific struggles, designing features that provide hints instead of just answers).

Students, working with a partner, design a paper prototype for a new type of smart watch for senior citizens. They clearly explain orally or in writing how they incorporated human-centered design (e.g., by making the buttons extra large, adding a voice-control feature for people who might have shaky hands).

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students gather data on how long it takes users to navigate their prototype during the testing phase of a prototype they created (e.g., app, new hardware). They create and use a line plot to identify where their design could use improvement (e.g., needs to be faster) and articulate how they plan to change the design of the prototype to fix it.

ela.standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
ela.description: Students read or watch a video about the development of the first computer mouse or touch screen and explain in a paragraph how the interaction between the designer and the user led to the invention.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
ela.description: Students write an opinion piece explaining why human-centered design is important when creating everyday technologies such as school websites, learning apps, or online games. They support their point of view with reasons and examples, such as the need to make tools accessible, safe, fair, and easy to understand for different users.

science.standard: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.
science.description: Students develop a user experience (UX) test for a computational solution (e.g., prototype of a homework app). The test should identify variables (e.g., age of the user, lighting in the room, complexity of the instructions) and observe where failures occur for the human user.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students apply human-centered design to an app that addresses an environmental problem, such as an app that helps sort recycling. They should define the criteria for success not just by how well the app works, but by how easy it is for a person in their community to use it correctly.

other.standard: Identify the beliefs, experiences, perspectives, and values that underlie their own and others' points of view about civic issues.
other.description: As a class, students discuss a local civic issue (e.g., where a new park should be). They articulate how a human-centered approach to building both the park and the park website would involve gathering the perspectives and values of everyone in the neighborhood, not just of the people who have computers at home.

standards.statement: Evaluate which human-centered design principles are present or missing in existing computing technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze familiar computing technologies (e.g., websites, mobile apps, video games, school platforms, recommendation systems) to determine how human-centered design principles are reflected in their features. Students should identify evidence of empathy, accessibility, user needs, fairness, sustainability, and accountability and explain where these principles are effectively incorporated or overlooked. Students should consider how different users (e.g., multilingual users, users with disabilities, users with limited internet access) might experience the technology differently and evaluate the potential impacts of design choices. Students may suggest improvements to the computing technologies examined.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or implement full computing technologies. Students are not required to conduct formal user research, perform usability testing, or apply detailed accessibility standards.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students analyze an existing self-service kiosk system (e.g., pizza-ordering kiosk, grocery store checkout). They evaluate how well the interface supports different user groups, such as people with limited dexterity, multilingual users, or visually impaired users, identifying where human-centered design principles like accessibility and empathy are present or missing. Students then propose specific improvements to make the system more inclusive.

Students evaluate an existing digital trivia game or educational app to determine how well it supports different users. They analyze features such as text-to-speech options, adjustable sound levels, and different input methods to identify evidence of human-centered design principles like accessibility and fairness. Students explain where these principles are missing and suggest improvements that would better support diverse users.

math.standard: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.
math.description: Students analyze survey data about how classmates use a school website or learning app. Using summary statistics and distributions of responses, they identify patterns in user experiences and evaluate whether the technology meets the needs of the broader student population. Students discuss how non-representative feedback might lead to design choices that overlook certain users.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 8 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students engage in collaborative discussions to evaluate an existing school website or online platform. Drawing on multiple perspectives, they identify how well the technology supports different users and where human-centered design principles such as accessibility or fairness are missing. Students build on each other's ideas to propose improvements that would better serve diverse members of the school community.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services.
science.description: Students evaluate an existing environmental awareness website or interactive simulation about a local ecosystem service, such as wetlands water filtration. They analyze whether the technology effectively supports diverse users and promotes understanding of ecosystem protection. Students compare the digital solution with other methods for engaging the public and evaluate how design choices influence its effectiveness.

other.standard: Document early stages of the creative process visually and/or verbally in traditional or new media.
other.description: Students analyze an existing digital art app used by younger students. Through sketches and written notes in a design journal, they document which interface features support intuitive use and accessibility. Students evaluate where human-centered design principles are evident or missing and suggest improvements to better support younger users.

standards.statement: Examine evidence of beneficial and harmful impacts, ethical issues, and biases of algorithms encountered in daily life.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and describe common ethical issues and biases in AI systems using familiar examples (e.g., photo apps misidentifying people, voice assistants misunderstanding accents, recommendation systems reinforcing prior interests). They should evaluate whether the outcomes of these systems seem fair and inclusive and explain why biases may occur in simple, concrete terms.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to program or modify AI tools, understand neural networks, or study global AI policy.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to analyze printed screenshots or mock scenarios of AI systems in daily life, such as a photo app misidentifying people, a voice assistant misunderstanding an accent, or a shopping site recommending only similar products. Each group identifies what the algorithm is trying to do, notes one beneficial impact (e.g., convenience, personalization) and one harmful impact or bias (e.g., exclusion, misidentification). Students then create an Impact Chart listing these examples and explain in simple terms why the bias might occur, such as limited training data or assumptions in design.

Students use a familiar AI tool like a digital photo organizer, voice assistant, or recommendation engine to test how it responds to varied inputs, such as voice commands with different accents or searches for diverse images. If direct access isn't possible, students watch video demonstrations or teacher-led tests of the same tools. They record observations of when the system works well and when it fails or shows bias, then produce a brief report or presentation with screenshots or notes and propose one simple idea to make the system fairer.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students collect data from their observations (e.g., number of times a voice assistant misinterprets commands) and summarize patterns, connecting math concepts to evaluating fairness and bias.

math.standard: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.
math.description: Students discuss why certain outcomes (e.g., misidentifications) might occur more often for some groups, linking probability concepts to algorithmic bias.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write an argumentative piece on whether a specific AI system (e.g., photo app, recommendation engine) is fair and inclusive, using evidence from their observations and/or credible sources.

ela.standard: Determine an author’s point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
ela.description: Students analyze an article or report about an AI system and evaluate how the author presents its benefits and risks. They identify evidence used to support claims and consider whose perspectives may be emphasized or overlooked.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students compare observed behaviors of different AI systems (e.g., voice assistants vs. photo apps) and analyze which seem fairer or inclusive.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare two AI systems (e.g., two recommendation engines or two voice assistants) and discuss which seems fairer and more inclusive based on observed evidence. They suggest one simple improvement (e.g., adding diverse training data) to reduce bias, applying the idea of evaluating and improving designs without technical implementation.

other.standard: Analyze ways that visual components and cultural associations suggested by images influence ideas, emotions, and actions.
other.description: Students examine AI-curated images or social media feeds and analyze how algorithmic selection influences representation, visibility, or stereotypes. They discuss who may benefit from these patterns and who may be excluded.

other.standard: Analyzes and applies technology as tools to support a healthy, active lifestyle.
other.description: Students explore how fitness apps or wearable tech algorithms (e.g., step counters, workout recommendations) might favor certain body types or activity patterns. They discuss fairness and inclusivity in health-related algorithms, linking ethical considerations to personal wellness.

standards.statement: Modify an algorithm to address a specific societal impact, ethical issue, or bias.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should design modifications to an existing algorithm, verbally or through diagrams or flowcharts, to make its outcomes fairer or more inclusive. Students should focus on reducing bias and improving equity through simple, conceptual modifications.
