For example, they might suggest adding a language option to a chatbot or adjusting a music playlist generator to include more diverse artists. Students should explain how their modification reduces bias or improves equity.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design complex algorithms from scratch or apply statistical fairness techniques.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs with printed flowcharts of a familiar recommendation algorithm (e.g., a playlist generator that predominantly suggests popular artists). Partners identify a specific bias such as lack of genre diversity and sketch a modification to the flowchart (e.g., inserting a step to include at least one underrepresented genre or language). Each pair then presents their revised flowchart and explains how the change could reduce bias and improve equity in recommendations.

Students use a prebuilt recommendation project in a block-based environment and adjust parameters or add a condition to diversify outputs (e.g., include songs from multiple genres or languages). They test the modified algorithm to observe changes in the recommendations and document what improved and what still needs work. Students submit a screenshot or short video of their changes and write a brief explanation of how their modification affects fairness and the behavior of the system.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.
math.description: Students analyze before-and-after data showing diversity in recommendations to see how algorithm modifications affect outcomes. They create a simple chart comparing original and modified results and explain what the changes reveal about fairness.

math.standard: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events. For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?
math.description: Students reason about why adding conditions to an algorithm changes the likelihood of certain results. They calculate probabilities for original and modified versions and discuss how these shifts relate to fairness.

ela.standard: Determine an author’s point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
ela.description: Students read an article about a computational system that has caused concerns about bias or inequitable outcomes. They determine the author's point of view about the issue and identify evidence used to support that perspective. Students analyze how the design of the algorithm reflects particular priorities or assumptions and propose a modification that would address the societal impact, ethical issue, or bias described in the text.

ela.standard: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, relevant descriptive details, and well-structured event sequences.
ela.description: Students pair up and write two short narratives: one from the perspective of a user impacted by the original algorithm (e.g., a music app that never recommends diverse artists) and one from the perspective of a user impacted by the modified algorithm. They present their narratives side by side to illustrate the difference.

science.standard: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
science.description: Students propose and test modifications to an existing algorithm (e.g., adjusting recommendation criteria to reduce bias). They predict how changes will affect outcomes and refine their design based on observed results.

other.standard: Demonstrate openness in trying new ideas, materials, methods, and approaches in making works of art and design.
other.description: Students redesign an AI-based image-tagging or recommendation system to better represent diverse users, explaining how their changes alter outcomes and improve inclusivity.

other.standard: Apply civic virtues and democratic principles in school and community settings.
other.description: Students identify a fairness concern in a school-related algorithm (e.g., club recommendations, event visibility) and propose modifications that promote equitable participation, justifying their design decisions.

standards.statement: Design computing technologies using human-centered design principles.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should design computing technologies that are inclusive and accessible by following a human-centered design process. This includes researching user needs, exploring design options, and anticipating the social and ethical impacts of their design. For example, when creating a website, students might ensure sufficient color contrast, keyboard navigation, and clear language for users with differing abilities. Students should also identify laws that set requirements for accessibility (e.g., ADA, IDEA, Section 508).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct large-scale user studies or meet every criterion of formal accessibility standards (e.g., Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG).

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students are assigned a "client" (e.g., a grandparent, a younger student, a person with a specific injury). They must interview their client to understand a daily struggle (e.g., remembering to take medicine). Students then sketch a paper prototype of a digital solution on index cards and simulate running the app for the client by swapping the cards. Based on the client's confusion or understanding, the students develop a revised sketch to better meet the user's needs.

Students design and implement the logic and interface of a digital Lunch Ordering System using a programming environment. After testing the beta version with a small group of users, they revise the ordering flow and decision logic to reduce confusion and improve accessibility. Students explain how their revisions better address user needs and reflect human-centered design principles.

math.standard: Model with mathematics.
math.description: Students design a school lunch ordering app and use mathematical modeling to analyze how long different users take to complete tasks in the interface. By comparing average completion times and error rates for different interaction options (e.g., menu layouts, button sizes), students evaluate which design better supports efficient and accessible use.

ela.standard: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects to answer a question (including a self-generated question) or solve a problem; narrow or broaden the inquiry when appropriate; synthesize multiple sources on the subject, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.
ela.description: Students research user demographics, accessibility needs, and existing solutions before developing their computational designs. They synthesize multiple sources to justify how their design choices address the needs of diverse users.

science.standard: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.
science.description: Students identify a real-world problem (e.g., such as improving access to emergency weather alerts) and define criteria and constraints for a computational solution. They consider user needs such as accessibility for visually impaired users, limited internet connectivity, and clear communication during emergencies. These criteria guide the design of a prototype alert system that accounts for both technical requirements and human-centered considerations.

other.standard: Analyze the impact and the appropriate roles of personal interests and perspectives on the application of civic virtues, democratic principles, constitutional rights, and human rights.
other.description: Students design a digital tool intended to increase participation in a community issue (e.g., voter information access or event sign-ups). They consider how their design choices may empower or disadvantage different groups and justify how their solution promotes equitable access and participation.

standards.statement: Evaluate the ethical implications, societal impacts, and potential biases of rule-based and data-driven algorithms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate how rule-based and data-driven algorithms can produce biased or inequitable outcomes. They should identify potential sources of bias, such as explicit decision rules embedded in a system (e.g., filtering candidates by ZIP code) or unrepresentative or historically biased training data in data-driven models. For example, students might analyze a hiring algorithm that excludes candidates living in certain ZIP codes or examine a résumé screening model trained on past hiring data that disadvantages applicants with names from underrepresented cultural or linguistic backgrounds. Students should provide recommendations on how algorithms can be refined. Students' analyses should remain conceptual, focusing on observable impacts and ethical reasoning.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to audit proprietary systems or use advanced statistical methods.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students evaluate two ways to assign "participation" grades. Algorithm A (rule-based) gives a point if a student raises their hand exactly three times. Algorithm B (data-driven) uses a camera to track engagement based on historical data of what "good" students look like. Students discuss the bias in B (what if a student is shy but focused?) and the societal impact on classroom culture for both A and B.

Students use an online simulator to see how predictive policing" works. They compare a system based on simple rules (patrol where the most 911 calls occurred) versus one that uses machine learning to predict "hotspots." Students must evaluate the results, identifying how the data-driven model might create a feedback loop that unfairly targets specific neighborhoods, leading to negative societal impacts.

math.standard: Evaluate reports based on data.
math.description: Students use a fictional university's  data-driven algorithm to predict student success based on SAT scores and extracurriculars. Students analyze the summary statistics (mean, median, proportions of the training set when compared to the general population) of the training data. Students then evaluate potential biases. For example, if 80% of the training data is from high-income ZIP codes, but the general population is only 20% high-income, students use proportional reasoning to show that the sample is not representative. Students then write a report to explain how this skewed distribution creates an ethical implication, unfairly penalizing low-income applicants.

ela.standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning (e.g., in U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents) and the premises, purposes, and arguments in works of public advocacy (e.g., The Federalist, presidential addresses).
ela.description: Students treat a Supreme Court majority opinion as a rule-based algorithm. They evaluate its logic using the same metrics used in CS (correctness, clarity, and bias). They translate the legal reasoning into a flowchart or if/then logic statements. They evaluate the efficiency (Did they establish legal precedents to make their argument?) and clarity (Is the logic clear?). Students then analyze the assumptions of the text looking for bias. Did the input data (historical context and assumptions) contain biases that led to a skewed output?

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students evaluate a data-driven algorithm that has been programmed to prevent a total blackout in an area by performing rolling brownouts. The algorithm prioritizes keeping the power on in neighborhoods with the highest economic productivity based on historical usage data. Students identify that the neighborhoods selected for power cuts are urban heat islands with less tree cover and more elderly residents. Students need to evaluate the trade-off the algorithm made, prioritizing reliability (ensuring economic output and the power grid) over safety and social impact (protecting vulnerable populations). Students propose a revision, also deciding if the algorithm should be rule-based (e.g., never cut power to a hospital zone) to ensure that ethical safety boundaries are maintained.

other.standard: Evaluate public policies in terms of intended and unintended outcomes, and related consequences.
other.description: Students will analyze a municipal policy that uses a data-driven algorithm to allocate police patrols based on historical crime data. Students will identify the policy's goal and investigate unintended outcomes caused by a feedback loop, such as overpolicing in specific minority neighborhoods rather than reducing crime rates. Students will then write a policy brief, deciding if the policy violates the principle of "equal protection" and propose a rule-based constraint (e.g., "do not use socioeconomic indicators") to mitigate the bias.

standards.statement: Articulate the values embedded in the design of algorithmic systems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and explain the values reflected in the design of algorithmic systems, recognizing that every design choice involves prioritizing certain outcomes or perspectives. Students should focus on identifying underlying priorities (e.g., efficiency, privacy, fairness, transparency) that shape algorithmic behavior. For example, students might examine a social media platform's recommendation system and discuss how its design favors engagement and attention over accuracy or civility.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to deconstruct proprietary systems or analyze full business models.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students use a digital mapping tool to compare Fastest Route, Avoid Tolls, and Eco-Friendly options. They articulate how the Fastest Route algorithm embeds the value of efficiency, and the Eco-Friendly algorithm embeds the value of environmental sustainability. Students then write a short Value Statement for a hypothetical Scenic Route algorithm, explaining the human values that it would prioritize (e.g., beauty, local business support) over saving time.

The teacher proposes three different algorithms for deciding who gets to go to lunch first: (1) Alphabetical order, (2)  By highest grades, and (3) A random lottery. Students must articulate the values embedded in each. They might explain that the first values order, the second values academic merit, and the third values equality. They then discuss the disadvantages to students who are always last in the alphabetical system.

math.standard: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.
math.description: Students explore how choosing a mathematical model (linear vs. exponential) embeds values into a system. Suppose a city designs an algorithm to predict population growth. Model A is linear, assuming steady growth, and Model B is exponential, assuming rapid and compounding growth. Students must decide which model to embed in the city's planning algorithm. If students choose a linear model, they may write about how they value sustainability or a planned infrastructure. If they choose an exponential mode, they may value market competition. Students should explain how their choice is not neutral because it embeds a value that decides how many resources the city will build.

ela.standard: Determine an author’s point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
ela.description: Students can treat the algorithmic system as a text and infer the author's (creator's) purpose and values based on the system's actions and outcomes.

other.standard: Analyze multiple and complex causes and effects of events in the past.
other.description: Students treat a major policy initiative (e.g., the Social Security Act of 1935) as an algorithmic system designed to solve the problem of the Great Depression. Students identify the inputs (e.g., tax revenue, age, employment status) and the output (i.e., monthly payments). Students analyze the original text to find the values that were included in the policy's logic. Students will then investigate unintended effects of the algorithm, explaining how priorities and values led to a system that produced unequal outcomes.

other.standard: Through experimentation, practice, and persistence, demonstrate acquisition of skills and knowledge in a chosen art form.
other.description: Students use code as the medium to create a piece of generative art that expresses a human value (e.g., chaos, harmony, isolation). If a student values harmony, they may focus on the use of linear algorithms to ensure that colors transition smoothly and that shapes are symmetrical. If a student instead values chaos, they might use random number generators to create clashing colors and/or jagged lines. Once the art is rendered, students should present their work and articulate the values embedded in the code. They should explain how their choice of variables and algorithms reflects their personal point of view.

standards.statement: Create a sequence of commands to complete a simple task or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should arrange a small set of commands in order (e.g., to help a character reach an object, tell a short story, follow a classroom routine). Using manipulatives, arrows, or simple digital programs is appropriate. Unplugged activities are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write code or use control structures beyond sequencing. Students are not required to use computers.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in small groups to arrange laminated picture cards showing daily activities such as getting dressed or washing hands. They order the cards to form a logical sequence. Students explain their sequence to the class and justify the reasoning behind each step, comparing similarities and differences among group responses.

As a class, students collaborate to create and perform a simple dance or movement sequence. They use visual cards labeled with actions like clap, jump, and spin to design the sequence. Together, they decide the order of movements, practice as a group, and attempt to recall the sequence from memory. Students perform the complete routine and reflect on how changing or adding movements affects the overall routine.

math.standard: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
math.description: Students create a program to count objects or move a character a certain number of times by 1s and 10s.

ela.standard: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.
ela.description: Students describe their program's steps orally or using drawings with the group.

ela.standard: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to narrate a single event or several loosely linked events, tell about the events in the order in which they occurred, and provide a reaction to what happened.
ela.description: Students sequence illustrations or words to tell a simple story program.

science.standard: Analyze data to determine if a design solution works as intended to change the speed or direction of an object with a push or a pull.
science.description: Students create a sequence of steps to build and test a simple ramp or movement task as a class.

science.standard: Use a model to represent the relationship between the needs of different plants or animals (including humans) and the places they live.
science.description: Students create a program or sequence of illustrated steps that show how plants and animals grow or move.

other.standard: Child demonstrates an understanding of narrative structure through storytelling and re-telling.
other.description: Students retell a simple story by putting pictures from a story in order and narrating what happened.

other.standard: Improvise dance that has a beginning, middle, and end.
other.description: Students create and follow a simple dance sequence using movement commands.

standards.statement: Create code from an algorithm that includes sequence to complete a task or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should translate algorithms with sequential steps into block-based code. Tasks such as translating an algorithm to move a character or navigate a maze are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design the algorithm themselves or use selection or iteration.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to translate a familiar classroom procedure into a coded sequence. The teacher provides preprinted paper blocks labeled with actions representing each step of the procedure (e.g., line up, wash hands, sit quietly). The groups physically arrange the blocks in the correct sequence on their desks to create their "paper program." Each group explains how their sequence represents the original classroom algorithm.

Students write code individually or in pairs using a grade-appropriate coding platform or an unplugged approach to make a character follow a morning routine. Based on a provided algorithm, students program a character to perform actions such as "wake up," "stretch," and "brush teeth." The program might be initiated by tapping the character (triggering event) and include a sequence of sound (alarm clock) and motion (get out of bed) blocks. Students run their programs and explain how the sequence and events work together to complete the routine.

math.standard: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.
math.description: Students create a program in a grade-appropriate platform that shows a character counting based on a written or illustrated algorithm (e.g., pictures showing Green Flag for the triggering event, character saying "113," character saying "114," etc.) provided by the teacher.

math.standard: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).
math.description: Students create code for a programmable floor robot on a large number line mat (0–20) based on a simple algorithm (e.g., a math problem) such as "Start at 4 and add 3." Students run the program and read the answer on the number line where the robot stops (7), using a coded sequence to solve the addition problem.

ela.standard: Write narratives in which they recount two or more appropriately sequenced events, include some details regarding what happened, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide some sense of closure.
ela.description: Students first write a simple, three-sentence story on paper, to serve as their algorithm. They translate their written sequence of events into a coded animation using an appropriate block-based coding platform starting with an event.

ela.standard: Retell stories, including key details, and demonstrate understanding of their central message or lesson.
ela.description: Students work in pairs to use picture cards to "code" a familiar story, such as "Goldilocks and the Three Bears," following a verbally given algorithm (the story) and arranging the cards in the correct sequence. They translate their cards into an animation using a block-based coding platform, demonstrating understanding of key details, the central message, and the sequencing of events.

science.standard: Use observations of the sun, moon, and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted.
science.description: In pairs, students use a block-based coding platform to create a simple day-and-night model with two characters, a sun and a moon, and program separate events: Tapping the sun changes the background to daytime, and tapping the moon changes it to nighttime. Students demonstrate understanding by showing how different events trigger different code sequences and explain how these patterns relate to predictable changes in the sun, moon, and stars.

science.standard: Read texts and use media to determine patterns in behavior of parents and offspring that help offspring survive.
science.description: In small groups, students use large printed code blocks and classmates as "robots" to model animal survival behaviors from a story or video, such as "When the fox appears, the mother quail moves in front of the chicks and the chicks hide." Students demonstrate understanding by arranging the event and action blocks in the correct sequence and then "running" their program, showing how parent and offspring behaviors follow predictable patterns that help offspring survive.

other.standard: Explain how all people, not just official leaders, play important roles in a community.
other.description: In pairs, students use a block-based coding platform to create a scene with community helper characters (e.g., a firefighter, a doctor) and single events, such as "When the firefighter is tapped, play a siren sound" or "When the doctor is tapped, play a heartbeat sound." Students will practice matching the correct starting event to the correct action for each community helper.

other.standard: Demonstrates a variety of locomotor skills with the concepts of space, effort, and relationship awareness.
other.description: In pairs, one student acts as the programmer and one as the robot. They use picture cards to code a movement sequence (e.g., hop, spin, stretch) provided by the teacher. The programmer gives the "Go!" command, and the robot completes the task by looking at the sequence of code cards and performing the physical actions.

standards.statement: Create code from an algorithm that includes sequence, events, and iteration to complete a task or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should translate a provided algorithm that begins with an event and includes sequential steps and iteration (e.g., loops) into a working program. Writing an animation in a block-based language from a storyboard or coding a robot in collaboration with a partner to dance from an algorithm of arrows are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to work with selection (e.g., conditionals [if/then statements]), variables, or nested loops. Teachers may provide the original algorithm, if desired.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to translate a previously written algorithm (e.g., a morning routine, recess preparation, a class procedure) into code using a block-based coding platform. Students convert each step into a sequence of code blocks, then add iteration (e.g., repeating an action three times) into the code. Students run their programs to verify that the sequence, events, and iteration correctly model the original routine.

Students work individually or in pairs to develop code that represents a teacher-provided music or dance routine (the algorithm). The routine includes a triggering event (e.g., pressing Start), a sequence of movements or sounds, and an iteration (e.g., repeating a set of steps or beats). Students use a block-based coding platform or use an unplugged approach to create the coded performance. Students run their completed code to show how the sequence, events, and iteration combine to produce a rhythmic or choreographed output.

math.standard: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces.5 Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
math.description: Students, individually or in pairs, create code for a robot or on a block-based coding platform to draw shapes like a square, focusing on its specific attributes based on a provided algorithm (e.g., Repeat four times: Draw a line of the same length, then turn right.)

ela.standard: Write narratives in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.
ela.description: Students individually write code based on a narrative they wrote that serves as their algorithm. The narrative should include details that could result in a program with events, sequence, and possibly iteration.

ela.standard: Describe how characters in a story respond to major events and challenges.
ela.description: Students, individually or with a partner, code a digital retelling of a story. Students retell a well-known story (e.g., "The Three Little Pigs") and use events to show cause and effect (e.g., When the Big Bad Wolf blows, then the house falls down) and iteration for repetitive parts of the story (e.g., "Little pig, little pig, let me come in!" chant).

science.standard: Use information from several sources to provide evidence that Earth events can occur quickly or slowly.
science.description: Students use a block-based coding platform to create animations that model how Earth's surface changes at different speeds. In one project or scene, students will code a rapid event (e.g., a volcano erupting) using the event to trigger a sequence of commands to show a quick, powerful change. In another project or a new scene, students code a slow event (e.g., erosion) using a loop to repeat a small change over and over triggered by an event.

science.standard: Develop a simple model that mimics the function of an animal in dispersing seeds or pollinating plants.
science.description: Working with a partner or individually, students create code that models a bee pollinating flowers. The code should include events (e.g., The bee touches a flower), sequence (e.g., The bee flies to a flower and collects nectar), and iteration (e.g., Repeat this sequence for multiple flowers).

other.standard: Compare life in the past to life today.
other.description: Students code a program that compares a daily routine (sequence) from the past with one from today using an event to trigger a sequence of actions and using iteration to show repetitive tasks, such as scrubbing clothes or harvesting crops.

other.standard: Improvise a dance phrase with a beginning, a middle that has a main idea, and a clear end.
other.description: Students, individually or with a partner, code a robot to perform a short dance that includes a beginning, a middle, and an end. They use an event (e.g., a sound, a light, a tap) to start the dance sequence and include iteration (a loop) to repeat dance moves.

standards.statement: Develop code from a student-created algorithm that includes sequence, events, iteration, and selection to solve a problem or express ideas.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should implement their own or a classmate's algorithm in a block-based environment using events, iteration (e.g., loops) for efficiency, and basic decisions (e.g., conditionals [if/then statements]). Students should also give credit to the algorithm author and implementer. For example, turning a storyboard for a game that includes a game character moving forward, jumping over obstacles repeatedly, and choosing different paths when encountering a fork in the road into a program using a block-based programming language is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use text-based languages or design multilevel projects. Students are not required to implement a single program that includes every control structure.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to translate a step-by-step morning routine algorithm into a coded program. Using a block-based coding platform, students implement an algorithm (e.g., hang up backpack, if homework is complete → then turn it in, else → keep it in the folder, then sharpen pencil. They create appropriate graphical elements and use appropriate coding blocks to show a student's movement around the classroom and choices at the start of the school day. Students include a visible credit in their program (e.g., a comment block or title screen stating "Algorithm by ___; Program implemented by ___") to acknowledge authorship and implementation. Students run their programs to show how the character moves through the morning routine, demonstrating both the sequence of steps and the selection that changes what happens next.

Students work with a partner to write code based on an algorithm they previously created that directs a robot to draw geometric shapes. Students translate the steps of the algorithm into code using event, loop, and motion blocks. The final program includes a comment or label crediting the algorithm designer and the student who implemented the code. They test the program to ensure it draws the shape correctly, then modify the algorithm and code to create new shapes (e.g., triangles, rectangles) by changing angles and the number of repetitions.

math.standard: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
math.description: Students create a program from the algorithm "repeatedly add five and check whether the result ends in zero or five" to demonstrate the arithmetic pattern with a visual representation of the pattern in the program. Students could use a platform that allows them to display groups of five images and the total number of items to help them recognize the pattern.

math.standard: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.
math.description: Students code a multiplication game based on an algorithm created by a classmate that starts based on an event, includes a sequence that asks users a series of multiplication questions, uses selection ("if" statements) to check if the user answers correctly, and optionally, iteration to give users three tries to answer correctly.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: Students write an explanation of how they used block-based code to create a game from an algorithm. They create a program for a game (e.g., "Rock, Paper, Scissors"), and they describe how they took specific parts of the algorithm (creating the selection rules to determine the winner) and determined which code blocks to use and in what order.

ela.standard: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
ela.description: Students outline a story for the "Choose Your Own Adventure" game to use as a logical plan (algorithm) to code the story. The code should include selection based on user decisions (e.g., IF the user chooses the "dark cave," the code triggers one sequence of events, ELSE IF they choose the "sunny path," a different sequence happens.).

science.standard: Develop models to describe that organisms have unique and diverse life cycles but all have in common birth, growth, reproduction, and death.
science.description: Using a plant or animal life cycle as an algorithm, students create a coded animation or interactive model that uses events to initiate a sequence of actions that illustrate each part of the life cycle and iteration to repeat the cycle.

science.standard: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence of the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object.
science.description: After completing an investigation, students code an animation illustrating the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object. The code should use iteration to show motion and selection to show the effects of forces (e.g., IF the sprite/character touches a mud puddle, THEN the speed of motion slows down.).

other.standard: Explain how rules and laws change society and how people change rules and laws.
other.description: Students model school rules using code to help students understand how rules affect a community. Students code a program illustrating a school rule about hallway behavior using selection to represent the rules (e.g., IF "Running" is true, THEN the sprite is sent back to the start.).

standards.statement: Use constructive feedback to improve programs.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should give and apply specific, helpful suggestions to improve the function or design of their programs. Incorporating feedback from peers, teachers, or users into a program is appropriate. Teacher-provided templates for giving constructive feedback are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to interpret complex error reports, use advanced tools, or overhaul program structure or design. Students are not required to defend against all critiques or implement all feedback.

implementation_examples.description: Students create a math facts quiz game for younger students using a block-based programming environment with selection (if/then statements) and events. The teacher asks a colleague to have their younger students (users) play the quiz games and fill out a feedback form about the games. Students then use the feedback gathered to revise their programs based on the suggestions, such as fixing problems with the conditional statements or improving the instructions to make it easier for younger students to know how to play the game.

The teacher assigns a programming project to the class that students complete individually. Once the projects are complete, students work in pairs to give and receive constructive and kind feedback to a peer. Each student tests their partner's program and completes a structured feedback form provided by the teacher with items like "What works well?" "What could be improved?" Students then review the suggestions made by their partner and iterate on their programs based on the feedback. Students also explain the feedback they used (e.g., "My partner said the character moved too fast, so I added a 'wait' block.").

math.standard: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.
math.description: Students individually create programs to calculate the area of a rectangle using the length and width provided by the user and then share their programs with a peer. The peer completes a form provided by the teacher to provide constructive feedback that the student who wrote the program uses to improve or fix their program.

ela.standard: With guidance and support from peers and adults, develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, and editing.
ela.description: Connect planning, revising, and editing in ELA with the program development process. Students both give and use structured constructive feedback on a programming project in the planning and coding stages, reinforcing that like writing, program development is a process of iterative refinement.

ela.standard: Ask questions to check understanding of information presented, stay on topic, and link their comments to the remarks of others.
ela.description: Students create a program to tell or recount a story and then sit with a peer to run, ask, and respond to questions (e.g., "I noticed the dragon disappears quickly. Did you want the reader to see him longer?") about one another's programs. Students then use the feedback from their conversation to improve their programs.

science.standard: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.
science.description: After being reminded by the teacher of how they planned and carried out tests in science and challenged to do the same with their programming project, students plan and conduct multiple tests (e.g., use different input values, stop and restart at different times, have a peer ) of their programs, noting failure points (e.g., program does not restart properly if stopped in the middle, peer does not understand how to start the program) on a structured feedback form. Students then use the results of the tests to make improvements to their programs.

other.standard: Learners work productively with others to solve problems by soliciting and responding to feedback from others.
other.description: After completing programming projects, students share their project with others (e.g., peers, others in the school, family members) asking for feedback using a digital form to structure the feedback. Students then categorize the feedback (e.g., bugs that must be fixed, cool ideas to do later) and improve their programs by fixing bugs and implementing additional items as time allows.

standards.statement: Compare different programming solutions to the same problem based on correctness and clarity.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should compare multiple short programs or code segments meant to solve the same task, noting which ones produce the correct result and which are easier to understand or follow. Examples that use short block-based or text-based code segments are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create multiple versions themselves, evaluate efficiency, or conduct formal code reviews.

implementation_examples.description: Students explore two block-based programs that move a character or a robot in a square: one uses repeated motion blocks, and the other uses a loop. In pairs, students run both programs and discuss which works correctly, which is easier to understand or change, and which seems to run most quickly. They share their reasoning with another group, the class, or their teacher (in written form), highlighting what made one solution easier to understand or more efficient.

Students explore two block-based programs that use a variable to keep score in a game. Program 1 uses the variable name "s" and Program 2 uses the variable name "score." Students test both programs to ensure they both properly keep score and then complete a written reflection explaining which program(s) worked correctly and which would be easiest to understand and modify and why.

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students solve a multistep word problem using  two different mathematical algorithms (e.g., adding repeatedly vs. multiplying) provided by the teacher. Students solve the problem using both algorithms and write a reflection on which algorithm was more "correct" for the specific problem and which would be easier to explain to someone else.

math.standard: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.
math.description: Working in pairs, students compare two different code snippets (provided by the teacher) that draw shapes to see which code snippet correctly produces the specific shape (e.g., right trapezoid). The class then discusses their findings and the clarity of each code snippet.

ela.standard: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
ela.description: Students maintain a design journal to track their work on comparing programming solutions for clarity and correctness and share journal reports with peers.

science.standard: Apply scientific ideas to design, test, and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another.
science.description: Students, working with a partner, read and test two different programs for a Smart Solar Heater to determine if they correctly activate a motor to track the sun's energy throughout the day. They then determine which solution better uses organized loops and labeled variables that would enable an engineer to easily troubleshoot the energy conversion process.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans.
science.description: Students work in small groups to design a prototype flood warning system based around a physical computing device that can measure rising water levels. Two groups then work together to test both of their prototypes to decide if each is correct and which program is easier to understand and modify.

other.standard: Explain how policies are developed to address public problems.
other.description: Students discuss two new proposed school rules for hallway behavior. The first is an unorganized, long, confusing rule, and the second is an organized, short, clear rule. In a class discussion, students discuss which "code" (rule) is more likely to be followed correctly and why, emphasizing the clarity of the second rule.

standards.statement: Collaborate with a team by offering a meaningful contribution to creating a program.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should work in small groups to plan and create a simple program, contribute ideas or code segments, or test functionality while practicing respectful communication, active listening, and shared tasking. Adding a feature, fixing an error, improving a design element, or helping organize the code are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use professional collaboration tools, manage large projects, or apply formal methodologies.

implementation_examples.description: Working in groups of three, students create a simple interactive story using a grade-level appropriate programming language by first using collaborative tools to plan their story and create the algorithms needed to code it. Students then create a program based on their planning with each student taking on a specific role (e.g., artwork, coding, testing). The roles are rotated among team members on a regular basis. As they build, each student documents their contribution on a shared project log. The group presents their completed story to the class or another group explaining what each person added and how it contributed to the final program.

In small groups, students create a collaborative piece of art using a coding platform or programmable robot. Each student is responsible for a specific element or feature of the artwork. Throughout the process, they record their individual contributions, decisions, and challenges in a shared digital or paper journal. The group presents their completed artwork to the class, explaining each member's role and how their combined efforts contributed to the overall design of the project.

math.standard: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.
math.description: Students work collaboratively to design and code a timer program with various features (e.g., start and stop timer, reset timer, making an LED blink every 10 seconds).

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students work in teams to program a calculator that solves multistep word problems. Each student codes one of the operations confirming that output from one operation correctly serves as input for the next operation.

ela.standard: Report on a topic or text, tell a story, or recount an experience in an organized manner, using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace.
ela.description: After completing a collaborative coding project, student teams present their code to another team or the whole class. Each team member must orally report on their specific meaningful contribution to the program, using descriptive details to explain how their code segment supports the main goal of the program (e.g., making a character avoid obstacles, calculating the score).

science.standard: Use a model to describe that animals receive different types of information through their senses, process the information in their brain, and respond to the information in different ways.
science.description: Working in a team, students create a physical computing project that represents an animal and models how that animal reacts to sensory input. Each student writes code to receive input from one of the device's sensors and produce an appropriate output. Students then collaborate with team members to test the completed program and ensure it works as intended, demonstrating how individual code contributions combine to build a complete biological model.

other.standard: Apply civic virtues and democratic principles in school settings.
other.description: Before starting a collaborative coding project, the whole class creates guidance on collaboration with rules for listening to partner ideas, determining who should be coding when, and so on. Students work in teams to create the program and complete a reflection describing how they followed the agreed-upon guidance and contributed to the program creation.

standards.statement: Create a novel program by modifying or combining elements of existing programs.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should make purposeful changes to a program by incorporating teacher-created, peer-created, or other code segments to create a unique variation of the original program, giving appropriate credit for code segments used. Remixing or adapting existing code to add new features, levels, or outcomes, including credit for code reuse through comments in code or in external documentation, is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write entirely original, complex programs from scratch or manage large-scale integrations of multiple projects. Students are not required to incorporate AI-generated code.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs to modify an existing program (e.g., a "Choose Your Own Adventure" game) to add a new ending, change the setting and what causes it to appear, or incorporate new sounds and actions. Students include comments in their code or a visible "Credits" section identifying the original program and its creator. After modifying the program, students test their version and share how their modification changes the player's experience.

As a whole class, students examine two simple computer programs (e.g., animations or games) to understand what is happening in the program. Students then select and combine elements from each of the programs (e.g., character movements, sounds, or interactions) to create a new, original program. Students document which elements were reused and include comments or a credit screen acknowledging the original sources. Students then share their completed projects and explain how remixing and modifying parts of existing code led to a new creation.

math.standard: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.
math.description: Students modify a math quiz game for multiplication to include additional types of operations, enabling users to select the type of operation they want to use.

math.standard: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.
math.description: Students are provided with two programs: One calculates area for whole numbers and the other visualizes a fraction on a grid. Students combine elements of both programs to allow for fractions or decimals that are visualized to create a new program that demonstrates why multiplying fractions results in a smaller area.

ela.standard: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
ela.description: Students remix a template program provided by the teacher to include their own narrative writing and plot development.

ela.standard: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; summarize or paraphrase information in notes and finished work, and provide a list of sources.
ela.description: Students are given a program template with code that handles text boxes and speech and are asked to modify it to include researched facts and primary source images to create a digital biography of a person from history. Students are required to attribute the original script to its creator and cite their research sources using comments in their code or in public-facing information about the program.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students adapt an existing simulation program to use code to simulate multiple possible solutions to a problem that they can test to determine the best option that meets the criteria within the constraints.

science.standard: Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen.
science.description: Students start with two basic programs: (a) one that moves dots randomly, modeling particle movement, and (b) one that includes a temperature slider. Students work with a partner to combine elements from both programs, adding selection (if/then) blocks to simulate what happens when the temperature changes, demonstrating how particles speed up and spread out in different states of matter.

other.standard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions and their environmental characteristics.
other.description: After researching regions within their state, students are provided with an interactive map program of another country. Students modify the program to include a map of their state and change the interaction so that when users click a specific region, the program displays facts about that region (e.g, climate, industry).

other.standard: Combine ideas to generate an innovative idea for art-making.
other.description: Students are given a program with code that draws repeating lines. They are asked to modify the program (e.g., changing the pen color, adding iteration, using sound or motion sensing) to create art based on a specific artistic style (e.g., Impressionism, Pop Art).

standards.statement: Construct individual components of a program that are collaboratively assembled into a programming project.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should individually build small code components and integrate them with teammates into a complete functional program. For example, in a block-based environment, one student might construct the code component for a scoring system using variables and selection, while another constructs the player movement component. They then integrate and test these pieces to ensure the final project works.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use version control or design full system architecture.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in teams of three using a block-based coding platform to create a simple maze game with three distinct scenes. Each student is responsible for one major component. Student A codes the player character's actions and dialogue. Student B programs a scoring system, including a variable to track points. Student C creates artwork and manages scene flow. After creating their individual components, each student imports their portion of the project into a shared project file which they collaboratively debug and refine to ensure that events (e.g., Next Scene) and variables (e.g., the score tracker) all work together. Teams present their completed maze game, describing how each member's contribution supports the overall functionality.

The entire class collaborates to build a simple digital yearbook. The class is divided into pairs, with each pair responsible for coding a specific component of the project (e.g., Student Photos, Favorite Quotes, Class Events, Next Page Button). A rotating class project manager coordinates integration by combining all components using a yearbook template and verifying that navigation works consistently across pages. Each pair submits their functional component and documentation explaining how their component connects to the other parts of the yearbook.

math.standard: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two- dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category. For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.
math.description: When creating a game, if the team decides all "enemy" components must move at a certain speed, a student constructing a Square Enemy must follow those inherited rules.

ela.standard: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
ela.description: Students work in teams to create a digital research report. Each student is responsible for constructing the code component for a different research aspect (e.g., one codes the data display for "History," another the interactive map for "Geography"). They collaboratively assemble these coded sections into one final presentation.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Each student constructs a distinct component of the simulation (e.g., Component 1: Animal movement, Component 2: Food growth, Component 3: Predator/prey interaction rules) and combines, tests, and refines to improve the overall simulation output.

other.standard: Explain why individuals and groups during the same historical period differed in their perspectives.
other.description: Students collaboratively create an interactive program showing a timeline. Each team member constructs the code component to display a historical event from a different perspective (e.g., one component codes the view of the colonists, another the view of the colonized). They assemble the components to show a unified timeline, where the user can select different perspectives programmed by the individual components.

standards.statement: Use procedures to structure code for clarity and reusability.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use procedures to make code easier to read and reuse by grouping a set of steps under a clear, descriptive name and calling the procedure in one or more places in the program. Students recognize an opportunity for a procedure (e.g., repeated or logically grouped steps), create the procedure, replace repeated code with procedure calls, and describe how this improves clarity and reusability (e.g., reduces duplication, makes updates easier, helps organize the program). Procedures may be teacher-provided, student-created, or developed from starter code.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to write procedures with parameters or return values, to design large modular systems, or to manage many interacting procedures, modules, or objects.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs or small groups to design and teach a "robot" classmate their own version of a  cha-cha dance sequence. Students create a written list of steps to define a procedure such as "cha-cha real smooth" or smaller procedures like "stomp" (stomp right foot, stomp left foot) and "hop" (hop twice, pause, hop twice, pause). Each group selects a song and develops one or more dance move procedures that can be called during the performance. One student plays the role of the programmer, giving commands, while another plays the robot following the procedure. After performing their programmed dance, students reflect on how using named procedures made it easier to organize and repeat sections of the dance without listing each step every time.

Students work individually or with a partner to program a game and revise it to incorporate at least two procedures. Students will use a programming platform to design a simple game that incorporates several repeated actions (e.g., cycling through multiple background images to simulate motion, dropping rain particles on the scene). Students identify at least two sections of code with repeated commands and replace them with procedures for clarity and reusability. Students present their completed game, explaining how the use of procedures reduced repetition and improved code organization.

math.standard: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers.
math.description: Students write a geometric art program where they define reusable procedures to draw shapes. Students will use variables within their procedures, enabling them to write clear, reusable code that can generate many different drawings by evaluating their procedures with different numeric arguments.

ela.standard: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
ela.description: After writing a program that uses procedures, students write a short technical explanation of their code. They must use computer science and programming vocabulary to clearly explain how their reusable procedures work and improve the program's structure.

science.standard: Develop a model that predicts and describes changes in particle motion, temperature, and state of a pure substance when thermal energy is added or removed.
science.description: Students use a programming language to create a simulation of thermal expansion. Students will write procedures to model how objects expand as the temperature increases, structuring the code so that they can reuse the procedure to simulate different materials or temperatures.

other.standard: Design, propose, and evaluate artistic ideas, plans, prototypes, and production processes for media arts productions, considering expressive intent and resources.
other.description: Students design a short digital animation, first proposing a plan and then creating it in a block-based coding environment. Students design and evaluate their production process by writing reusable procedures to build their scenes efficiently, enabling them to focus their resources on refining the artistic expressive intent of their final piece.

standards.statement: Use reference documentation in program development.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use reliable documentation that helps write, debug, and refine their programs. They should use teacher-provided or self-selected documentation to understand functions or blocks and search for common error messages to identify causes and solutions.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to read professional-level documentation or apply coding concepts beyond their grade level.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in small groups to analyze and debug a printed computer program using provided reference documentation. The teacher supplies students with a program written in a familiar language that contains several types of errors (e.g., syntax, runtime, logic bugs) and a printed list of programming features with explanations of correct usage. Students are told what the program should do and what errors occur when it runs. Using highlighters and pens, students mark buggy lines and annotate corrections directly on the paper. Students share their annotated programs and explain how they identified and fixed the errors using the documentation. They reflect briefly, orally or in writing, on how consulting reference materials supported their debugging process.

Students work individually or in pairs to learn and apply a new coding feature using official documentation or online resources. Each student chooses a feature they have not yet used (e.g., event triggers, sound blocks, conditional statements). Using the programming language's wiki or help documentation, they learn how the feature works and apply it in a small, self-designed project. After testing their project, students create a brief, 15-minute lesson to teach classmates how to use the feature. All lessons include a citation for the documentation source used. Students present their mini lessons in class, showing how the new feature functions within their code.

math.standard: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.
math.description: Students will use a programming language to write a small program that solves one-step or two-step equations. When their program produces incorrect results, students will use language documentation or online coding references to debug logic or syntax errors.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students write a program that summarizes a small numerical data set. A student calculates the mean/median and range of a set of quiz scores or daily temperatures. When their results are incorrect, they use reference documentation to debug issues such as loop logic, indexing, or data types. Students present their summary in a simple table and describe what the statistics show about the data in context.

ela.standard: Introduce a topic clearly, previewing what is to follow; organize ideas, concepts, and information into broader categories; include formatting (e.g., headings), graphics (e.g., charts, tables), and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
ela.description: Students write an informative "how it works" explanation for a program they built. Using official documentation, they organize the explanation with clear headings that include its purpose and key features. Students include a brief table or graphic to support comprehension. Students cite the documentation source used.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students create and test two program solutions for the same task. Students create two versions of a simple game or data tool and compare results using basic criteria (accuracy, reliability, usability). When one version fails or behaves unexpectedly, students use reference documentation to debug and improve it. They use test data to identify which design characteristics best meet the success criteria.

other.standard: Apply relevant criteria to examine, reflect on, and plan revisions for a work of art or design in progress.
other.description: Students create a digital artwork or interactive design using a programming tool and consult documentation to learn an unfamiliar feature, such as layering, transformations, or interaction. After a structured peer critique, students revise their work and use reference documentation to troubleshoot and refine their code. They briefly reflect on how the documentation supported their revisions.

standards.statement: Justify the importance of attribution and intellectual property when developing computing technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should define intellectual property and explain why giving credit to original creators matters. They should recognize that programming and computing technologies make use of multiple artifacts (e.g., code, images, music, text), and understand the difference between learning from others' code and plagiarizing it. Identifying whether code is open source, free to use, or proprietary and providing basic attribution in their own work are appropriate. Students should focus on ethical awareness and responsible use of others' work.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to study copyright law, fair use, or licensing in depth or to license their own code.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to debate whether computer code should be considered intellectual property. Each group selects a position (i.e., for or against) and develops at least three arguments to support their stance. The teacher provides specific scenarios for consideration, such as open-source licensing, AI-generated code, and software patents. Students cite these examples in their arguments and prepare a rebuttal to one argument from an opposing group. Groups present their debates to the class, using evidence and reasoning to support their claims. Afterward, students reflect on how attribution, ownership, and collaboration influence ethical decision-making in programming.

Students work individually or in pairs to evaluate how a web developer credits external code and design assets on a live website. The teacher provides a list of the code snippets and media assets used to build a given site, none of which were originally created by the developer. Students navigate the website to locate attribution statements for each resource and determine whether credit is correctly provided. Students document which items include proper attribution and which do not, then write a short reflection explaining: (a) the importance of giving credit in programming and design, (b) their own definition of intellectual property, and (c) one practice they can adopt to ensure they always attribute others' work in their own projects.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students take an existing data set they are plotting in math (e.g., temperatures, survey results, sports statistics) and discuss why knowing the source of the data and the methods used to gather it matters for accuracy and fairness. They connect this to programming by explaining how attribution of data sources in code ensures transparency and trustworthiness, just as citing sources in math prevents misinterpretation and allows for more careful inferences about the data.

math.standard: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle sum and exterior angle of triangles, about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similarity of triangles. For example, arrange three copies of the same triangle so that the sum of the three angles appears to form a line, and give an argument in terms of transversals why this is so.
math.description: Students use informal geometric arguments (e.g., angle–angle similarity, exterior-angle facts) and explicitly cite the theorems or sources that support their reasoning ("Triangles △ABC and △DEF are similar by AA; see Theorem AA in our notes."). They then draw a parallel to programming by including attribution comments and a credits section in a small project ("Distance-calculation function adapted from Open Source Geometry Toolkit, v1.2 (link), CC BY 4.0"). In both cases, clear sourcing (i.e., naming the mathematical facts in a proof, crediting borrowed code or assets) makes work traceable, verifiable, and ethical, distinguishing legitimate learning and reuse from plagiarism.

ela.standard: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, using search terms effectively; assess the credibility and accuracy of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard format for citation.
ela.description: Students practice ethical research and attribution in writing and draw parallels to giving credit for code, images, and other programming artifacts.

ela.standard: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, using search terms effectively; assess the credibility and accuracy of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard format for citation.
ela.description: Students analyze why attribution matters in writing and apply the same reasoning to programming, recognizing original creators' intent and respecting intellectual property.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students compare two versions of a project (one with proper attribution and one without) and analyze which better supports reproducibility and ethical standards in scientific programming.

science.standard: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
science.description: Students create a simple flowchart showing steps for incorporating attribution when using external code or media in a scientific simulation, reinforcing systematic thinking and ethical responsibility.

other.standard: Apply civic virtues and democratic principles in school and community settings.
other.description: Students explore how respecting intellectual property in programming parallels civic responsibility in society. Just as citizens credit sources when sharing information or ideas, programmers must attribute code, images, and media to maintain trust and fairness in digital spaces. This reinforces ethical participation in both civic and technological communities.

other.standard: Demonstrate willingness to experiment, innovate, and take risks to pursue ideas, forms, and meanings that emerge in the process of art-making or designing.
other.description: Students demonstrate how artists often draw inspiration from existing works or styles when creating new pieces. They learn to acknowledge these influences in their own art projects, which parallels attribution in programming (crediting original creators when incorporating code, images, or design elements).

standards.statement: Develop a program utilizing inclusive collaboration practices.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should actively share ideas during planning, provide and receive constructive feedback in all stages of program development, and collaborate effectively on shared digital tools. Students should focus on productive teamwork and inclusive communication. Practicing equal participation, clear communication, and respect for others' contributions is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use formal collaboration methods, like Agile or Scrum, or professional project management software.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to design a simple program concept (e.g., a game or quiz) using paper-based storyboards or flowcharts. Each student contributes at least one idea during planning. Groups practice inclusive collaboration by assigning rotating roles (idea generator, note-taker, presenter) and using a feedback protocol (e.g., "I like …," "I wonder …," "What if …").

Students use a shared digital coding platform to co-create a program. They practice inclusive collaboration by dividing and completing separate parts of the code, commenting on each other's code, suggesting improvements, and documenting contributions in a shared space.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Reporting the number of observations.
math.description: Students collect and summarize data on group participation (e.g., number of ideas shared per person) to evaluate fairness and inclusivity in collaboration.

math.standard: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events. For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected.
math.description: Students reason about how randomizing roles (e.g., coder, tester, presenter) ensures equal participation, connecting fairness in collaboration to probability concepts.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 7 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students practice structured discussions during program planning, using active listening and respectful turn-taking to ensure inclusive collaboration.
