Observing and identifying a block that led to an unexpected result in a block-based coding app or a command card that was incorrect in an unplugged activity are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explain why the error occurred, analyze program logic, or use formal debugging strategies.

implementation_examples.description: Students follow step-by-step instruction cards that display a visual sequence of four or five steps for assembling a small structure with blocks. The teacher provides the student with the correct blocks but intentionally gives students a step-by-step instruction card that contains an incorrect step (e.g., one step shows a block being placed in the wrong location,one step is intentionally out of sequence). Students follow the visual commands and when they reach the incorrect step or the step that is out of order, they identify the item (the block or the instruction card) that does not work as expected by pointing to it and describing the expected action versus the observed/instructed action.

In small groups or centers, students work with a simple programmable robot and unplugged materials (e.g., arrow cards showing directional commands) to create a path from a starting point to a target (e.g., moving a robot to a picture of a flower on a floor grid). Partners take turns placing command cards or pressing buttons to create a sequence. When they test the sequence and the robot doesn't reach the target, students work together to identify which command caused the problem. The teacher provides sentence frames like "This step doesn't work" or visual supports (thumbs up and thumbs down cards) to help students communicate which specific command did not work as expected.

math.standard: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
math.description: Students create sequences of commands to move something (e.g., robot, toy, character) to a specific location using directional and positional vocabulary. When testing their sequences, they identify which directional command (forward, backward, left, right) doesn't work as expected, connecting spatial reasoning with debugging skills.

math.standard: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
math.description: Students review a sequence of steps for a math problem (e.g., "Start with two apples. Add one more apple."). The teacher acts out the sequence with an intentional error (e.g., adds two more apples). Students  identify the error in the sequence of actions by describing how the action does not match the sequence of steps.

ela.standard: Confirm understanding of a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media by asking and answering questions about key details and requesting clarification if something is not understood.
ela.description: Students review instructions for a craft activity or a class procedure. The teacher demonstrates completing the instructions but with an intentional error. Students identify the instruction/step that was executed incorrectly.

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions in order to seek help, get information, or clarify something that is not understood.
ela.description: To connect the debugging process with communication skills, students identify a command that doesn't work as expected and practice asking questions like "Why didn't this work?" or "What should we do instead?"

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: To connect the debugging process to scientific inquiry and observation, students observe a program's behavior and identify what needs to change.

other.standard: Child persists in tasks.
other.description: Students follow a short sequence of steps during a simple problem-solving task (e.g., completing a puzzle or using a shape sorter). When a step does not work as expected, they identify the step that caused the problem and continue working by trying the step again or moving to the next step. Through this process, students demonstrate persistence while recognizing errors in a sequence.

other.standard: Child explores the positions of objects in space.
other.description: Students create sequences of commands to move objects (e.g., toys, manipulatives) to specific locations using positional vocabulary. When testing their sequences, they identify which directional command (forward, backward, up, or down) doesn't work as expected, connecting spatial reasoning with debugging skills.

standards.statement: Debug programs that include a sequence.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and fix simple errors in block-based programs they have developed or were provided by the teacher. Students should focus on identifying and correcting simple, visible mistakes. For example, if a character is supposed to move and then jump, but the code blocks are in the wrong order, the student should be able to identify the problem and reorder the blocks.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to find complex logical errors or debug programs that include loops or conditionals.

implementation_examples.description: Students act as debuggers to spot the mistake in a simple picture algorithm for a task, like getting ready for recess (e.g., 1. Push in chair. 2. Put on coat. 3. Line up quietly.). On the board, the teacher models this algorithm with picture cards, but intentionally creates a bug by putting the steps in the wrong sequence (e.g., 1. Line up quietly. 2. Push in chair. 3. Put on coat.). After spotting the mistake in the sequence, students physically move the cards back into the correct order, fixing the bug so the plan makes sense.

Students test a simple block-based coding program that has a clear goal, like "make the character walk to the apple on the right." They discover that the program has a bug: the code block says "move left" instead of "move right." Students debug the code by finding the incorrect block and replacing it with the correct one to match the algorithm and fix the bug.

math.standard: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false. For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 – 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.
math.description: Students test whether an equation is true or false. Looking at the teacher-provided equation, 2 + 2 = 5, they identify the bug (the answer is incorrect) and debug the equation by replacing the 5 with the correct answer, 4.

ela.standard: Produce and expand complete simple and compound declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts.
ela.description: Students act as editors to debug a sentence the teacher writes on the board (e.g., "Cat the sat mat the on."). To fix the bug, students rearrange the words into the correct sequence (e.g., "The cat sat on the mat,"), connecting debugging a sequence in code to fixing a problem in word sequence.

science.standard: Use observations of the sun, moon, and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted.
science.description: Students are shown a four-picture sequence of a day (sunrise, noon, sunset, night) but with a bug in the order. They identify the mistake in the predictable sequence and debug the model by putting the pictures in the correct order.

other.standard: Construct maps, graphs, and other representations of familiar places.
other.description: As a whole-class activity, the students, along with the teacher, create a simple map of the classroom. The teacher then provides a set of directions to get to the bookshelf using directional cards, but the directions have a bug (e.g., "turn right" instead of "turn left"). Students try to follow the directions. They then identify the bug and debug the instructions.

other.standard: When analyzing selected music, read and perform rhythmic patterns using iconic or standard notation.
other.description: Students listen to find the bug in a rhythm's sequence (the teacher claps out a simple, repeating rhythm but adds a bug on the third repeat). They then clap it the correct way to debug the pattern.

standards.statement: Debug programs that include sequence, events, and iteration.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should test a simple, block-based program that includes sequence, events, and iteration, identify one obvious bug, and correct it. Bugs may involve commands in the wrong order (sequence), an event not triggering the intended action, or a loop repeating too few or too many times (iteration). For example, if a robot does not respond when clicked, moves in the wrong order, or draws only three sides of a square instead of four, students should locate the issue and adjust the relevant block.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to fix multiple or complex errors or explain problems using technical terms.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs on a block-based coding platform to fix a premade program. The goal of the program is to make a character draw a square. The provided code correctly uses a "move forward" block and a "turn 90 degrees" block inside a repeat block (iteration). However, the program has a bug: the repeat block is set to "repeat 3 times" instead of 4. Students run the program (event) and observe that the character only draws three sides of the square. They will then debug the program by finding the error in the iteration block and changing the value from 3 to 4, successfully refining the program to solve the problem.

In a whole-class activity, students are at tables in groups of five. The teacher, acting as a robot, hands out worksheets. The goal is to give one worksheet to every student at a table group (e.g., a table with five students). The teacher shows the algorithm on the board:
(Event) When the class says "Go!",
(Iteration) Repeat 3 times:
(Sequence) [Take one paper from the stack, Give it to a student at the table].
Return to the main desk.
The teacher runs the program exactly as written. After students say "Go!", the teacher walks over, gives a paper to three students, and then immediately returns to their desk, leaving two students empty-handed. The class identifies the bug and the students work in their groups to debug the algorithm by identifying that the iteration (the repeat block) has the wrong number. They tell the teacher to fix the bug by changing the repeat value from 3 to 5 to match the number of students at the table.

math.standard: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
math.description: Students act as math debuggers to test a teacher-provided sequence pattern (e.g., "2, 4, 6, 7, 10"), find the number that breaks the repeating "+2" rule, and debug the sequence by changing the 7 to an 8.

math.standard: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.
math.description: Students identify the bug in a skip-counting sequence on the board that breaks the "+10" pattern (e.g., "10, 20, 30, 35") and debug the sequence by changing the 35 to a 40.

ela.standard: Describe how words and phrases (e.g., regular beats, alliteration, rhymes, repeated lines) supply rhythm and meaning in a story, poem, or song.
ela.description: Students read or listen to a short poem with a repeating line (a refrain). They notice when a word is changed in one of the repeating lines breaking the iteration..

ela.standard: Describe the overall structure of a story, including describing how the beginning introduces the story and the ending concludes the action.
ela.description: Students examine a simple three-panel comic strip or a set of three sentences describing a short story that is out of order (e.g., 1. The girl cries. 2. The girl gets a balloon. 3. The balloon pops.). They identify the part of the sequence that does not make sense and debug the story by rearranging the events into a logical order (e.g., 2, 3, 1).

science.standard: Make observations to construct an evidence-based account of how an object made of a small set of pieces can be disassembled and made into a new object.
science.description: Students follow a set of steps to build a toy car from a set of parts (e.g., a base, 4 wheels, 2 axles): (1) (Event) When you start building, (2) (Sequence) Get the car base, (3) (Iteration) Repeat 2 times: [Get a wheel, put it on an axle, attach it to the car]. The steps contain an iteration bug. When the object does not turn out as expected (e.g., the car only has two wheels), they identify the step that caused the problem and change the repeat value from 2 to 4.

science.standard: Develop a simple model that mimics the function of an animal in dispersing seeds or pollinating plants.
science.description: Students follow or observe a step-by-step algorithm of how a bee pollinates a garden with five flowers. The algorithm has a bug inside its iteration loop: (1) (Event) When the bee starts, (2) (Iteration) Repeat 5 times: [Fly to a flower, Fly to a new flower, Get pollen, Drop pollen]. When the algorithm does not work as expected, they identify the step in the sequence that causes the problem (e.g., leaving a flower before collecting the pollen) and debug the algorithm by correcting the order of actions (e.g., "Fly to a flower, Get pollen, Fly to a new flower, Drop pollen").

other.standard: Improvise rhythmic and melodic patterns and musical ideas for a specific purpose.
other.description: Students perform a simple four-beat rhythmic pattern that is intended to repeat (iteration), but contains a bug. For example, the pattern may be "Stomp, Clap, Clap, Stomp," followed by a repeated sequence with an error such as "Stomp, Clap, Stomp, Stomp." Students test the pattern by clapping it aloud and debug the rhythm by identifying the "Stomp" that should be a "Clap," fixing the iteration.

other.standard: Identify practices and behaviors that support health and well-being of self and others.
other.description: Students examine a chart showing a sequence of steps for washing hands that contains a bug in the order. For example, the chart may show: (1) Get soap. (2) Rinse hands. (3) Turn on water. (4) Dry hands. Students test the sequence by thinking through or acting it out, identify the step that does not work as expected (e.g., rinsing before turning on the water), and debug the sequence by rearranging the steps into the correct order.

standards.statement: Debug programs that include sequence, events, iteration, and selection.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should locate and fix common logical or structural errors in programs using a combination of sequence, events, loops, and conditional choices. For example, debugging a block-based program in which commands in the wrong order (sequence), a character that does not move when clicked (event), a loop that runs too many times (iteration), or an "if" block triggers the wrong action (selection) are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to debug syntax errors in text-based languages or correct complex programs involving variables, functions, or nested conditions or loops. Students are not required to debug a single program that includes all control structures (i.e., sequence, events, iteration, and selection). However, across multiple debugging experiences, students should work with programs that collectively include all of these control structures.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to identify and fix iteration errors in a program that animates a character performing a dance routine. The teacher provides several versions of a program in which the character's dance sequence includes errors in the loop structure (e.g., repeating too many or too few steps, performing actions in the wrong order). Students analyze the code to locate the faulty iteration logic (e.g., misplaced repeat blocks, missing end loops) and make corrections to ensure that the character performs the intended sequence smoothly. Students test and run their corrected programs to confirm that the dance moves now repeat correctly.

Students work individually or in pairs to debug a narrative program that includes both character movement and background changes. The provided code includes one or more intentional errors in selection (e.g., incorrect use of if or if/else statements) and iteration (e.g., loops that don't run as intended). Students analyze the logic to determine why certain actions don't trigger correctly or repeat as expected. They use testing and reasoning to isolate the problem and revise the conditional or loop structure accordingly. Students present the corrected version of their story, showing that character movements and scene changes now follow the intended pattern.

math.standard: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students debug a math-themed program (e.g., a calculator or pattern generator) by finding where logic or selection statements cause incorrect results. This integrates reasoning about operations with debugging iterative or conditional errors in code.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students use loops and conditionals to create or fix a simple program that automatically generates a bar graph from class-collected data, connecting the debugging process to interpreting and organizing mathematical data.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 3 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students work in pairs to identify and fix bugs in a shared program, using precise academic language to explain their debugging strategies and reasoning.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: After debugging a program, students write a concise explanation describing the type of error (iteration vs. selection) and how they resolved it, reinforcing both coding vocabulary and clear explanation skills.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: When debugging a simple simulation or model (such as a water cycle animation), students test different solutions to fix iterative loops or conditional logic, reflecting the engineering design process.

science.standard: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.
science.description: Students test versions of a looping or conditional program, observing how changes affect performance, mirroring scientific testing to refine code behavior.

standards.statement: Debug programs incrementally and repeatedly as they are developed.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should test and fix their code as they develop programs rather than completing all coding and then testing. For example, students can add a short sequence of blocks and then run the code to confirm that it does what is expected. If the code does not behave as expected, students can find, reproduce, and fix the error easily in the code they added incrementally. Students can use tracing skills to identify where code does not behave as expected. Debugging programs that include a combination of sequence, events, iteration, and selection are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to debug programs involving procedures or nested structures. Students are not required to debug one single program that includes all control structures (sequencing, events, iteration, and selection); however, all control structures should be included throughout programs that students debug.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to develop a program by adding short sequences of commands and testing regularly. Students can be provided a worksheet to repeatedly record what they added, whether bugs were observed, and how the bugs were resolved.

Students design a Choose Your Own Adventure game using numbered cards. They start writing their story on card 1. The player chooses one of two actions and is directed to a new card number based on that option. As students add new cards to their game, they repeatedly test that their story makes sense or invite peers to test it.

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students use guided worksheets to solve multistep word problems or develop programs. Students assess the reasonableness of answers in multistep word problems by comparing them to repeatedly testing code as it is developed.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: In a worksheet or a paragraph, students write a short explanation of how they debugged their program. They describe the bug, how they reproduced it, and how they fixed it.

ela.standard: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
ela.description: Students write a narrative about the process they followed developing their program. Each time they test their code, they record this as an event with descriptive details about what was observed.

science.standard: Apply scientific ideas to design, test, and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another.
science.description: Students apply the technique of repeatedly doing incremental work before testing their computing project to the context of developing a physical device.

other.standard: Compare the benefits and costs of individual choices.
other.description: Students compare two debugging strategies (e.g., "change lots of blocks quickly," "change one block and test") and discuss the costs and benefits of each (e.g., time, confusion, accuracy). They then apply the more efficient strategy and explain how their choice improved results.

other.standard: Explain how culture influences the way people modify and adapt to their environments.
other.description: Students discuss how team culture (e.g., helpful feedback, patience, careful testing) changes how a group works in a coding environment. During debugging, they practice that culture explicitly, using kind, specific language, and note how it helps the group solve problems faster.

standards.statement: Debug programs using systematic strategies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should apply more than one systematic debugging strategy. Strategies such as reproducing the problem, reading error messages, tracing code, changing one element at a time, or adding temporary outputs (e.g., sounds, text, other alerts) to locate issues are appropriate. Students should focus on using clear, repeatable methods to find and fix syntax, logic, or runtime errors.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use professional debugging tools or automated testing frameworks.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to use systematic strategies to debug intentionally buggy programs provided by the teacher that include a variety of common issues (e.g., incorrect loops, misplaced variables, flawed logic). Students use a debugging checklist to analyze the code step by step and apply a specific strategy, such as using print statements, isolating sections of code, or tracing program flow. They might debug a Fibonacci sequence program by inserting print statements to verify each iteration's output. Students share their corrected programs and explain which debugging strategies helped them identify and fix the errors.

Students apply systematic debugging methods to their own coding projects, incorporating strategies they've previously practiced. Students create or use provided test cases to check whether their program functions correctly across a variety of inputs, including edge cases. As they test, they identify bugs and use structured debugging approaches (e.g., targeted print statements, incremental testing, code tracing, checklists) to resolve issues. Students present their completed programs along with evidence of their debugging process (e.g., notes, screenshots, brief reflection).

math.standard: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 0, and given the rule “Add 6” and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.
math.description: Students debug programs that generate number patterns (e.g., Fibonacci, geometric sequences, arithmetic sequences) or create coordinate pairs by analyzing whether the pattern logic is correct and identifying where the sequence breaks down.

ela.standard: With guidance and support from peers and adults, develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
ela.description: Students will fix issues (e.g., errors in logic, problems in the interface, suggested improvements) in programs they created based on feedback from peers or their teacher to systematically improve their final program.

science.standard: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.
science.description: Knowing that debugging can be framed as a fair test, students design a set of tests to determine if the code behaves correctly with both typical inputs and boundary cases. Students predict the outcome and record results in a table.

other.standard: Use deliberative processes when making decisions or reaching judgments as a group.
other.description: Systematic strategies for debugging are one example of deliberative processes that students can follow either individually or in groups. Their goal is to reach a judgment regarding what is broken so they can decide how to fix it.

standards.statement: Use systematic strategies to test, refine, and document changes to a computing technology to meet the intended purpose.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should select and implement a variety of techniques to find and fix errors, explain code, refine a user interface, and give and receive constructive feedback during code review. Appropriate techniques might include testing input and output, using watchers, testing individual procedures, or using AI to make suggestions for alignment with design specifications.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use debugging software, unit testing frameworks, or version control systems or to follow documentation standards beyond basic commenting practices.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small teams to design a paper‑based "app" that processes inputs on a backend flowchart (e.g., calculating a score or sorting items) and displays results on a front‑end paper interface. Teams run structured test cases by feeding sample inputs into their backend logic, noting incorrect outputs or broken decision paths on a debugging checklist. Classmates then act as users, interacting with the paper interface and leaving feedback on clarity, layout, labels, and accessibility. Teams refine both the backend logic and the front‑end design, documenting their changes directly on the artifacts and briefly explaining which testing strategies led to the improvements.

Students test their own or a partner's program to evaluate whether it functions as intended. They identify at least one issue, revise the code to address it, and add comments explaining the change. Students then complete a brief peer-review checklist describing what works well and what could be improved.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students record pass/fail counts and time‑on‑task for each test case before and after debugging, then compute measures of center and variability to describe improvement. They present a simple before and after chart and explain how the summarized results verify that the revised code is more correct and usable.

math.standard: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.
math.description: Students treat a program routine as a function, and they design input–output tables to test edge cases and typical cases. Mismatches flag bugs to fix. After debugging, they rerun the same table to demonstrate that each input now deterministically produces the correct output.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students author a one‑page developer note that explains the major defects discovered, the debugging steps taken, and the rationale for code changes, embedding short code excerpts as evidence. They revise the note after peer feedback to improve precision and clarity, ensuring documentation accurately reflects the final program.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 7 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Pairs lead a brief code‑review conversation using sentence starters such as "I notice…," "I wonder…," "Consider renaming…," and so on. They capture agreed‑upon action items and prioritize fixes. They implement one high‑impact suggestion and demonstrate how the change improved correctness, readability, or user experience.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Teams compare two debugging approaches (e.g., print‑statement tracing vs. input partitioning) on the same bug set, logging defects found and time to fix. They select the approach that produced better results and justify their choice with the collected testing data.

science.standard: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
science.description: Students create a lightweight test model (e.g., task list, expected results, acceptance criteria) and use it to drive multiple debug–retest cycles. They show how the model produces consistent evidence that the program improved with each iteration.

other.standard: Compare deliberative processes used by a wide variety of groups in various settings.
other.description: Students adopt a simple code‑review protocol (e.g., roles, timebox, criteria) and reflect on how structured deliberation leads to fair decisions about what to fix first. They document one instance where the process helped resolve a disagreement and improved the final code.

other.standard: Apply relevant criteria to examine, reflect on, and plan revisions for a work of art or design in progress.
other.description: Students work in pairs to develop criteria to evaluate the user interface design of each other's programs. After revising based on the critique, they present side‑by‑side screenshots and a short rationale explaining how the feedback improved the piece, just as artists refine a work before exhibition.

standards.statement: Refine a computing technology based on user feedback to improve its usability and accessibility.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should discuss user feedback with peers, consider the needs of diverse users, and identify which suggestions would most improve a computing technology's usability or accessibility. Students should focus on developing awareness of others' needs and incremental improvement.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform formal audits or implement complex accessibility frameworks.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students conduct a quick usability test of a prototype for a simple app (e.g., a homework tracker) by running classmates through two short tasks while using a think‑aloud script. Testers note barriers related to readability and access (e.g., tiny text, low contrast, unclear labels, no keyboard‑only path) on sticky notes and a one‑page checklist. Designers revise their prototype to address the top feedback items and annotate the changes directly on the mockup. Groups then demo before and after task flows and explain how revisions improved usability and accessibility for more users.

Students build or import a basic project (e.g., quiz, clicker game) and recruit three peer "users" to complete a task while timing success and logging pain points on a short feedback form. Using the data, teams implement at least three accessibility and usability refinements (e.g., larger fonts and color‑contrast checks, clearer instructions, keyboard controls, reduced motion, alt text for sprites and images). They retest the same task with new peers and compare success rate and time‑on‑task before and after. Each team submits a brief changelog with screenshots highlighting the specific feedback that drove each improvement.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Reporting the number of observations.
math.description: Students collect task‑completion times and success rates from user tests (baseline vs. revised build), then compute measures of center and variability to describe improvement. They present a simple before and after chart and explain how the summarized data shows that the program became more usable and accessible.

math.standard: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
math.description: Students calculate percent change in errors, task success, and time‑on‑task after implementing accessibility fixes (e.g., +25% successful attempts, −40% average time). They interpret these changes to evaluate whether refinements meaningfully improved the program for users.

ela.standard: With some guidance and support from peers and adults, develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach, focusing on how well purpose and audience have been addressed.
ela.description: Students write a brief design rationale explaining how specific user feedback led to concrete revisions (e.g., labels, contrast, input methods) that improved usability and accessibility. They revise the rationale after peer review to clarify evidence and strengthen claims about the program's improvement.

ela.standard: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate.
ela.description: Students integrate information presented in different media or formats. They synthesize feedback forms, observation notes, and test videos to identify the highest‑impact barriers users faced. They produce a two‑paragraph summary that integrates these sources to justify which program refinements most improved access.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare two alternative interface changes (e.g., color‑contrast palette A vs. B, on‑screen buttons vs. keyboard controls) using the same usability criteria and user tasks. They select the better option based on test evidence and explain how it improves accessibility for more users.

science.standard: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
science.description:
Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed tool.
Students define a mini test plan (e.g., tasks, success criteria, timing) as a model for gathering consistent feedback on their program. They iterate, retest, and use the generated data to justify how modifications improved usability and access.

other.standard: Assess specific rules and laws (both actual and proposed) as means of addressing public problems.
other.description: Students research basic digital accessibility expectations (e.g., captions, readable contrast, keyboard navigation) and connect them to the idea of equitable access in public services. They then document how specific refinements to their program align with inclusive policy goals for broader participation.

other.standard: Apply relevant criteria to examine, reflect on, and plan revisions for a work of art or design in progress.
other.description: Students generate a short, student‑friendly accessibility and usability rubric (e.g., readability, clarity, navigation) and use it to critique and refine their program's interface. They present side‑by‑side screenshots and briefly justify how the applied criteria guided their revisions.

standards.statement: Evaluate a computing technology's alignment with design specifications and responsible design values, including its correctness, effectiveness, and user experience.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should systematically evaluate a computing technology that they or someone else created to determine whether it functions correctly, aligns with original design specifications, and reflects responsible design values. For example, a student might test a range of inputs to verify accuracy and reliability, examine edge cases, and assess usability, accessibility, clarity, and overall user experience. Students should compare the completed project to the intended features and purpose to confirm alignment.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use formal verification methods or master industry-specific tools.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given a "specification sheet" for a school vending machine that outlines the requirements (e.g., must accept coins, must display calories, must be easily accessible). They are then shown three different "designs" (sketches/descriptions). Students must evaluate which design aligns best with the specifications and which best embodies responsible design values (e.g., is the coin slot at a height accessible to someone in a wheelchair?).

Using a simple Study Timer app that they had previously coded, along with the original project proposal (design specifications), students perform a self-evaluation: (1) Does the timer actually count down accurately (correctness)? (2) Does the alarm sound even if the screen is off (effectiveness)? (3) Is the interface distracting or helpful (UX)? (4) Does the app collect unnecessary data about the user (responsible design)?

math.standard: Attend to precision.
math.description: Students calculate compound interest and loan amortization using a teacher-provided pseudocode and a program. Students verify that the program works as intended, decide whether the algorithm uses an efficient formula, and evaluate how the results are presented.

ela.standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words in order to address a question or solve a problem.
ela.description: Using a teacher-provided technical specification document (text) and the finished software product (media), students write a comparative critique that evaluates how accurately the functional program represents the written requirements.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students evaluate a software simulation used for environmental modeling (such as a climate change predictor). They check for scientific accuracy (correctness) and analyze the underlying data sets for potential geographic or socioeconomic bias (responsible design/impacts).

other.standard: Evaluate public policies in terms of intended and unintended outcomes, and related consequences.
other.description: Students analyze the ethical implications of using algorithmic decision-making in public policy, such as software used for jury selection or resource allocation. They evaluate how responsible design values (transparency, fairness, and accountability) could be used to prevent unintended systemic bias in these civic processes.

standards.statement: Refine a computing technology based on user feedback, testing results, and responsible design values to improve its effectiveness and impact.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use testing results and user feedback to make meaningful refinements to a computing technology's functionality, usability, accessibility, accuracy, and efficiency, but not necessarily all at the same time. For example, a student might add a help command, simplify instructions, or adjust text size and contrast to improve readability and accessibility.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to correct every functional or user-related issue or achieve full optimization.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a simple board game and have another group play it. The designers watch without helping, noting where players argue over rules (functionality) or struggle to read the board (accessibility). Students then patch the game by rewriting rules and redesigning the board based on these testing results.

Students create a digital flashcard app. They perform two tests: (1) a stress test to see if the app crashes with 1,000 cards (efficiency and accuracy), and (2) a "user interview" during which they ask a classmate to find the Shuffle button (usability). Students then refine the code by optimizing the shuffle algorithm and changing the button color and/or size to improve accessibility for users with low vision.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students test a computing technology (e.g., a website or app) by gathering user feedback and performance data (e.g., time to complete a task, navigation errors). They evaluate the results using criteria such as usability and efficiency, then refine the design to improve performance and user experience, explaining how trade-offs influenced their revisions.

other.standard: Analyze how people use and challenge local, state, national, and international laws to address a variety of public issues.
other.description: Students revise a computing technology after gathering feedback from diverse users (e.g., improving color contrast, language clarity, or navigation). They explain how their changes address accessibility, fairness, or potential bias, and how refining the technology can better support different communities.

standards.statement: Use collected data to help answer questions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should collect data to answer a question about a grade-appropriate topic involving two to three variables. Having students wonder about the world to create questions to answer is appropriate. Collecting simple survey data or recording measurements and creating graphs as a class in order to answer a question are also appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to work independently. Students are not required to use digital tools or collect large sets of data.

implementation_examples.description: Students collect weather data daily by looking outside and putting a check next to the type of weather (e.g., sunny, windy, rainy, snowy). Students determine the type of clothing and activities for outside recess and lessons based on the data they collected about the weather.

Upon receiving a list of three ice cream flavors, students put an X next to their favorite, creating a bar graph. After the students have recorded their answers, they determine which flavor was chosen most often or least often.

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Students sort weather days into categories like sunny days and non-sunny days. They then count how many good weather days there were and compare it to the number of bad weather days.

math.standard: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).
math.description: Students write the numbers 0 through 20, each on its own line. They then collect information from each of their classmates (e.g., number of siblings they have, how many teeth they have lost).

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions in order to seek help, get information, or clarify something that is not understood.
ela.description: Students ask questions of their peers or adults to collect data and then look at the data to answer a question (e.g., they ask peers what their favorite pizza topping is to determine what to buy for the class party).

ela.standard: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.
ela.description: Students describe daily weather conditions based on data they have collected about the weather using appropriate vocabulary to describe the weather.

science.standard: Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time.
science.description: Students observe and share current local weather conditions. As a class, they record the observations (e.g., sunny, rainy, cloudy, temperature) on a chart and use the collected data to look for patterns over time.

other.standard: Child analyzes results, draws conclusions, and communicates results.
other.description: Each morning during calendar time, students place an icon (e.g., coat, sweater, T-shirt) on a calendar based on what they wore because of the weather. On Friday, students look at the calendar and use the data they collected to answer the question "Was it a coat week or a sweater week?"

other.standard: Child shows interest in and curiosity about the world around them.
other.description: Looking at a chart with the categories of bunny, hamster, and fish, each student adds a sticky dot to the category of their favorite. Students then count the number of dots in each category to answer the question.

standards.statement: Use multiple methods to collect both numeric and non-numeric data to help answer questions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use different ways (e.g., observation, measurement, surveys) to gather numbers and descriptive words to help answer questions. For example, students might ask their classmates about their favorite fruit (descriptive words) or measure the height of a bean plant in cubes or with a ruler (numeric data).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to analyze or organize data into complex charts. Students are not required to use digital tools or formal statistical methods.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a whole-class survey about their favorite fruit. The teacher writes fruit options (e.g., apple, banana, orange, grapes) on chart paper. Each student states their choice, and the teacher records responses using tally marks. The teacher also writes down descriptive words students use to explain their choice (e.g., "sweet," "juicy," "crunchy"). After collecting data, students count the tallies together and discuss which fruit is most and least popular. They compare the numeric results with the descriptive words collected to help determine what is the favorite fruit of the class. Students then copy the tally chart into their journals and draw pictures to represent the results.

During a supervised nature walk, students collect leaves and observe their characteristics (e.g., color, shape, texture), recording descriptive words about each leaf. Back in the classroom, students measure the length of their leaves using cubes or a ruler and count how many leaves fall into each category (numeric data). Using a tablet with a simple graphing app or digital drawing tool, in groups students create a pictograph using digital leaf stamps or icons to represent their data. Groups present their digital pictograph to the class, explaining both the numbers and the descriptive characteristics they recorded (e.g., "We found five green leaves, and most were smooth and small.").

math.standard: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.
math.description: Students ask a question such as "Which classroom object is the longest?" They measure several objects using a string or linking cubes and record the lengths (numeric data). They also describe the objects using words (e.g., "long," "short," "about the same length") (non-numeric data). Students then order three objects by length and use one object as a reference to indirectly compare the lengths of two others.

math.standard: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.
math.description: Students ask a class question such as "Which snack do you like best?" (e.g., apples, crackers, yogurt). They collect responses using a survey (non-numeric data) and record tallies for each category (numeric data). Students organize the results into a simple class graph and answer questions such as "How many students chose apples?" "How many more students chose crackers than yogurt?" "How many total responses were recorded?"

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
ela.description: After reading a short informational text (e.g., about animals, about weather), students ask and answer questions about key details from the text (e.g., "What does the animal eat?" "Where does the animal live?"). The class records the answers on chart paper, using tallies or simple counts to organize repeated details.

ela.standard: Describe people, places, things, and events with relevant details, expressing ideas and feelings clearly.
ela.description: After collecting and organizing class data (e.g., favorite fruits, weather observations), students orally describe their findings to the class using relevant details (e.g., "Five students chose apples. Apples were the most popular fruit."). Students practice speaking clearly and explaining what the data shows.

science.standard: Use materials to design a solution to a human problem by mimicking how plants and/or animals use their external parts to help them survive, grow, and meet their needs.
science.description: Students are challenged to solve the problem of retrieving a marble from a deep, narrow crack in the floor. Through observation or by watching a video, students collect data on how a woodpecker gets food, creating a tally chart to count how many times the bird pecks in a minute and drawing a detailed diagram of the shape of the beak. Using the data, students create a device that will work like the woodpecker's beak to solve the problem.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: After noticing bottles in the trash at lunch, students ask questions and gather information in two ways: they count how many bottles are thrown away each day (numeric data) and record descriptive observations about the bottles (e.g., plastic or metal, full or empty, found near which tables) (non-numeric data). Using both types of data, students define a recycling problem and suggest improvements to their collection system.

standards.statement: Compare numeric and non-numeric types of data in terms of how they are collected and what information they provide.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should compare how numeric (quantitative) data can be used for math and measurement and non-numeric (categorical) data can be used to sort, group, and describe. Having students identify the kinds of pets the class has (non-numeric data), count the total number of pets in each category (numeric data), and make simple comparisons (e.g., more students have cats vs dogs) is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform more sophisticated data transformations or analyses, nor are students expected to identify finer-grained data types (e.g., integers, characters). Students are not required to use technology to collect or compare different types of data.

implementation_examples.description: Students collect, organize, and analyze simple classroom or environmental data (e.g., favorite colors, types of pets, insects in the schoolyard). They identify which data is numeric (counts, totals) and which is non-numeric (categories, labels). They use both to draw conclusions.

In a citizen science project tracking local weather, students record descriptive observations (e.g., "cloudy," "windy," "humid") as non-numeric data and measure temperature or rainfall amounts as numeric data. Students compare how the descriptive data helps describe conditions, and the numeric data allows for measurement and comparison over time.

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students collect classroom data (e.g., favorite colors). They identify the colors as non-numeric categories and the vote counts as numeric data. They then use this data to create a bar graph, explicitly labeling the parts of the graph as representing numeric or non-numeric information.

ela.standard: Recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
ela.description: As a pre-writing or research step, students formulate a question about a story's characters (e.g., "Which character is the bravest?"). They survey classmates, collecting character names (non-numeric) and vote counts (numeric). Students then use both the text evidence and the collected data to help answer the question in their writing.

science.standard: Make observations of plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.
science.description: When observing a schoolyard habitat, students gather data on the living things they find. They record the types of insects or plants (non-numeric data) and the count for each type (numeric data). They then compare their findings, discussing how both types of data are needed to understand the habitat's diversity.

standards.statement: Evaluate numeric and non-numeric data for accuracy and completeness.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on checking for missing data and recognizing data that seems unreasonable (e.g., values that are much too large or much too small, data that is the wrong type). Students may use a survey to collect data that they record on a chart. Students may also use data supplied by the teacher.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create complex graphs or work with large datasets. Students are not required to use technology for collection, recording, or evaluation of data.

implementation_examples.description: In small groups, students create a survey and tally chart to record students' favorite within a category (e.g., color, food, holiday). Students then ask their classmates the question they created and record the answers on the tally chart. After all data is collected, they update the total tally count for each option. Groups swap tally charts and look for missing data (e.g., fewer tally marks than students in the class) and data that seems inaccurate (e.g., total tally count does not equal the tally marks, more total tally marks than there are students). Students answer questions about the data posed by the teacher(e.g., "Which is the most popular?" "Which is the least popular?").

Students look at a teacher-provided dataset that has missing and invalid data (e.g., a bar graph of the average temperatures for the last two years with one month missing, a bar graph with one month being way too high a temperature or way too low a temperature). Students are asked to look at the data and work with a partner to figure out what data might be missing, what data might be incorrect, and why they think that.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: After students collect data about their classmates' favorites, they draw a scaled bar graph to represent the results. The teacher or their peers then ask one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" questions using information presented in the graph.

math.standard: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units— whole numbers, halves, or quarters.
math.description: Students measure the growth of a plant over time and create a line plot of the measurements. Then they could check the numeric data collected for anything missing (e.g., a day that a measurement wasn't done) and problems with accuracy (e.g., the plant appears to have shrunk from one day to the next).

ela.standard: Form and use regular and irregular plural nouns.
ela.description: Students work independently or in small groups to list as many plural nouns as they can remember and sort them into regular and irregular categories. As a class, they can review the lists to identify inaccuracies (e.g., a word placed in the wrong category) or incompleteness (e.g., missing examples). Students discuss how checking for errors and missing information improves the accuracy and completeness of their data.

science.standard: Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season.
science.description: Students are provided with a dataset showing average seasonal weather conditions (e.g., temperature, precipitation). They create a table or bar graph to represent the data. Before describing the typical weather for that season, students review the dataset to check for missing values, incorrect units (e.g., mixing inches and centimeters), or unreasonable measurements (e.g., extremely high temperatures). They discuss how identifying inaccuracies and incomplete data affects their ability to describe typical seasonal weather accurately.

science.standard: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence that plants and animals have traits inherited from parents and that variation of these traits exists in a group of similar organisms.
science.description: Students examine a completed dataset showing traits of a group of plants or animals (e.g., leaf shape, height, fur color, ear length). They organize the information into a table and check for missing entries, mislabeled traits, or inconsistent measurements. Students discuss how incomplete or inaccurate data affects their interpretation of similarities and differences among organisms and whether the evidence supports conclusions about inherited traits and variation.

standards.statement: Organize collected data into tables using digital tools, with rows representing records and columns representing attributes.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should practice organizing small sets of collected or provided data into simple tables, ensuring that each row represents one record (e.g., a survey respondent, a pet) and each column represents an attribute (e.g., age, favorite color, type of animal). Students may use paper-based tables and templates prior to using digital tools for this work.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design complex databases, manage large datasets, or use advanced spreadsheet functions. Students do not need to understand relational databases, formulas, or data visualization techniques.

implementation_examples.description: Working in small groups, students receive raw school lunch participation data (number of students buying lunch each day for one month) from the cafeteria. Groups use a digital tool to create a table where each row represents one school day and columns include date, day of week, number of hot lunches sold, and number of cold lunches sold. Students determine appropriate column headers based on the available data. Groups then use their organized table to calculate which day of the week has the highest lunch participation and present their findings to the class, explaining how organizing the data into a table helped them identify the pattern.

Working in pairs, students research three different animals and their defensive structures using provided texts or digital resources. Using a spreadsheet tool, pairs create a table with columns for "Animal," "External Structure for Defense," and "How It Helps Survival." Each row represents one animal (e.g., "Turtle," "Hard Shell," "Protects from predators by allowing turtle to retreat inside"). After completing their table, pairs compare their data with another pair to identify patterns in how animals use external structures for defense. Each pair selects one animal and explains to the class how organizing the information in the spreadsheet helped them analyze the connection between structure and survival.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots. For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
math.description: Students create a line plot. First, students measure various classroom objects to the nearest 1/4 inch. They then organize their collected measurement data into a structured table with columns for "Object" and "Length (inches)" and create the line plot showing how many objects they found for each fractional length.

ela.standard: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
ela.description: After reading an informational text (e.g., about animal habitats, about weather patterns), students extract key facts and organize them into a digital table, with each row representing one animal or location and each column representing an attribute (e.g., habitat, diet, average temperature). Students then interpret the organized table and explain how structuring the information in rows and columns helps them better understand the relationships and key details presented in the text.

science.standard: Construct an argument that plants and animals have internal and external structures that function to support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction.
science.description: During a study of plant or animal structures, students organize their observations into a digital table. Each row represents one organism (record), and each column represents a structure or trait (attribute), such as roots, thorns, fur, or wings. Students use the organized table to identify patterns and construct an argument explaining how specific internal and external structures support survival, growth, behavior, or reproduction.

standards.statement: Use digital tools to collect and organize different types of data.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should demonstrate their ability to use digital tools to collect (e.g., surveys, sensors) and organize (e.g., spreadsheets) data. Students should collect and distinguish between quantitative (numeric) and qualitative (descriptive and non-numeric) data. When organizing the data, students should use a computational tool to efficiently sort and group similar data (e.g., sort from highest to lowest temperature, sort non-numeric responses alphabetically).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create their own data collection tools from scratch. Students are not required to create data visualizations or to analyze or interpret the data collected.

implementation_examples.description: Working in pairs, students use a microcontroller to collect environmental data in different classroom locations over one school day. Students program their microcontroller to record temperature and light levels at three different times. Pairs export the collected data into a spreadsheet and organize it with columns for location, time, temperature, and light level. Students sort their data from highest to lowest temperature to identify the warmest location in the classroom. Pairs share their organized data and explain one observation, such as which area has the most light or how temperature changes throughout the day.

Working in small groups, students use tablets to observe and record traffic near their school for one week. Groups collect numeric data (number of vehicles), categorical data (type of vehicle, e.g., car, bus, truck), and yes/no data (crosswalk usage). Students organize their observations in a shared spreadsheet with columns for date, time, vehicle count, vehicle type, and crosswalk usage. Groups analyze their data to identify one pattern or safety concern and share their findings with the class.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students use the temperature or light level data collected with microcontrollers to create line plots showing measurements over time, then analyze the data using mathematical operations to find differences between highest and lowest readings or calculate average values.

ela.standard: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
ela.description: For a research project, students use a tool like a school library database or a teacher-provided spreadsheet of websites. They use the tool's sort and filter features to collect and organize their sources (e.g., by filtering to show only articles from the last five years, sorting sources by author).

science.standard: Develop a model using an example to describe ways the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and/or atmosphere interact.
science.description: Students use spreadsheet tools to organize the data from a teacher-provided public weather dataset (e.g., temperature, precipitation, wind speed) by sorting and filtering (e.g., filtering for days with high precipitation and then sorting by temperature). Using the organized data, students identify patterns that help them describe interactions between Earth systems, such as how precipitation (hydrosphere) relates to temperature (atmosphere).

standards.statement: Evaluate how different levels of precision and granularity in data collection affect accuracy, storage, and analysis.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explain the difference between precision and granularity in data collection and evaluate how these choices affect data accuracy, storage requirements, and interpretation. Students should identify and explain situations in which higher precision or granularity might be more important. For example, students might compare tracking daily step counts (lower granularity, less storage) versus tracking steps every minute (higher granularity, more storage) or recording ages in years (lower precision) versus years and months (higher precision). Comparing medical monitoring data (requiring high precision and granularity for patient safety) with casual fitness tracking data (where lower precision and granularity are sufficient) is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to collect data at varying precision or granularity levels. Students are not expected to understand the technical details of data collection processes.

implementation_examples.description: To experience how data precision and granularity affect conclusions, students test two different paper airplane designs. First, they use a low-precision, low-granularity method by flying each plane once and estimating the distance using floor tiles or whole feet. Then they use a higher-precision, higher-granularity method by flying each plane five times and measuring the exact distance in centimeters for each trial. Students calculate the average distance for each design and compare how the level of precision and number of data points influence their confidence in determining which plane flew farther.

Students use a pedometer or activity app to measure their steps over the course of a week, collecting total steps for each student for each day of the week. Students enter their hourly totals into two separate spreadsheets, one collecting hourly data and one collecting daily data. Hourly data is represented in a line graph, and daily data is represented in a bar graph. Students will evaluate which level of granularity and precision is needed for determining which day a student is most active versus determining what time of day a student is most active.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students collect the same data at different levels of granularity (e.g., measuring plant growth daily vs. weekly) and then summarize each data set using measures of center and variability to quantitatively evaluate how the granularity impacts the interpretation of the plant's growth trend.

math.standard: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.
math.description: Students analyze how changing the precision of measurements (e.g., rounding to the nearest inch vs. quarter-inch) in a proportional relationship, such as a scale model, affects the accuracy of the calculated result for the full-sized object.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 7 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students participate in a collaborative debate. They clearly express and defend their choice of precision and granularity for a data collection project, building on and challenging each other's ideas about the trade-offs between accuracy, storage, and interpretability.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write a short argumentative paragraph defending their chosen level of precision and granularity for a specific data collection task, using evidence about the impacts on accuracy, storage, and interpretation to support their claim.

science.standard: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
science.description: Using performance data from tests of a prototype collected at different levels of precision and granularity (e.g., one dataset with single trial measurements in whole centimeters and another with multiple trials measured to the nearest millimeter), students compare the datasets to evaluate how precision and granularity influence their ability to identify patterns and determine effective design modifications.

science.standard: Use mathematical representations to describe a simple model for waves that includes how the amplitude of a wave is related to the energy in a wave.
science.description: Students use sound wave sensor software to collect data at different sampling rates (granularity) and bit depths (precision), then analyze how these choices affect the accuracy and file size of the recorded waveform used for their mathematical representations.

other.standard: Apply visual organizational strategies to design and produce a work of art, design, or media that clearly communicates information or ideas.
other.description: Students create a data-driven artwork (e.g., an infographic) where they must strategically choose the precision and granularity of the included data to balance visual clarity (interpretation) with the accurate communication of their intended idea.

other.standard: Evaluate the relevancy and utility of a historical source based on information such as maker, date, place of origin, intended audience, and purpose.
other.description: Students analyze census records or population data from different historical periods, evaluating how the precision of data collection (e.g., occupational categories) and the granularity of the data (e.g., city-level vs. national-level figures) affect the utility and relevance of those sources for answering specific historical questions.

standards.statement: Explain how data and its associated metadata can be used to answer questions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to explain how data and metadata serve different but complementary purposes when answering questions. Students should understand that metadata is data about data (i.e., it provides context that helps interpret the primary data content). For example, a photo's image data shows what was captured, whereas its metadata (e.g., timestamp, location, camera settings) provides context about when, where, and how the photo was taken. Students should be able to use computational tools to view metadata (e.g., viewing file properties, examining web page source code). Students should recognize that metadata can be collected automatically without their explicit knowledge (e.g., their phone adding location and time data to photos).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand technical standards for metadata formats or structures. Students are not required to focus on any particular metadata tool or to manually create or edit metadata fields. Students are not expected to provide exhaustive lists of all possible metadata types for different file formats.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to examine a set of digital artifacts, such as photos, documents, or web pages, and use built-in tools to view both the data and its associated metadata. Each group identifies questions that can be answered using the primary data (e.g., what is shown) and questions that require metadata (e.g., when or where it was created). Students discuss how the metadata changes or deepens their interpretation of the data and note cases where metadata may be collected automatically. To demonstrate understanding, students create a brief explanation or annotated example showing how data and metadata together can be used to answer a specific question.

Students examine a screenshot of a news article or social media post along with its metadata (e.g., publication date, author, URL, geolocation tag). Students identify which questions can be answered by the content itself and which require metadata (e.g., "Who wrote this?" "When was it published?"). They discuss how missing or misleading metadata might affect credibility and explain how metadata helps determine whether information is current or reliable.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.
math.description: Students examine a dataset alongside contextual information such as units, time collected, or location and explain how that metadata affects which mathematical questions can be accurately answered.
