other.description: To lessen the noise during readaloud time, students use an app that visually shows on the screen how noisy it is. They look at the data (e.g., needle moving into the "red" zone, balls bouncing wildly on the screen) and use it to make the decision to use "whisper voices" so everyone can hear the story.

standards.statement: Distinguish between data collection approaches, including those that may lead to inaccurate or biased data.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should articulate how different ways of gathering data could affect different people or communities they are familiar with (e.g., classroom, family, school, neighborhood). Students should identify which communities might be unfairly represented or left out by specific data collection methods. Students should compare similar approaches to describe how they might produce different results. Students should connect these differences to real-world situations where biased data collection could lead to unfair decisions for their community.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to analyze data at this stage. Students are not required to collect data.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students compare two proposed methods for determining which lunch foods students like best: surveying students only during the first lunch period and surveying all classes in the school. They identify advantages and drawbacks of each method and discuss which groups of students might be left out or unfairly represented. Students explain how the choice of method could affect the results and lead to unfair decisions.

Using a simple digital polling tool or a shared spreadsheet, the class records their favorite pets. The teacher intentionally "skips" recording the answers of students who like cats to show how missing data makes the final chart inaccurate. Students work in pairs to identify the error on the screen and explain how leaving out certain responses changes the results and could lead to an unfair conclusion.

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students create a graph based on a survey where they asked only their best friends, noticing that the results don't match what the whole class thinks. They then survey the rest of the class and redraw the graph, learning that gathering data from the whole group makes the picture "true" for everyone.

math.standard: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.
math.description: Students compare measurements taken with variable nonstandard units (like body parts) versus standard tools, identifying that the lack of consistency in the former creates measurement bias. They conclude that using standardized tools is a critical data collection strategy to ensure that results are accurate and comparable across the class.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or book they are writing about, state an opinion, supply reasons that support the opinion, use linking words (e.g., because, and, also) to connect opinion and reasons, and provide a concluding statement or section.
ela.description: The teacher presents a new policy (e.g., "Recess is cancelled because Table 1 prefers reading.") based on a survey of that single group, prompting students to identify this data collection approach as unfair (biased). Students write an opinion piece arguing that the decision is unfair, supporting their claim by explaining that valid rules require gathering input from the whole community.

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to clarify comprehension, gather additional information, or deepen understanding of a topic or issue.
ela.description: In response to a "news reporter" making a big claim (e.g., "The whole school loves broccoli!") based on hidden data, students act as news editors and ask clarifying questions (e.g., "Who exactly did you ask?" or "How many people?") to reveal that the reporter only asked one person, identifying the data collection approach as biased.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.
science.description: Students test two ways to vote for a class reward: "raising hands" versus "secret ballot box." They compare the results and find that the box is a better tool because it lets people be honest without copying their friends, creating more accurate data.

science.standard: Plan and conduct an investigation to describe and classify different kinds of materials by their observable properties.
science.description: Students test the hardness of a material by pressing it gently versus scratching it firmly, discovering that inconsistent testing methods lead to inaccurate data. They decide on a standardized data collection approach (e.g., "Everyone uses the same scratch tool.") so their scientific classification is fair and reliable.

other.standard: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions while responding attentively to others when addressing ideas and making decisions as a group.
other.description: During a presentation by a guest speaker, students practice "passing the microphone" to ensure that quiet students get a turn, not just the ones who always volunteer. They learn that if we don't hear everyone's voice (collect all data), our group decision won't be fair to the community.

other.standard: Describe roles and responsibilities of people in authority.
other.description: Looking at a new rule based on a survey of only one table group of students, the class identifies the rule as biased and unfair. Students describe the leader's responsibility to collect input from the whole group, expressing that a fair authority figure ensures their decisions reflect the needs of the entire community.

standards.statement: Design a data collection process that addresses the needs of people from different backgrounds or groups.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should consider different data collection plans and how they would affect accuracy and representation. Students' plans should include what data to gather, which tools to use, and which sources to access for an investigation. Tools like class surveys or tally charts marking observations are appropriate. Students should identify different groups and describe how they would be affected by different data collection strategies. Students can obtain consent by including an opt-out box for the survey a student is designing. Students should learn that they have a right to tell authority figures (e.g., teachers, website) that they don't want to share their information.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not required to use advanced data collection techniques or statistics. Students are not required to consider the ethics associated with data collection or design a process for more than two or three variables.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students evaluate different aspects of sample data collection strategies, such as two versions of a simple class survey question (e.g., "What's your favorite sport?" vs. "Do you play soccer, basketball, or baseball?") or two collection techniques (e.g., tallying what people are playing at recess vs. asking classmates which sport they like best) and discuss how each might affect who feels included and what data is captured.

In small groups, students design a simple data collection plan to address a class need (e.g., which new book to add to the classroom library). They explain why their chosen method (e.g., survey, tally, sticky notes) would be fair and representative.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: In small groups, students design a survey to collect data about how fellow students get to school, ensuring they include categories for walkers, bus riders, car riders, and those using mobility aids or bikes. Using the data collected from their inclusive design, students produce a scaled bar graph and explain how having specific, inclusive categories enabled them to accurately represent every student in the group.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons.
ela.description: Students design a data collection plan (e.g., survey on paper, using a polling app that collects information from all of their classmates) to find out their classmates' opinions on a school issue. After collecting the data using their inclusive design, they write an opinion piece arguing for a change based on the "fair" data they gathered from everyone in the class.

science.standard: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.
science.description: Students plan and carry out a fair comparison of two data collection methods (e.g., surveying only one class vs. surveying multiple classes). They control other variables (same question, same response options) and examine how the method affects representation. Students identify failure points in each approach (e.g., certain groups being left out) and propose improvements to create a more inclusive data collection process.

other.standard: Identify the beliefs, experiences, perspectives, and values that underlie their own and others' points of view about civic issues.
other.description: In a whole-class discussion, students identify different groups in their community (e.g., elderly people, younger children, non-English speakers). They then work in small groups to design a process for the town to collect data on a new library's hours, ensuring their process respects the different schedules and needs of each group identified.

standards.statement: Investigate how data collected about people may affect individuals and groups.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should investigate simple scenarios to identify who is affected by data collection and what the effect is, including concerns about privacy and fairness. Students should ask clarifying questions (e.g., "Who is collecting this information?" "What information are they collecting?" "Why do they need it?"). Students should identify who is affected, distinguishing between individuals and groups (e.g., the whole class). Students should describe what the effect is for the individuals and groups using simple, descriptive terms (e.g., "helpful," "harmful," "unfair"). Gathering facts and identifying clear effects rather than weighing pros and cons is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct formal research projects or make evaluative judgments about whether the data collection is overall good or bad. Students are not expected to understand the technical aspects of how data is collected online.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Working individually or in pairs, students complete a digital citizenship lesson that includes examples of websites and apps collecting personal data (e.g., location, search history, preferences). Using screenshots, short videos, or guided prompts, students identify what data is collected and who might use it. Students create a brief written response or participate in a class discussion explaining how this data collection could affect individuals and groups differently. Students also identify at least one action a person can take to protect their privacy.

As a whole class, students participate in a simulation where the teacher collects "data cards" representing personal information such as age, interests, or location. The class groups the data for different purposes (e.g., advertising, school planning, safety decisions) and discusses how the data might be used. Students explain how collecting and sharing the same data can have different effects on individuals and groups. Students reflect on which types of data should be shared and which should be protected.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots. For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
math.description: Working in pairs, students collect class-generated data about non-sensitive attributes (e.g., number of pets, time spent reading) and represent the data on a line plot. Students explain how the line plot shows patterns for groups while discussing how collecting, sharing, or misusing similar data about people could affect individuals and groups differently.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 4 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students engage in collaborative discussion with diverse partners about a teacher-posed scenario (e.g., "An app offers you 100 free coins, but you have to enter your name and email. What are the privacy concerns? What should you do?").

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans.
science.description: Students examine examples of data collected about people during emergencies (e.g., location data used for evacuation planning, shelter needs). They discuss how collecting this data can help protect communities while also considering how it might affect individuals differently.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students explore a scenario where a school collects data about students (e.g., lunch choices, transportation needs) to improve services. They compare different ways to collect the data and discuss how each approach might affect individuals or groups in fair or unfair ways.

standards.statement: Analyze the benefits and risks of computing technology that uses collected data.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should examine everyday technologies that rely on collected data (e.g., weather apps, fitness trackers, AI tools like voice assistants or recommendation systems) and identify both benefits (e.g., convenience, personalization, improved predictions) and risks (e.g., privacy concerns, inaccurate results, or bias).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand technical details of algorithms, machine learning model training, or data storage infrastructure. Students are not required to evaluate statistical methods, encryption, or policy frameworks.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students investigate a common AI-based tool (e.g., movie or music recommendation system). They first discuss the benefits of using data (e.g., it helps them quickly find shows or songs they might enjoy) and then explore potential risks (e.g., recommendations may reinforce the same choices, personal data could be misused). The class records their findings in a two-column chart labeled Benefits and Risks. To extend the activity, students write a short reflection explaining one way data-driven AI can improve people's lives and one way it might cause problems.

Working in small groups, students analyze printed scenario cards describing how everyday technologies (e.g., voice assistants, recommendation systems, school apps) use collected data. Using a T-chart, each group sorts examples of data use into benefits (e.g., personalization, convenience) and risks (e.g., privacy concerns, bias, errors). Groups share their charts and explain how the technology's use of data could help or harm individuals or groups. Students demonstrate understanding by justifying one benefit and one risk using evidence from the scenario.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Working in small groups, students collect measurements of a non-sensitive classroom variable (e.g., minutes classmates spend on a favorite app) and record the data in fractional units (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) to create a line plot. They use the plot to answer questions, then discuss one benefit (e.g., understanding overall app usage and identifying learning patterns) and one risk (e.g., highlighting individual behaviors that could create pressure if shared publicly) of this kind of data collection, connecting their analysis to computing technologies.

ela.standard: With some guidance and support from adults, use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of two pages in a single sitting.
ela.description: Working in small teams, students use a shared online document to collaboratively research and write a short guide on the benefits and risks of everyday computing technologies (e.g., fitness trackers, recommendation systems, voice assistants). Teams publish their document and explain how their research supports identifying one benefit and one risk of these computing technologies.

science.standard: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth’s resources and environment.
science.description: Students analyze how technologies that collect data (e.g., weather sensors, air-quality monitors, traffic cameras) help communities make safer and more sustainable decisions. They discuss both the benefits (e.g., better predictions, improved safety) and risks (e.g., privacy concerns, misuse of location data) of collecting and using this information.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students examine a problem (e.g., improving school safety, managing transportation) using data-collecting technologies. They analyze how collecting data can help solve the problem while also introducing risks, such as unfair use of data or over-collection of personal information.

standards.statement: Explain the benefits and risks of allowing personal data and metadata to be collected and used in datasets, including issues of data ownership, privacy, and sovereignty.
standards.boundary_includes:
Students should be able to explain the benefits and risks of allowing personal data and metadata to be collected by websites, apps, and other computing technologies. Students should understand that benefits may include personalized recommendations, improved services based on user data, or free access to platforms in exchange for data collection. Students should recognize risks including loss of privacy (e.g., location tracking, browsing history collection), unauthorized sale or sharing of personal data, and reduced control over how information is used (data ownership). Students should also understand basic concepts of data sovereignty, such as how data collected in one country may be stored or governed under another country's laws.
Students are not expected to understand technical data protection methods (e.g., encryption, secure protocols) or analyze specific legal frameworks (e.g., General Data Protection Regulation [GDPR], the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act [COPPA]). Students are not required to create technical explanations of cybersecurity systems or evaluate the technical adequacy of privacy policies.

implementation_examples.description: Students read a short story about a wearable fitness tracker. Working in groups, they list the benefits (e.g., tracking progress or motivating exercise) and the risks (e.g., companies sharing their health data).
Students explore the privacy settings of a sample social media account or mock app. They make decisions about which information to share and explain why.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Reporting the number of observations.
math.description: Students collect class survey data (e.g., favorite apps) and report the total number of responses collected. The teacher then introduces the idea that in addition to the survey responses, metadata (e.g., time submitted, device used, location) could also be collected, prompting discussion about how this additional data might be used and what risks it could pose.

ela.standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
ela.description: Students read an opinion piece about data privacy and identify the author's main claims and evidence.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students brainstorm improvements to devices that collect data (e.g., smart watches) to make them safer for users.

other.standard: Distinguish the powers and responsibilities of citizens, political parties, interest groups, and the media in a variety of governmental and nongovernmental contexts.
other.description: Students hold a debate on whether people should have ownership rights over data collected by companies.

standards.statement: Analyze how decisions made at different stages of working with data can lead to biased data, misleading conclusions, and compromised AI models.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to recognize that decisions made during data collection, data processing, data analysis, and data presentation all involve human choices and that those choices can, often unintentionally, introduce bias or distort results. Students should examine simple examples to identify how limitations or assumptions at different stages can affect interpretations and conclusions and how those same limitations may influence the performance of AI models trained on the data. Students should be able to explain how these limitations shape conclusions and outcomes.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not required to learn advanced statistical methods, the technical details of AI training algorithms, or programming-level solutions to bias. Students are not required to have deep knowledge of machine learning mathematics or data science processes.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a survey about favorite school lunches, but collect responses from only one grade level. They compare those results to a schoolwide dataset and identify how limiting data collection affected representation and conclusions. Students analyze how the initial decision about whom to survey introduced bias and discuss how using the smaller dataset to train a simple recommendation system (e.g., suggesting future lunch menus) could lead to unfair outcomes for other grade levels.

Students examine two graphs created from the same dataset, one with a consistent scale and one with a manipulated scale that exaggerates differences. They analyze how presentation choices influence interpretation and discuss how misleading visualizations could affect decision-making.

math.standard: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions. For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.
math.description: Students draw multiple random samples from a larger dataset (e.g., student preferences, school survey data) and calculate an estimate such as the mean or proportion. They compare how their estimates vary across samples and discuss how random sampling helps reduce bias. Students then examine a nonrandom (biased) sample and analyze how conclusions differ, explaining how data collection decisions can lead to misleading results.

ela.standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
ela.description: Students read a news article that uses data to support a claim and identify whether the data is presented fairly or in a misleading way.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students develop a simple model to test two competing design solutions (e.g., two website layouts, two survey formats). They generate test data by collecting user responses or simulated data and compare which design appears more effective. Students then analyze how biased test data (e.g., only testing one user group) could influence which solution seems "best" and revise their testing model to ensure more representative data before refining their design.

other.standard: Compare the central arguments in secondary works of history on related topics in multiple media.
other.description: Students analyze how graphs, charts, or polls in the news might be presented in ways that change public opinion.

standards.statement: Evaluate the societal, environmental, and ethical implications of large-scale data collection and processing, including AI applications.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to analyze and articulate the societal, environmental, and ethical trade-offs associated with large-scale data collection and processing. This includes evaluating issues such as individual privacy and consent, data sovereignty, algorithmic bias, the spread of misinformation, and the environmental impact of data centers. For example, students could evaluate a social media platform's data collection policy and discuss the ethical implications of using that data for targeted advertising.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform a formal legal or economic analysis of data policies or otherwise focus on the technical or legal specifics.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students hold a mock town hall meeting regarding the construction of a new Hyper-Scale Data Center in their community. Different students represent different interests: a local farmer concerned about water use (environmental), a tech worker focused on job opportunities (societal), and a privacy advocate concerned about the data being stored (ethical). Students must evaluate the proposal and suggest modifications.

Students use a large-scale AI image generator or chatbot and evaluate its outputs for bias. They investigate the origin of the training data and whether the original creators were compensated. They then write a brief Impact Report detailing the ethical concerns associated with using copyrighted work to train AI and the societal risks of AI-generated misinformation.

ela.standard: Integrate quantitative or technical analysis (e.g., charts, research data) with qualitative analysis in print or digital text.
ela.description: Students evaluate a news article or report that makes claims about large-scale data by critiquing the quantitative data and technical analysis presented. They then write a report that integrates their own qualitative analysis of the ethical implications alongside the technical information.

science.standard: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces impacts of human activities on natural systems.
science.description: In a science class, students evaluate the environmental impact of data centers and the digital infrastructure that supports large-scale data. They research a technological solution (e.g., more efficient cooling systems, renewable energy sourcing) and evaluate its effectiveness in reducing the environmental footprint, thereby applying engineering principles to a real-world problem.

standards.statement: Debate the efficacy of policies and regulations to ensure responsible data use.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of existing data policies and regulations. This could look like students researching a specific data privacy issue and preparing arguments for a classroom debate on whether a new law is needed to protect consumer data. Students should include the efficacy of social approaches (e.g., social movements, political resistance, personal behavioral change) aimed at shaping the design and use of computing systems.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to read the text of laws.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students debate the efficacy of a new teacher-proposed Classroom Data Policy that allows the teacher to read any student's digital notes at any time to "ensure focus." They discuss multiple topics (e.g., Does it actually improve learning? Is it an ethical violation? How would they "regulate" the teacher's access?).

Students use a site like Terms of Service; Didn't Read (tosdr.org) to compare the data policies of two major apps. They then debate whether the current "self-regulation" of these companies is enough to protect teens or if a government-mandated age verification law would be more efficacious, discussing the privacy trade-offs of such a law.

math.standard: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.
math.description: Students analyze a dataset related to data policy outcomes (e.g., number of reported data breaches over time and strength of state privacy laws, amount of consumer data collected and number of privacy complaints). They create a scatter plot to represent the relationship between the two variables and describe the pattern of association. Students use their analysis to evaluate claims about the effectiveness of data policies and incorporate this evidence into a structured classroom debate.

ela.standard: Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grades 11–12 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.
ela.description: Students use formal debate structures to present evidence-based arguments regarding the effectiveness of facial recognition bans in public spaces.

standards.statement: Examine the use of tools to accomplish tasks or solve problems for different users.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore and talk about how everyday tools, both digital and non-digital, help people complete activities. Students should also recognize that different tools are designed to solve specific problems for different people. Age-appropriate examples include using a pencil or pen to write, using a paintbrush or drawing app to create a picture, using a magnifying glass to see small things, or using an app on a tablet or physical book to read a story.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explain technical details about how the tools work or compare them based on efficiency. Students do not need to develop knowledge of specialized hardware, software, or design processes.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students examine a teacher-provided problem (e.g., needing to move a large pile of blocks) and sort different tools (e.g., a small spoon, a bucket, a toy truck) to decide which tool works best for each "user" (a small stuffed animal and a student) to solve the problem. To demonstrate understanding, students point to the chosen tool and verbally explain to a partner why that tool helps their specific user.

Students go on a hunt in their classroom to find objects (tools) that help them with things they need to do during the school day (e.g., pencils for writing, scissors for cutting, a tablet for learning games). They could then sort these tools by the problem they solve (e.g., tools for drawing, tools for building) and talk  with a peer or teacher about who uses each tool and why.

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Individually or in pairs, students examine and sort various tools in a bin and pictures of various users of those tools into categories based on the user they are best for. Students demonstrate understanding by creating a physical bar graph of the tools on the floor for each user and counting which category has the most tools.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about kindergarten topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: During circle time, students share experiences using different tools at home (e.g., a TV remote, a spoon, a tablet) and explain who in their family uses the tool and for what purpose.

ela.standard: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
ela.description: Students explore a variety of apps as examples of tools that let them express their ideas through writing and drawing.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students look at a simple problem (e.g., "How can we clean up toys faster?") and examine different tools people might use (e.g., bins, labels, carts). They discuss how different users (e.g., children, teachers, custodians) might need different tools to solve the same problem.

science.standard: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of pushes and pulls on the motion of an object.
science.description: Students explore tools like wagons, toy scoops, or ramps and observe how pushing or pulling helps move objects more easily. They discuss how these tools help different users (e.g., small children, adults) accomplish the same task in different ways.

other.standard: Child shows interest in and curiosity about the world around them.
other.description: Students explore classroom tools (e.g., scissors, crayons), use them appropriately, and talk about when people would want to use them.

other.standard: Child demonstrates increasing control, strength, and coordination of small muscles.
other.description: Students draw a picture (e.g., the sun, a flower, a person) with crayons, using the correct grip, and then with a drawing app They express how artists use each tool differently (e.g., pressing down, tapping) to complete the same task and state which tool they preferred.

standards.statement: Describe the purpose of basic hardware components of a computing system, using accurate terminology.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use correct academic language to both identify the name and explain the basic function of external computing system hardware (e.g., laptop computer, tablet device, keyboard, mouse). Expressing that a laptop or tablet is used to run apps to complete school work or relating that headphones are used to hear sounds on a device is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to identify or describe the function of internal computer system hardware. Students do not need to determine whether peripherals serve as input or output for a computing system.

implementation_examples.description: After students learn about computing system hardware (e.g., by reading a book, by watching a short video, by participating in a teacher-led lesson), students go on a scavenger hunt taking pictures of hardware and recording/writing about the function of the hardware component.

When using robots, students draw and label the sensors on a robot and describe the function of each sensor. They share their description with a peer. Alternatively, they make audio or video recordings of their description.

math.standard: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
math.description: In small groups, students use pattern blocks or 3D building blocks to build a model of a computer system using specific shapes to represent specific hardware (e.g., "Use a rectangular prism for the monitor and a smaller cube for the mouse."). Students explain which shapes they chose to represent each hardware component and describe that component's purpose.

ela.standard: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using frequently occurring conjunctions to signal simple relationships (e.g., because).
ela.description: Students create a drawing of a computing system and label its major components with appropriate terminology and then describe the function of each component.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 1 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: When working with a partner using robots, students discuss the parts of the robot and identify the sensors and what they do.

science.standard: Develop a simple sketch, drawing, or physical model to illustrate how the shape of an object helps it function as needed to solve a given problem.
science.description: Students work with peers to use their bodies to represent parts of a computing system and describe how their component part functions.

other.standard: Learners engage with new knowledge by following a process that includes generating products that illustrate learning.
other.description: Students create a video showing the components of a computing system and describing what each part does

standards.statement: Explain how the basic hardware components of a computing system work together to perform input and output (I/O) operations.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should use academic language to name components of a computing system, identify whether they are input or output components, and explain how the components work together to take in information from the real world and produce an action that can be seen or heard by people. Explaining input and output operations of components like keyboards, monitors/screens, microphones and sound sensors, headphones, speakers, webcams/cameras, printers, light sensors, sound sensors, and distance sensors is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explain the technical details (e.g., I/O ports and buses, data digitization) of how inputs and outputs work. Students do not need to explain processing and storage.

implementation_examples.description: When working with a partner using robots, students discuss which components, including sensors, are input components and how the input received from the components controls the output from the robot.

After a lesson, a read-aloud of an age-appropriate book, or an age-appropriate video on I/O operations, students work in groups to explain how data enters a computer, how it is processed, and how it produces output. They demonstrate input and output by creating computing components from craft materials or acting them out.

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students, working in groups, sort pictures of various computer parts and peripherals (e.g., keyboard, speaker, mouse, webcam) into two categories: input and output. Students then create a bar graph showing how many of each type they identified and explain their graph to the class or another group. In their explanation, they identify which category contains more hardware components and describe how a specific input device from their graph works with an output device to perform a task.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 2 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: Students create a drawing of a computing system, label its major components with the name of the component and whether it is input or output, and then explain to a peer or teacher how components work together to take in input and produce output.

science.standard: Develop a simple sketch, drawing, or physical model to illustrate how the shape of an object helps it function as needed to solve a given problem.
science.description: Students create a paper or cardboard model of a computing system from craft materials, designing each component to reflect its real-world shape (e.g., a keyboard with keys, a monitor with a screen surface). They explain how the shape of each component helps it perform its function and how the components work together to take in input and produce output to solve a specific problem (e.g., typing and displaying a message).

other.standard: Learners engage with new knowledge by following a process that includes generating products that illustrate learning.
other.description: Using puppets or computing components created from crafting materials, students work with a partner or in a small group to create a video showing how a computer takes in input and produces output.

standards.statement: Describe the role of software in a computing system to accomplish tasks or solve problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should understand that software consists of programs and applications that tell hardware what to do and that different types of software serve different purposes (e.g., word processors for writing, web browsers for accessing information, games for entertainment, educational apps for learning). Students identify common software applications and describe how they process specific user inputs (e.g., typing, clicking) into meaningful outputs (e.g., a document, a game action) to complete tasks.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students do not need to learn about operating system structures, cloud storage administration, or version control systems.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups with picture cards showing different computing tasks (e.g., writing a letter, drawing a picture, playing music, solving math problems, video chatting with family). Each group receives software cards (e.g., word processor, drawing app, music player, calculator app, video chat app) and matches each task to the appropriate software. Groups then discuss and record why each software is suited for its task, explaining: "To [accomplish task], we need [software] because it tells the computer to [specific function]." Groups share one example with the class.

Students use a computer to complete a multipart task, such as creating a digital card. They identify that they used the operating system software to find the apps and files they needed, including an app that lets them draw to create a picture for the card. They describe how the software turned their mouse movements into colors on the screen.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students use spreadsheet or graphing software to organize data they've collected (e.g., favorite lunch foods, number of pets) and create bar graphs or picture graphs. Students describe how the software's role is to help them organize numbers and create visual representations that would be difficult to draw by hand, making it easier to compare data and identify patterns.

math.standard: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students use calculator software or math apps to solve multistep word problems, explaining how the software's role is to perform calculations quickly and accurately, allowing them to focus on understanding the problem and determining which operations to use. They describe how the software accomplishes the computational task while they accomplish the problem-solving task.

ela.standard: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
ela.description: Students use word processing software to write narratives and name and save appropriately. Then they could describe why they used the software they did and how they named and organized the file they created.

ela.standard: Create engaging audio recordings of stories or poems that demonstrate fluid reading at an understandable pace; add visual displays when appropriate to emphasize or enhance certain facts or details.
ela.description: Students use audio recording and/or presentation software to create recordings with visual elements. They describe the role each software plays: recording software captures their voice clearly, and presentation software organizes images and text to enhance their message, with each telling the computer how to accomplish different tasks.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students examine a problem (e.g., "How can we share information with the class?") and identify how software (e.g., presentation tools, drawing apps, word processors) helps solve that problem. They discuss how software gives instructions to the computer so it can complete tasks people want to do.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare different types of software that can accomplish the same task (e.g., typing a story in a word processor vs. recording it with a voice-to-text app). They discuss how software choices affect how easily and effectively a computer can help solve a problem.

standards.statement: Apply basic troubleshooting processes to identify and fix common hardware and software issues.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on following a consistent set of steps (e.g., define, plan, try, reflect) to address common hardware and software issues such as a device not responding, no network access, or an app crashing. Students should apply basic troubleshooting strategies such as restarting the device, checking connections, or closing and reopening applications.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to solve all hardware and software issues they encounter. Students do not need to open devices to diagnose or troubleshoot internal hardware problems.

implementation_examples.description: Students encounter "broken" stations with nonfunctional setups (e.g., a keyboard unplugged from a computer, a tablet with the brightness turned all the way down, a low battery warning sign). Working in small groups, students use a printed troubleshooting checklist to diagnose the issue and propose a fix. Students complete a digital or paper "repair ticket" provided by the teacher. They explain what the problem was, what they tried first, and how they fixed it.

Students learn about information technology (IT) careers, including help desk roles, and invite a school district IT support personnel or IT director to visit the classroom to talk about the troubleshooting process in their job.

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students work individually to calculate the total cost of the troubleshooting repairs for scenarios in which a school has a budget to fix common hardware issues (e.g., replace five mouses at $10 each, repair three chargers at $15 each). Then students prioritize which fixes to do first if the budget is limited, justifying their choice based on which hardware is more critical for daily tasks.

ela.standard: Produce complete sentences, recognizing and correcting inappropriate fragments and run-ons.
ela.description: Students apply the computational thinking skill of debugging by treating a broken sentence structure as "buggy code" that fails to communicate clearly. They use the troubleshooting cycle to locate the syntax error (define), select the correct punctuation tool (plan), edit the text (try), and reread to verify that the "program" flows smoothly (reflect).

ela.standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
ela.description: Students read technical how-to guides for common classroom hardware and software. In pairs, they identify the specific steps recommended for a problem (e.g., frozen screen) and summarize the procedure into a three-step anchor chart for the classroom, explaining the reason behind each step (e.g., "We restart to give the computer a fresh start.").

science.standard: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.
science.description: Students recall the steps to carry out tests in science and then apply that knowledge to the steps that might be required to troubleshoot problems in CS.

science.standard: Make observations to provide evidence that energy can be transferred from place to place by sound, light, heat, and electric currents.
science.description: Students participate in a "circuit debugging" lab where there is a simple circuit with a switch and lightbulb that refuses to turn on. They systematically check the "hardware" components to find the failure point and fix it.

standards.statement: Explain how hardware and software components of a computing system work together to perform input and output (I/O), processing, and storage.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on everyday examples of how hardware and software interact to complete a task (e.g., pressing a key on a keyboard sends input to the computer, which is stored in memory and processed with software to display a letter on the screen as output). Age-appropriate models, such as flow diagrams, role-play activities (e.g., students acting as a computer with input, processor, memory, and output), and physical computing projects that use sensors are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or analyze actual logic gate diagrams, understand machine-level binary representations, or study complex computer architecture. Students do not need to develop knowledge of circuitry or number base systems.

implementation_examples.description: Students take on the roles of different hardware and software components (e.g., keyboard, mouse, word processor, monitor, hard drive). They act out a scenario, such as writing a story. The keyboard acts out input, the word processor acts out processing, the monitor acts out output, and the hard drive acts out storage, with each component explaining its role in the process.

Students create a physical computing project that uses sensors to collect data and then present their project to peers or their teacher showing. Using accurate terminology, they explain how hardware and software work together in their project.

math.standard: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.
math.description: Students create a hierarchy chart for computing components similar to how shapes are classified into hierarchies (e.g., a square is a rectangle, which is a quadrilateral). They might place a touchscreen under both the Input and the Output categories or place SSD under "Storage." They explain the properties that allow a component to fit into multiple parts of the I/O cycle.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: Students write an explanatory text about how a computer works, describing the roles of hardware and software components and providing examples of input, output, processing, and storage.

ela.standard: Summarize a written text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.
ela.description: Students listen to a podcast as audio input and organize the key details through cognitive processing to create a written summary. This written output demonstrates their ability to filter and transform information just like a computer program.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students analyze a design problem (e.g., "How can a computer help students create and save a presentation?") and identify the hardware and software components needed for input, processing, output, and storage. They explain how each part must work together to meet the goal of the system.

science.standard: Support an argument that plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air and water.
science.description: Students draw a plant system, labeling sunlight and water as input and the leaves as the hardware that processes these resources. They identify oxygen and sugar as the output, visualizing photosynthesis as a biological system of inputs and outputs.

other.standard: Identify examples of the variety of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) that are used to produce goods and services.
other.description: Students analyze a product's journey, identifying raw materials as input and the factory machines as the hardware that processes them. They map the finished goods as output, illustrating how economic systems use resources and tools to produce value.

other.standard: Explain how groups of people make rules to create responsibilities and protect freedoms.
other.description: Students simulate a town council where citizen complaints serve as input that the council processes through debate to create new laws. They place the final written laws in storage, showing how public policy is developed through an information-processing cycle.

standards.statement: Examine differences between computing systems based on user needs, system requirements, and potential societal, environmental, and ethical impacts.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should compare multiple computing systems based on features and system requirements (e.g., storage capacity, connectivity, accessibility features). Students should identify user needs (e.g., portability, cost, battery life) and provide reasoning for system choices. Students should connect at least one societal, environmental, or ethical impact to system choice (e.g., digital divide due to cost, energy consumption and e-waste, privacy and accessibility concerns).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explain detailed technical specifications (e.g., processor clock speeds, low-level architecture).

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students research and debate the societal, environmental, and ethical implications of different computing systems (e.g., cloud vs. local storage, proprietary vs. open-source software). Teams are assigned to represent different stakeholders (e.g., users, developers, environmentalists, policymakers).  Students present arguments and propose recommendations in response to guided questions (e.g., How does each system meet user needs? What are the trade-offs in energy use, accessibility, and privacy?).

Students use a simulation tool to model two computing systems. One is optimized for speed and the other for energy efficiency. Students define user needs (e.g., gaming vs. data archiving). They simulate system performance under different conditions And analyze trade-offs in usability, environmental impact, and ethical concerns (e.g., data privacy, accessibility).

math.standard: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.
math.description: Students display numerical data (e.g., energy consumption, processing speed, cost) from different computing systems using dot plots, histograms, or box plots. Using these visualizations, students compare systems based on user needs (e.g., gaming vs. school use), system requirements, and environmental impacts (e.g., energy usage). Students discuss trade-offs and evaluate which system would be most appropriate for specific contexts.

ela.standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
ela.description: Students evaluate claims about computing systems (e.g., cloud vs. local storage) and assess their societal and environmental impacts.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write persuasive essays comparing computing systems based on ethical considerations and user needs.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students are given a scenario (e.g., selecting computers for a community center with a limited budget and sustainability goals). They define the criteria for success (e.g., performance requirements, durability) and constraints (e.g., cost limits, energy consumption, environmental impact) before comparing computing systems to determine which best meets the defined criteria.

science.standard: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
science.description: Students apply scientific principles related to energy consumption and resource use to design a method for monitoring the environmental impact of classroom computing devices (e.g., tracking electricity use, device life span). Based on their data, they propose and justify strategies to minimize impact, such as selecting energy-efficient systems or reducing e-waste.

other.standard: Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society.
other.description: Students compare computing systems as an economic and ethical choice by weighing user needs (e.g., cost, portability, accessibility) against system requirements (e.g., storage, connectivity, battery life). They identify how different choices affect well-being for different groups (e.g., students with disabilities, families with limited internet, school budgets) and connect at least one broader impact (e.g., digital divide, privacy, e-waste) to their recommendation.

standards.statement: Describe computing devices used in various industries, their basic functions, and how they are used to accomplish tasks or solve problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should learn about computing devices used in various industries and describe their basic functions. Devices might include robots, electronic control units in vehicles, medical imaging devices, automated manufacturing equipment, and agricultural sensors. Students should identify how these devices use input, output, processing, storage, and (when applicable) mechanical interactions to accomplish specific tasks or solve problems within industries such as medicine, agriculture, or manufacturing. Students should have agency in selecting industries and devices to study.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build or program devices. Students do not need to demonstrate advanced technical fluency in hardware or software integration.

implementation_examples.description: Students select an industry (e.g., agriculture, medicine, manufacturing) and investigate a computing device used in that field, such as a robotic arm, a medical imaging device, a vehicle control unit, or an agricultural sensor. Using a simulation or interactive model, students identify and describe the device's basic functions, including its inputs, processing, outputs, and storage components, and any mechanical interactions involved. Students explain what problem the device is designed to solve, how it accomplishes its task within the industry, and what trade-offs or limitations (e.g., cost, accuracy, environmental impact) affect its use.

Students select and analyze a real-world computing device used in an industry of their choice (e.g., robotic arm in manufacturing, wearable health monitor, smart agricultural sensor) and then follow these steps:
1. Read and analyze: Students examine a case study and identify the device's purpose and the problem it solves.
2. Break down functions: In small groups, students describe how the device uses input, processing, output, storage, and (if applicable) mechanical interaction to accomplish its task.
3. Create a model representation: Students create a labeled physical model using classroom materials (e.g., cardboard, pipe cleaners, paper circuits) that represents the device's basic components and illustrates how information flows through the system.
4. Present and reflect: Students present their model, explaining: (a) the device's basic functions, (b) how it solves an industry-specific problem, and (c) any societal or environmental considerations related to its use.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Reporting the number of observations.
math.description: Working in groups, students count hardware in their classroom and create addition problems (e.g., "We have four keyboards and four mouses. How many total pieces do we have?") They sort components by function (e.g., input vs. output devices) and use subtraction to compare quantities (e.g., "How many more monitors than speakers do we have?").

math.standard: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.
math.description: Students explore how changes in input (e.g., voltage, code parameters) affect output in computing devices like sensors or motors.

ela.standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
ela.description: Students analyze videos and articles about industrial computing devices and synthesize how they function and solve problems.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students write an explanatory report on how a specific computing device (e.g., robotic arm) is used in manufacturing.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students investigate how computing devices are designed to meet specific industrial needs and constraints.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare different computing devices (e.g., types of medical imaging tools) based on cost, accuracy, and usability.

other.standard: Evaluate alternative approaches or solutions to current economic issues in terms of benefits and costs for different groups and society as a whole.
other.description: Students investigate how a computing device used in an industry (e.g., agricultural sensors, medical imaging equipment, manufacturing robots, vehicle control systems) changes how work is done and how value is created. They explain the device's role using input, processing, storage, and output, then analyze economic impacts (e.g., productivity, job roles and skills, safety, cost, access). Students compare trade-offs for different stakeholder groups and propose one realistic improvement, policy, or practice that could reduce harms while preserving benefits.

standards.statement: Differentiate operating systems (OS) as a special type of software that manages both the hardware and other software components of a computing system, including handling memory and peripherals.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to differentiate an operating system from other types of software by identifying its role in managing hardware and software resources. For example, students might describe a computer's operating system, explaining that the operating system manages the computer's basic functions (e.g., allocating memory, connecting to peripherals).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the intricacies of how an operating system is coded or to perform advanced tasks like configuring system drivers.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a role-play. The "hardware" is the kitchen; the "application" is the customer; and the "operating system" is the waiter. The customer (app) cannot go into the kitchen (hardware) themselves. They give an order to the waiter (OS), who manages the resources (ingredients/memory) and brings back the result. If two customers order at the same time, the waiter (OS) decides who gets served first.

Students open the Task Manager (Windows) or the Activity Monitor (macOS). They observe how the OS is currently handling memory by showing how much RAM each app is using. They then plug in a peripheral (e.g., USB drive, webcam) and observe how the OS recognizes it and makes it available to other software.

science.standard: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.
science.description: Students analyze the problem of managing a computer's resources and design a high-level conceptual model for a simplified operating system, breaking down the complex task of resource management into smaller, more manageable components (e.g., handling input, output, and processing).

other.standard: Distinguish the powers and responsibilities of local, state, tribal, national, and international civic and political institutions.
other.description: Students compare the structure and function of an operating system to different forms of government (e.g., centralized monarchy, distributed democracy), discussing how each system manages its "resources" and "citizens" (hardware and software).

standards.statement: Demonstrate the capabilities and limitations of a physical or simulated computing device to address a task or problem.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to select and use a computing device to solve a practical problem. For example, a student could use a device to manage project deadlines and task assignments for a group project, using its apps and cloud synchronization features to coordinate with team members while also identifying limitations, such as battery life or screen size.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build their own computing device, understand the internal architecture of the device, or write code that directly controls the device's hardware components.

practices.practice: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students address three real-world problems (e.g., tracking a lost pet, monitoring soil moisture in a massive farm, counting people entering a building). Using a deck of "Device Cards" (e.g., smart watch, satellite tag, soil sensor, infrared camera), students must match the device to the problem and present a risk and reward list identifying the limitations of their choice (e.g., "The satellite tag is accurate, but the battery only lasts two days.").

Students use a physical microcontroller or a simulation tool to solve the problem of overheating plants. They connect a temperature sensor and a small fan. Students must demonstrate the working solution and then write a Device Reflection explaining its capabilities (automated cooling) and its limitations (the sensor only reads the air immediately around it, not the soil).

math.standard: Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.
math.description: When applying a physical sensor (e.g., a sensor that only reads whole numbers) to a problem, students analyze the precision of the device and explain how those hardware limitations affect the reliability of their data.

ela.standard: Follow precisely a complex multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks; analyze the specific results based on explanations in the text.
ela.description: Students follow a technical manual to set up a specific computing system (e.g., a Raspberry Pi server) and write a technical reflection on whether the device meets the requirements of the task.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students use a simulated environment (e.g., PhET, a circuit simulator) to model energy efficiency in a home. They apply the simulation to find the sweet spot for insulation, identifying the limitations of the model's accuracy compared to real-world variables.

standards.statement: Differentiate between public and private information.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on being able to describe the differences between information that can be safely made public (e.g., favorite food, favorite animal) and information that should be kept private (e.g., home address, family photos). Real-life scenarios, like deciding what is okay to share with a friend versus with a stranger, are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to use technical vocabulary like "confidential." Students do not need to understand detailed internet safety rules or the technical aspects of data privacy or cybersecurity.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: In response to being shown cards with pictures (e.g., pizza topping, house key), students move to one side of the rug if the picture is something public and to the other side if it is something private. Students move to the public side of the rug for the pizza topping and the private side for the house key and describe why (e.g., "Anyone can know what type of pizza we like, but only family should have the key to our house.")

Students view a puppet show or videos, then discuss personal information (e.g., favorite color, first name) versus private information (e.g., full name, phone number) to determine how to stay safe online.

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Working in pairs, students sort a set of picture cards into two piles labeled "Public" and "Private." They then count and record how many cards are in each pile and describe to another pair of students why they sorted their cards the way they did, identifying why something is public or private.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about kindergarten topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: In a discussion circle facilitated by the teacher, students explore the questions "What's safe to share with friends?" and "What's safe to share with strangers?"

ela.standard: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose informative/explanatory texts in which they name what they are writing about and supply some information about the topic.
ela.description: Students use drawing and oral storytelling to present something they would share (or not share) about themselves.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students compare everyday situations (e.g., sharing a name vs. sharing a home address) and identify which information is safe to share publicly and which should stay private. They discuss how understanding this difference helps solve problems like staying safe when using tools and technology.

other.standard: Child asks and answers questions about a book that was read aloud.
other.description: After the class hears a story about what is okay to share and what they should keep private, students sort pictures from the book into public and private categories.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: Students focus on rules and guidelines around what is appropriate to share (public information) and what is not (private information).

standards.statement: Describe how to keep devices and online accounts safe from unauthorized access.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on how authentication (e.g., passwords, QR codes for signing in) and good habits like signing out/logging off help keep their information protected online. Demonstrating how they sign out of devices and accounts and keep their authentication details secret from others is appropriate if students have online accounts that require authentication.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to create their own passwords or other authentication methods or to describe more complex authentication methods (e.g., multifactor authentication, passkeys, biometrics). Students do not need to have online accounts that require authentication. They can learn and describe these concepts without online accounts.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students complete a digital literacy/citizenship lesson on how to keep devices and online accounts safe and then share examples of how to keep their own information safe online with a teacher or peer or by recording a video or creating a poster.

After a read-aloud of a picture book related to not sharing passwords and to following rules, students discuss what should be added to their classroom's agreed-upon rules and guidelines for keeping their online accounts safe.

math.standard: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.
math.description: Working as a class, students record how many times they sign in and sign out of a classroom learning tool during the day and organize the counts into categories on a picture graph. Students demonstrate understanding by explaining why signing out after use and not sharing passwords helps keep their accounts protected from unauthorized access.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they name a topic, supply some facts about the topic, and provide some sense of closure.
ela.description: In pairs, students devise one rule and a drawing of the rule. Then as a class, students create a safety rule book for the devices they use.

ela.standard: Describe people, places, things, and events with relevant details, expressing ideas and feelings clearly.
ela.description: Students describe to a partner, a small group, or a teacher ways to keep online accounts safe.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: Students connect not sharing passwords or QR codes and signing out of accounts and devices to personal responsibility and classroom/school rules.

standards.statement: Explain how online actions have real-world consequences.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on age-appropriate examples that connect how their online actions (e.g., sharing information, posting comments, using a device) can have effects in the real world (e.g., hurting someone's feelings, compromising personal safety).
