Writing a story or drawing a picture to show how a specific online behavior (e.g., sharing a picture without asking) can lead to a consequence (e.g., making a friend angry) is appropriate. Discussing the consequences of copying someone's work online is also appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to identify specific laws (e.g., Children's Internet Protection Act, COPPA) or legal frameworks like copyright or intellectual property law. Students do not need to have online accounts. They can learn and describe these concepts without online accounts.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Working individually or as a class, students complete a digital citizenship lesson focused on recognizing and responding to meanness online, using age-appropriate videos or interactive scenarios. Students identify an example of unkind online behavior and describe a real-world consequence, such as hurting someone's feelings. Students demonstrate understanding by drawing or writing one respectful response they could use instead. The class reflects on how positive online choices help create safer, kinder communities.

As a whole class, students listen to short scenarios describing online actions (e.g., copying someone's work or sharing personal information) and discuss possible real-world consequences. Students then draw a picture showing one online action and its outcome, using labels to show cause and effect. Students demonstrate understanding by explaining their drawing to a partner or the class. Students have a discussion, guided by the teacher, on how rules for online behavior help keep people safe and help ensure that people are treated fairly.

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: The class collects data about the rules they follow and creates a bar graph comparing classroom rules to online rules. By analyzing the data, students see that some rules appear in both categories (e.g., being kind), helping them explain that rules apply in multiple environments.

ela.standard: Write narratives in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.
ela.description: Working individually, students write a short story about a character's online action (e.g., sharing a picture without permission, copying a friend's work) and the real-world consequence that results (e.g., hurting a friend's feelings, losing a friend's trust). Students demonstrate understanding by including details of the action, the effect on others, and how following rules could prevent harm, showing the connection between online behavior and real-world outcomes.

ela.standard: Build on others’ talk in conversations by linking their comments to the remarks of others.
ela.description: In small groups, students discuss short online behavior scenarios (e.g., posting unkind comments, sharing personal information) and identify the real-world consequences for the people involved. Students demonstrate understanding by sharing their ideas with the group, explaining why rules are important online, and building on peers' examples to show the connection between online actions and real-world effects.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.
science.description: In small groups, students compare two classroom safety rules for using their devices (e.g., "Only use the app the teacher says is okay to use." vs. "Use any app you would like.") They gather data on which rule leads to more consequences (e.g, getting in trouble, seeing popups, losing access to their device) and present their findings, explaining that the online action of following a rule is a way to prevent real-world consequences.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students explore scenarios where online behavior causes a problem (e.g., sharing something unkind or unsafe). They discuss why rules and laws are needed to help keep people safe and solve problems, both online and offline.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: As a whole class, students compare rules for the classroom, playground, and online spaces using picture cards (e.g., take turns, be kind, log out when finished). Students demonstrate understanding by explaining how rules in digital spaces help prevent harm and guide behavior, just as rules do in school and the community.

standards.statement: Evaluate how sharing information online might reveal personally identifiable information (PII) and other details.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on developing skills to help them recognize risks in online situations and assess what information to share online and when to share it. Activities using age-appropriate real-world situations (e.g., sharing their favorite book with a classmate, providing their address in response to a pop-up on a website saying they won a prize) are appropriate. Students should practice identifying how seemingly harmless information shared in contexts like online gaming (e.g., screen names, team names, game schedules) can unintentionally reveal PII to unintended recipients.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to evaluate all risky online situations, including things like catfishing and data breaches. Students do not need to participate in situations where they could reveal their personally identifiable information.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students complete digital citizenship lessons around what PII is, risks, and things like phishing. They then create a presentation or poster about avoiding the risks.

Students work in small groups to analyze printed scenario cards describing common online situations, such as creating a gamer tag or sharing a practice schedule in a chat. Groups sort information cards (e.g., name, city, school mascot, favorite book, team name) into "safe to share" and "reveals PII" categories for each scenario. Students record their decisions on chart paper and explain how seemingly harmless details could combine to reveal personal information. Students demonstrate understanding through their group explanations and completed charts.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 3 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students participate in class or small-group discussions about how sharing information online might reveal PII and other details.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons.
ela.description: Students write an opinion piece suggesting when one should and should not share information online in order to avoid revealing unintended information.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: In response to online-sharing scenarios (e.g., posting a photo, joining a game, filling out a form), students identify what personal details might be revealed. They compare different choices for sharing information and evaluate which options best protect personal safety while still allowing participation.

science.standard: Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season.
science.description: Working in pairs, students examine examples of online weather tools (e.g., a weather website or app screenshot) to identify what information is shared or displayed and then sort those details into categories (e.g., weather data and personal information). Students create a simple chart showing patterns in weather data shared online and explain how recognizing patterns in shared data helps predict weather while also considering how sharing information online might reveal personal details.

standards.statement: Distinguish between authentication and authorization in protecting devices and private information.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on authentication and authorization as two distinct but related concepts for protecting private information and devices. Using an analogy of a house is appropriate: authentication is proving you have the key to get in the door, whereas authorization is a parent telling you which rooms in the house you're allowed to enter once you're inside.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to learn about different types of authentication (e.g., biometrics, multifactor authentication) or technical details of how authentication and authorization work. Students do not need to use a variety of authentication methods.

implementation_examples.description: Students act out situations in which they try to access a protected device or account. One student plays the role of a user, and another plays the role of the system. The system asks the user for a password (authentication). If the password is correct, the system grants access to certain applications or files, but not to others (authorization). For example, the user might be granted access to a drawing program, but not to a settings menu.

Students analyze a variety of real-world scenarios and use a T-chart to organize them as examples of authentication or authorization. For instance, putting a key in a lock is authentication, whereas a parent giving permission to use a certain toy is authorization.

ela.standard: Report on a topic or text, tell a story, or recount an experience in an organized manner, using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace.
ela.description: Students present their understanding of authentication and authorization to the class, using their own examples and analogies to distinguish the difference.

ela.standard: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
ela.description: Students craft a narrative in which a character proves their identity (authentication) by showing a ticket, pass, or badge and then accesses only the resources or areas they are allowed to use (authorization). Students demonstrate understanding of cause and effect by showing what happens when the character follows the rules versus trying to access something they are not authorized to use.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students define the problem of needing to protect information on a shared device and brainstorm simple solutions related to authentication (e.g., using a picture password) and authorization (e.g., creating separate user profiles for different games).

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information.
science.description: Students play a game where they will generate and compare multiple secret patterns (e.g., rhythmic taps, light flashes) to authenticate teammates and identify "intruder spies" trying to sneak into their station. After testing, students evaluate which signal best authorizes entry to their private data zones while successfully blocking unauthorized intruders from seeing their work.

other.standard: Explain how policies are developed to address public problems.
other.description: The class explores policies that address public problems related to authentication and authorization (e.g., library cards give access to books [authentication], but not all books are available to children based on their age [authorization]).

standards.statement: Describe the concepts of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) Triad and how each part is important in protecting information.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to explain the CIA Triad at a conceptual level and describe how each element (confidentiality, integrity, and availability) helps protect information. For example, students might describe confidentiality as keeping a password secret and not sharing personally identifiable information online. They might describe integrity as ensuring that data is accurate and unchanged (e.g., checking whether a photo is real or AI-generated, ensuring that grades in a gradebook haven't been improperly changed). They might describe availability as ensuring that they can access their accounts, devices, apps, or gaming systems when they need them (e.g., the system isn't down or blocked).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement technical security measures such as encryption or access control lists. Students do not need to understand cybersecurity systems or networks beyond how they affect students' daily lives.

practices.practice: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students have slips of paper with a "secret code" written on them. Some students keep their code private, and others share it. The class discusses what happens when secrets are shared (e.g., does it still stay safe)? This helps them see why keeping a password or personal information private protects confidentiality.

The class discusses how weather alerts (e.g., tornado or wildfire warnings) are sent to phones or TVs. If those systems are down or unavailable, people can't get important information in time. This highlights how availability can affect safety in real life.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students collect data, plot it, and then explore what happens if someone changes or removes a data point that illustrates how data integrity matters.

ela.standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
ela.description: The class discusses the importance of integrity within the context of quoting text or sharing information. Students recognize how changing information can cause problems (e.g., getting the wrong grade, believing false news).

ela.standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
ela.description: Confidentiality, integrity, and access in the context of CS are examples of domain-specific words and phrases relevant to the subject area. Students read a text relevant to the topic of CIA or cybersecurity that uses these terms.

other.standard: Explain how policies are developed to address public problems.
other.description: The CIA Triad can be connected and applied to the importance of protecting information in government, historical record keeping, and voting systems.

standards.statement: Explain the effects of not using the CIA Triad when working with data.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should recognize and explain what happens when each element of the CIA Triad is not maintained. When confidentiality is compromised, sensitive data is exposed (e.g., leaked passwords, shared personal information). When integrity is compromised, data becomes corrupted or altered (e.g., incorrect grades in a school database). When availability is compromised, systems become inaccessible (e.g., a denial-of-service attack blocking a website). Students should apply the CIA Triad to age-appropriate, relatable contexts (e.g., school accounts, social media, online gaming), demonstrating understanding of how failures connect to real-world impacts.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct professional-level security audits or develop deep cryptography knowledge.

practices.practice: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: In small groups students receive scenario cards (e.g., password leaks, altered grades, denial-of-service) and identify which CIA element failed, describe the consequences for users and systems, and propose age-appropriate prevention strategies. Groups present findings and compare cases across contexts (e.g., school accounts, social media, online gaming). They respond to multiple teacher prompts (e.g., "Which CIA element failed?" "What were the consequences?" "How could this be prevented?")

Students work individually or in pairs to identify the specific failures in teacher-run simulations that intentionally demonstrate failures (e.g., overly broad sharing settings to show confidentiality loss, silent modification of a document to show integrity loss, temporary account lockouts to show availability loss). They explain the effect of the failure on tasks and users and recommend safeguards. In a wrap-up discussion, students talk about how those safeguards would change behavior or system settings.

math.standard: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.
math.description: Students calculate the percentage of students in class who reuse passwords across accounts and analyze risks.

math.standard: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.
math.description: Students model probability of data breaches under weak versus strong password policies.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 7 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students role-play as security analysts discussing which CIA failures led to different case study incidents.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write a persuasive essay arguing which element of the CIA Triad is most critical to protect in schools.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students evaluate different school-level security measures (e.g., two-factor authentication, password resets, backups) to determine which best prevents CIA failures.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students review case studies of school Wi-Fi outages, identify availability issues, and propose system improvements.

other.standard: Draw on multiple disciplinary lenses to analyze how a specific problem can manifest itself at local, regional, and global levels over time, identifying its characteristics and causes, and the challenges and opportunities faced by those trying to address the problem.
other.description: Students debate whether schools should prioritize confidentiality (protecting student data) over availability (keeping systems always online).

other.standard: Combine concepts collaboratively to generate innovative ideas for creating art.
other.description: Students collaboratively design posters or infographics that illustrate the consequences of neglecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability in real-world scenarios.

standards.statement: Evaluate common types of cyber attacks and preventions.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and describe common types of cyber attacks, such as phishing, malware, ransomware, and social engineering. They should be able to evaluate how these attacks exploit human behavior and system vulnerabilities. Students could also explore real-world examples of cyber incidents and their consequences. Students should learn to apply basic prevention strategies, such as using strong passwords, enabling multifactor authentication, and recognizing suspicious activity.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to investigate complex cyber attacks or use professional security tools. They do not need to break into systems, test network defenses, or analyze how malware is built. Students are also not expected to configure advanced security settings or understand technical protocols used in industry.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to analyze brief, realistic cyber attack scenarios (e.g., phishing emails, fake tech-support calls, infected downloads/malware). For each scenario, groups identify the attack type, how it works, who is vulnerable and why, and key warning signs. As a synthesis activity, each group produces a prevention artifact (e.g., an unplugged Prevention Poster, a plugged meme/short video) that lists warning signs, clear steps to avoid the attack, and a memorable slogan or PSA-style message for peers.

Students work in small groups to create a meme/short video that lists warning signs, clear steps to avoid the attack, and a memorable slogan or PSA-style message for peers based on an analysis of cyber attack scenarios (e.g., phishing emails, fake tech-support calls, infected downloads, malware).

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students analyze frequency data from simulated cyber attacks (e.g., types of malware detected) and summarize patterns.

math.standard: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.
math.description: Students evaluate the likelihood of different types of cyber attacks based on user behavior or system vulnerabilities.

ela.standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
ela.description: Students analyze phishing emails or cyber propaganda to identify manipulative language and unsupported claims.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write a persuasive PSA or blog post warning others about a specific cyber threat and how to prevent it.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students design a cybersecurity protocol or awareness campaign that meets constraints like accessibility and cost.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare different password protection strategies or authentication methods for effectiveness and usability.

other.standard: Demonstrate persistence in developing skills with various materials, methods, and approaches in creating works of art or design.
other.description: Students create a visual artwork that represents a specific cyber attack (e.g., phishing as a baited hook, malware as a spreading virus) and illustrates at least one prevention strategy. Through visual metaphors and iterative design, students show how the attack exploits vulnerabilities and how protective measures (e.g., strong passwords, multifactor authentication) reduce risk.

other.standard: Analyze how art reflects changing times, traditions, resources, and cultural uses.
other.description: Students analyze contemporary artworks (e.g., digital art, posters, media campaigns) that address cybersecurity, data privacy, or digital ethics, discussing how these works reflect modern technological challenges and societal concerns. Students then create their own artwork that comments on a current cyber threat and includes a prevention message.

standards.statement: Identify different types of cybersecurity and physical security measures and the trade-offs for users, data, and devices.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to identify and describe different types of cybersecurity and physical security measures, as well as their associated trade-offs. They should be able to articulate how a security measure may benefit one aspect (e.g., data protection) while posing a challenge to another (e.g., user convenience, cost). For example, students could identify how multifactor authentication enhances security for a user's account, but makes it less convenient for the user to access. Students should focus on conceptual understanding of security principles and their practical implementation.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement these security measures or demonstrate technical expertise.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students design a security plan for a high school computer lab. They must list three cybersecurity measures (e.g., strong passwords, software updates) and three physical measures (e.g., locking the door, bolting computers to desks). For each, they must identify a trade-off (e.g., "Bolting the computers down prevents theft, but makes it impossible for students to move them for group work.")

Students use a personal security checklist to audit their own digital habits. They explore the settings on their smartphones to find biometric options and encryption status. They then participate in a classroom debate: "Is a 20-character password worth the extra security if it takes you a full minute to type it every time you check your phone?"

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
ela.description: Students write an argumentative essay in which they analyze the trade-offs of a specific security measure and argue for or against its implementation, using evidence from their research to support their claims.

other.standard: Critique relationships among governments, civil societies, and economic markets.
other.description: Students investigate and debate real-world scenarios where security measures have led to a conflict between individual privacy and public safety. They can examine how different governments and societies have approached this balance.

standards.statement: Classify the causes and impacts of security breaches and social engineering attacks for individuals, industries, communities, and governments.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to research and categorize the consequences of a security breach or social engineering attack, differentiating between the effects on various stakeholders. The classification should go beyond a simple list of impacts and demonstrate an understanding of how the same breach can have different types of consequences (e.g., financial, reputational, legal, operational) for different groups. For example, a student could classify the impacts of a data breach at a hospital, analyzing the effects on patients (individuals), the hospital (industry), the local healthcare system (community), and regulations (government). Students should focus on understanding the broad, interconnected impacts of an attack.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct a forensic investigation of a real-world breach or to use professional cybersecurity tools for their analysis. Students do not need to focus on the technical details of the attack itself.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students hold a set of "Attack Cards" (e.g., "A hacker shuts down a city's power grid." "A student falls for a fake Netflix login email."). They must place these cards into a matrix that classifies the attack type (e.g., technical vs. social) and the primary group affected (e.g., individual, industry, community, government). They then present the chain reaction of how one attack on an individual (e.g., a CEO) could lead to an impact on an entire industry.

Students use a safe, educational simulator to identify the red flags of a social engineering attack. They then research a real-world breach, such as the Colonial Pipeline attack, and classify its causes (a leaked password) and its massive impacts on the community (gas shortages) and government (emergency declarations).

ela.standard: Assess the extent to which the reasoning and evidence in a text support the author’s claim or a recommendation for solving a scientific or technical problem.
ela.description: Students read a series of articles, reports, or government documents about a security breach and write a paper or create a presentation that assesses the various claims made about the impacts of the event, using evidence to support their own classifications.

other.standard: Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to construct an argument for or against an approach or solution to an economic issue.
other.description: Students investigate the economic and legal ramifications of security breaches, examining how they affect consumer trust, stock prices, and government regulations. They could conduct a mock hearing or debate on proposed legislation to address cybersecurity issues.

standards.statement: Formulate a solution to a security flaw in a given system.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to analyze a simulated or described scenario involving a security flaw and propose a high-level solution. The proposed solution should explain the identified vulnerability, the potential consequences, and the recommended steps for mitigation. For example, a student could be given a case study of a school's network being compromised by a phishing attack and be asked to propose a solution that includes both technical measures (e.g., email filtering that detects suspicious links, multifactor authentication) and nontechnical measures (e.g., user training, security policies) to prevent future attacks.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement the solution.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Using a flawed floor plan (e.g., glass window next to a keypad, door that stays open for 30 seconds after a badge swipe, server rack with no lock) for a secure data center, students must formulate a physical security solution for each flaw and justify how it prevents specific types of unauthorized access.

Using a simple script for a login page that is vulnerable to a "tautology attack" (where entering ' OR 1=1 -- bypasses the password), students formulate a code-based solution using query parameters or input filters to stop the attack. They test their solution to verify that legitimate users can still log in and that hackers are blocked.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
ela.description: Students write a persuasive report or argumentative essay proposing their solution to the security flaw. The report must use evidence from the case study to justify their claims about the vulnerability and argue for why their proposed solution is the most effective.

science.standard: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.
science.description: To propose a solution to a security flaw, students define the problem (the security flaw), research potential solutions, and then design and evaluate a plan. The activity directly mirrors the engineering design process and can be framed as an engineering challenge.

other.standard: Analyze how people use and challenge local, state, national, and international laws to address a variety of public issues.
other.description: Students research and discuss the societal and ethical implications of security flaws, particularly for public institutions or critical infrastructure. They propose solutions that consider the impact on various stakeholders, including individuals, businesses, and government agencies.

standards.statement: Explain how people access the internet to gain information and communicate with each other.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to describe, in age-appropriate terms, how people use different devices to connect to the internet and communicate. Examples of devices that can be used to access the internet include computers, cell phones, and tablets. An example of accessing information is using a search engine to look up facts for a report. An example of communicating through technology is using video chat to talk with people across long distances.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe technical infrastructure such as IP addressing, routing protocols, domain name systems, or data packet transmission. Students do not need to consider network configuration or errors.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students compare different ways of communicating via the internet and gaining information from the internet to identify advantages and limitations of each in real-life scenarios. Working in pairs, students use a kid-safe search engine on a computer or tablet to find the answers to questions (e.g., "What is the state bird of California?" "What is the tallest mountain in the world?"). This shows how the internet helps students look up facts for school work.

Students work in small groups to sort picture cards of devices (e.g., computer, tablet, phone, TV, game console, book, chalkboard) into the categories "Connects to the internet" and "Does not connect to the internet." For each internet-connected device, students explain how it could be used to find information or communicate with others, such as video chatting or sending messages. Students demonstrate understanding by verbally describing how people use different devices to access the internet and communicate.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students work in pairs to survey classmates about which devices they use to access the internet (e.g., computer, tablet, phone) and record the responses. They create a scaled bar graph to display the data and explain which devices are most commonly used for finding information or communicating, connecting data representation to real-world internet usage.

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
ela.description: Students use a kid-safe search engine to answer a simple factual question (e.g., "What is the tallest mountain in the world?") They then write or share orally how they found the answer and what steps they took, demonstrating understanding of both the information and how the internet was used to access it.

ela.standard: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge about a topic.
ela.description: Students conduct a short research project on a chosen topic (e.g., an animal, a planet, a historical figure) using kid-safe search engines. They record three key facts about their topic in a graphic organizer and then create a poster or slideshow explaining how they found the information online and how different devices (e.g., computer, tablet, phone) helped them gather and share it.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students examine a problem (e.g., "How can our class share information with students in another school?") and identify internet tools (e.g., email, video chat, shared documents) that help solve the problem. They discuss how internet access enables people to choose tools that best meet communication needs.

other.standard: Compare life in specific historical time periods to life today.
other.description: Students compare how people communicated long ago (e.g., letters, telegraph, landline phones) with how they communicate today (e.g., email, video chat, texting). They create a simple timeline or Venn diagram. Then, as a reflection, they discuss how the internet lets communities stay connected globally (e.g., talking with family in another country).

standards.statement: Compare wired and wireless methods that computing devices use to connect to the internet.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on comparing the advantages and disadvantages of different ways of connecting to the internet. Important factors include distance, speed, convenience, and safety considerations (e.g., connecting to trusted networks at home or school vs. unknown public networks). Tasks in which students determine when it is advantageous to have either a wired connection or a wireless connection are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explore other ways of connecting between devices to share information (e.g., Bluetooth) or the protocols used to connect devices (e.g., TCP/IP). Students do not need direct access to routers or hubs.

implementation_examples.description: Students explain why different methods work better in different situations. Using a rope to model an Ethernet cable, they see how a "tug" travels quickly and reliably without weakening the rope, representing the stability of wired signals. With a flashlight, they model Wi-Fi, observing how the beam spreads out, weakens with distance, and can be blocked by obstacles, just like wireless signals. Through discussion and real-world scenarios, such as a classroom full of desktops versus a student with a laptop at home, students compare the advantages and disadvantages of each method.

Students work in pairs to analyze a set of teacher-selected scenarios showing devices connecting to the internet in different settings (e.g., home desk, classroom, library, coffee shop). Using either a digital tool or printed charts, students decide whether a wired or wireless connection is more appropriate for each scenario and record factors such as distance, speed, convenience, and safety. Pairs discuss and justify their choices using evidence from the scenario. Students demonstrate understanding by explaining the advantages and disadvantages of each connection type across the situations.

math.standard: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two- column table. For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), ...
math.description: Students work in pairs to measure distances between classroom devices (e.g., from a computer to a wall outlet, from a student desk to a wireless access point) using different units (feet and inches) and record the measurements in a two-column data table. Using the table, students decide whether a wired or wireless internet connection would be more appropriate for each setup and explain how distance and unit choice influenced their decision.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
ela.description: Students write an opinion piece on whether wired or wireless internet is better, using data (e.g., speed tests, cost, reliability) to support their claim.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information.
science.description: Students generate and compare multiple methods for transferring information, such as wireless signals (modeled by a spreading flashlight beam) and wired connections (modeled by electricity traveling through a wire). Students analyze how signal strength changes with distance and discuss how each method maintains or weakens patterns used to transmit information.

standards.statement: Distinguish between the components of wired and wireless networks.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore and describe the basic components of networks, such as devices (e.g., computers, tablets, phones), connecting hardware (e.g., routers, switches, cables), and wireless connections (Wi-Fi signals).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand detailed networking protocols, IP addressing, or the technical differences between LANs, WANs, and the internet. Students do not need to understand packet structures, routing tables, or advanced network design.

implementation_examples.description: Students individually create a labeled diagram of a simple home or school network on poster paper or digitally. They should include at least three devices (e.g., computer, tablet, phone) and one router, and show both wired (drawn as solid lines) and wireless (drawn as wavy lines) connections. Students add labels identifying each component and draw arrows showing how information might travel from one device to another (e.g., from a tablet to a printer). Students then explain their diagram to a partner, describing the role of each component and why they chose wired or wireless for specific connections.

Students work in pairs to test and compare wired and wireless connections using provided devices. Each pair receives a worksheet with scenarios (e.g., playing an online game, printing a document, video-calling grandparents, using a laptop in different rooms) and discusses which connection type would work best for each situation and why. Pairs then create a T-chart listing advantages of wired connections (e.g., faster, more reliable) and wireless connections (e.g., can move around, no cables needed). Students present one scenario to the class, demonstrating their reasoning about which connection type to choose.

math.standard: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.
math.description: Students plot network devices (e.g., router, computer, tablet, printer) on a coordinate plane as ordered pairs then calculate horizontal and vertical distances between each device and the router.

math.standard: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.
math.description: Students compare network connection speeds in megabits per second (Mbps)—wired Ethernet, nearby Wi-Fi, and distant Wi-Fi—by using base-10 blocks or area models to subtract and determine speed differences. They then explain their reasoning for their calculations.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: Students write explanations of how network components work together.

ela.standard: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
ela.description: Students research different types of network hardware or investigate how home and school networks differ.

science.standard: Make observations and measurements to identify materials based on their properties.
science.description: Students measure and compare properties of network cables (e.g., length, flexibility, conductivity vs. non-conductivity) and  wireless signal strength at different distances. They categorize devices by their input/output properties.

standards.statement: Model how information in a network is broken down into packets, transmitted between devices, and reassembled.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to model how data is split into packets, encoded into binary, transmitted independently across a network, and reassembled at the destination. Students should also identify common issues such as packet loss, explain possible causes (e.g., congestion, interference, faulty hardware), and describe basic strategies to reduce or prevent packet loss.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explore networking protocols in detail (e.g., TCP/IP) or to configure real-world networking hardware (routers, switches, servers).

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to model network transmission by breaking a short message into numbered "packets" using cards or strips of paper. Group members act as network devices, sending packets along different paths across the room before reassembling them at the destination. The class then simulates packet loss by removing or delaying a packet and discusses what happens when information is missing or out of order. To demonstrate understanding, students explain or document how packets are transmitted and reassembled and describe one cause of packet loss and one strategy to reduce its impact.

Students use a simple network simulator to visualize how packets are transmitted across a network. They observe how packets from one message may take different paths and still arrive at the destination in the correct order.

math.standard: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, “The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak.” “For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes.”
math.description: Students model a message as equal-sized packets and use ratios to describe how many packets were sent, received, or lost during transmission.

ela.standard: Follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks.
ela.description: Students describe the packet transmission process as a sequence of steps, explaining how information is divided, transmitted, and reassembled and identifying where breakdowns can occur.

science.standard: Integrate qualitative scientific and technical information to support the claim that digitized signals are a more reliable way to encode and transmit information than analog signals.
science.description: Students model sending a message as digitized packets by converting a short phrase into a simple binary representation (e.g., using a provided encoding key), splitting it into "packets," and transmitting packets along multiple paths in a classroom simulation where some packets are delayed or lost. Students compare what happens when the message is sent as discrete pulses versus a single continuous "analog" message (e.g., one long uninterrupted strip) when interference is introduced. To demonstrate understanding, students write a brief claim-evidence statement explaining why digitized signals can be more reliable for transmitting information, using observations from their model (e.g., easier error detection, missing packets resent, less distortion).

standards.statement: Explain how the resilience of the internet depends on interconnected devices and their roles and functions within the network.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to explain how the internet is made up of interconnected devices that each serve specific roles. For example, routers direct traffic between networks, servers host information, clients (e.g., laptops, phones) request and use data, and switches connect devices within a local network. Students should also describe how redundancy (multiple pathways between devices) supports resilience, allowing communication to continue even if some devices or connections fail.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to demonstrate technical knowledge of networking protocols (e.g., TCP/IP) or to configure or analyze real-world enterprise-level networking systems.

implementation_examples.description: Students create a physical "map" of the internet in the classroom using index cards for devices (servers, routers, clients) and string for connections. They simulate what happens when one connection or device "fails" and trace how data still finds another path, modeling internet resilience.
Students use online tools to explore real internet infrastructure. They compare how many "hops" it takes to reach different websites and discuss why multiple routes exist.

math.standard: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.
math.description: Given a diagram of how messages travel across the internet and the time it takes various messages to reach different end points on the diagram, students construct equations to calculate the time it takes for a message to reach its destination if a particular server or router is out of service. They express the lower and upper bounds of time needed for each scenario.

math.standard: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope of the graph. Compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways. For example, compare a distance-time graph to a distance-time equation to determine which of two moving objects has greater speed.
math.description: Students graph data on how many messages are sent between various points on the internet each minute and how many errors occur in that time period that require messages to be resent.  They determine which internet data route is the most efficient.

ela.standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
ela.description: Students identify technical vocabulary in an article about how an email is sent from one location to another via the internet. Students then identify any clues in the text that shed light on the meanings of the vocabulary terms.

science.standard: Integrate qualitative scientific and technical information to support the claim that digitized signals are a more reliable way to encode and transmit information than analog signals.
science.description: Students compare the speed of various methods of data transmission, both digital (e.g., fiber optic, bluetooth) and analog (e.g., radio waves, coax cable), and investigate which methods of transmission are used in all parts of a web page being loaded onto a screen and then read aloud by a screen reader into headphones.

standards.statement: Diagram a network of computing systems, including hardware and software.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to create a diagram of a computing systems network that includes both hardware (e.g., servers, routers, storage, user devices) and software (e.g., operating systems, applications). Students should focus on recognizing and representing the concept of a network and the role of each component in the network. Students should show how these components connect and interact to process information, accomplish tasks, or solve problems.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build a network using hardware or software.

implementation_examples.description: Students act as hardware and software. Some students are "Computers," one is a "Router," and another is the "Firewall." They use colored string to connect to one another. Once the physical layout is set, they draw a diagram of their human network, labeling which "nodes" represent hardware and which roles (e.g., Firewall) represent software rules.

Students use a digital diagramming tool (e.g., Lucidchart, Draw.io, Canva) to diagram their own home network. They must include the ISP connection, the modem/router, and at least three hardware devices (e.g., a gaming console, a laptop, a smart fridge). They label the software used to manage the network (e.g., the Router's firmware, a VPN).

ela.standard: Translate quantitative or technical information expressed in words in a text into visual form (e.g., a table or chart) and translate information expressed visually or mathematically (e.g., in an equation) into words.
ela.description: Students read a technical description of a network and translate that information into a visual diagram. They can then write a paragraph or a short presentation explaining the key elements of their diagram.

science.standard: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.
science.description: Using the concept of a computer network being analogous to biological systems, students compare and contrast the hierarchical structure of a computer network to the interacting systems within an organism (e.g., the digestive and circulatory systems).

other.standard: Evaluate and implement improvements in presenting media artworks, considering personal and local impacts, such as the benefits for self and others.
other.description: Students create and present a visual diagram of a network of computing systems, using principles of visual design to communicate hardware and software relationships clearly. After presenting their diagrams, students evaluate how effectively their visuals communicate the network to an audience and revise their design—adjusting layout, symbols, labeling, or organization—to improve clarity and usefulness for others.

standards.statement: Analyze how the internet functions as a network of networks and how it differs from other types of networks.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to conceptually analyze the internet's layered structure and its role as a global network connecting smaller, local networks. They analyze its layered structure, key components (e.g., routers), core protocols (e.g., TCP/IP), and the client/server model. For example, a student could compare a simple LAN in a classroom to the global structure of the internet in terms of structure, scalability, addressing, and data transfer. Students should focus on developing a high-level, conceptual understanding of networking principles.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to implement specific networks, configure or troubleshoot professional-grade networking equipment, write network protocols, or perform packet analysis.

implementation_examples.description: Students simulate how a letter gets from a desk in a classroom (LAN) to a desk in a different country. They identify the different "networks" the letter must pass through (Classroom → School Office → Local Post Office → International Hub). They discuss the "protocols" needed, such as a standardized address format, and why the system would fail (due to scalability issues) if everyone had to know everyone else's exact location.

Students use a command-line tool to see the hops a packet takes from their computer to a website. They analyze the results to identify when the packet leaves their local network and enters the broader internet, noting the different routers and networks it passes through.

ela.standard: Translate quantitative or technical information expressed in words in a text into visual form (e.g., a table or chart) and translate information expressed visually or mathematically (e.g., in an equation) into words.
ela.description: Students can create detailed diagrams, flowcharts, or infographics that explain the structure and function of the internet, translating their technical understanding into a clear visual representation.

science.standard: Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning that the complex interactions in ecosystems maintain relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms in stable conditions, but changing conditions may result in a new ecosystem.
science.description: Understanding that the internet can be analogized to a complex ecosystem, students compare the structure, interactions, and resilience of the internet to those found in biological ecosystems.

other.standard: Explain how current globalization trends and policies affect economic growth, labor markets, rights of citizens, the environment, and resource and income distribution in different nations.
other.description: Students can investigate the geopolitical and economic implications of the internet as a global infrastructure, including issues of control, access, censorship, and the "digital divide."

standards.statement: Identify responsible behavior when using computing systems and tools.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to identify the responsible use of hardware and software in terms of tangible, classroom-level expectations, including caring for hardware (e.g., handling devices gently, keeping food and drink away from devices), making safe choices (e.g., asking permission before using a device, using only the app specified), and being a good citizen in a shared technology environment (e.g., not using someone else's account, using headphones instead of playing sound out loud). Students should focus on understanding that computing systems in schools are tools for learning and should be used appropriately, in the same way other tools are used in the classroom.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand complex cybersecurity or digital citizenship topics.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: The class listens to a read-aloud or watches a short video about the proper use of computing systems and tools. Students work in pairs or small groups to identify and sort the pictures of people using computing technology into responsible (e.g., carrying devices correctly, using a learning app, wearing headphones when using a device) and not responsible (e.g., eating while using a device, playing a game while the teacher is giving instructions and other students are listening) categories.

After an interactive lesson on properly caring for the computing devices, the class will be using, students draw pictures of how to properly care for computing devices and write or dictate a sentence about their picture.

math.standard: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
math.description: Students learn about using positional words (e.g., "Put the headphones beside the tablet." "Place the charger under the shelf.") to help them understand the role of a good citizen in keeping technology safe and organized. Students identify their responsible role by correctly positioning the hardware and verbally stating what they did (e.g., "I put the charger on the shelf." "I put my headphones beside my tablet on the desk.").

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Students are given a set of Behavior Cards showing different ways to treat technology (e.g., eating near a tablet, using two hands, sharing with a friend). Students classify and sort these into the categories "Responsible" and "Not Responsible." They then count how many behaviors are in each set to see which group has more.

ela.standard: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., listening to others and taking turns speaking about the topics and texts under discussion).
ela.description: Students follow the class rules of discussion to work with a partner to categorize teacher-provided images of appropriate (e.g., student using a device on a clean table or desk) and inappropriate (e.g., student using a device while drinking a juice box) use of computing systems and tools describing why the behavior is responsible or irresponsible.

ela.standard: With prompting and support, describe the relationship between illustrations and the text in which they appear (e.g., what person, place, thing, or idea in the text an illustration depicts).
ela.description: Students view Safety Signs for using devices (e.g., a "No Food" sign, a "Headphones" icon). Students describe the relationship between the picture and the classroom rule it represents, identifying the specific "Do" or "Don't" required for responsible use.

science.standard: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air, and/or other living things in the local environment.
science.description: Students learn that computing systems use electricity. They demonstrate their role in being responsible for the environment when using computing systems by "putting the computer to sleep" or turning off the screen when finished to save energy.

science.standard: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of pushes and pulls on the motion of an object.
science.description: When using a touchscreen or mouse, students demonstrate responsible use by using the correct "strength" (a gentle tap vs. a hard poke). They observe that the technology only works as intended when the "push" is gentle, connecting physical science to responsible hardware care.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: Students learn that adults in their lives (e.g., teachers, parents) set rules to keep them safe. Students demonstrate and describe how to respect digital boundaries (e.g., not sharing passwords, using only allowed apps) set by adults.

other.standard: Child appropriately handles and takes care of classroom materials.
other.description: Prior to using classroom devices or robots, students work with their teacher to create a poster illustrating proper care and handling of technology. Students help identify the rules (e.g., Wash hands before using. Stay on the app the teacher picked,.Take turns.) and add their handprint to the poster to make a commitment to responsible behavior.

standards.statement: Describe an individual's role in responsibly using computing systems and tools.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to explain why rules for responsible use of computing systems and tools exist and why following them is important for themselves and their classroom community. They should describe their individual role in meeting these expectations and explain both individual and classroom consequences when expectations are not followed. For example, students could explain that careful handling of hardware (e.g., using devices gently, keeping food and drinks away) ensures devices remain available for everyone and that being a good digital citizen in a shared technology environment (e.g., not using someone else's account, using headphones instead of playing audio aloud) helps maintain a safe and respectful learning space.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe complex digital citizenship topics. Students do not need to understand intellectual property (e.g., copyright), plagiarism, how to identify misinformation, or the nuances of a digital footprint.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: As a class, students brainstorm a list of promises for using classroom technology. Students respond to teacher prompts (e.g., "How do we show we respect our tools?" "What should you do if you see something that makes you feel worried?"). Students' ideas are recorded on an anchor chart with simple text and drawings.

Students work individually or as a class to examine images showing responsible and irresponsible uses of computing tools (e.g., carrying a tablet carefully vs. spilling water on it). They label each image as "Responsible" or "Not Responsible" and discuss what the person is doing and why the choice matters. Students explain the possible consequences of each action, including how it affects the person individually (e.g., losing device privileges, damaging their own work) and how it affects the classroom community (e.g., fewer devices available for others, disruptions to learning). Students demonstrate understanding by explaining one image to the class and describing both the behavior and its impact.

math.standard: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.
math.description: Students apply their understanding of data and graphing to the topic of digital citizenship, analyzing responsible technology use in their classroom. The class identifies three key responsible behaviors for using tablets (e.g., "Use Two Hands," "Take Turns," "Put Away Correctly"). At the end of the week, students collect and organize data on how consistently each behavior was followed and create a class graph. Students interpret the data by answering questions (e.g., "Which behavior happened most?" "How many more times did we use two hands than forget to put tablets away correctly?") and discuss the consequences of the results, including that responsible behaviors help protect devices and ensure everyone has access, and irresponsible behaviors may lead to damaged devices or fewer opportunities for use.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 1 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: Students create a "tech agreement." Its creation is a collaborative conversation during which students both listen to the ideas of others and contribute their own ideas to build a shared set of classroom expectations.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students discuss situations where devices (e.g., computers, tablets) are not being used responsibly (e.g., not plugging them in, mishandling them). They talk about how individual actions can help solve these problems by taking care of tools so they work properly for everyone.

other.standard: Explain the need for and purposes of rules in various settings inside and outside of school.
other.description: Students connect the concept of being a good citizen in the classroom to being a good digital citizen, describing how classroom rules of respect and sharing apply equally to using technology. They discuss classroom responsibilities (e.g., cleaning up) and describe their responsibility to "digitally clean up" by closing unused tabs and logging out of the computer so it is ready for the next person.

standards.statement: Describe the benefits and harms that arise from an individual's use of computing systems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should describe benefits and harms in the context of their own personal experiences, feelings, and well-being. The concepts should be simple and concrete. Describing benefits such as learning new things (e.g., watching a video about animals), having fun (e.g., playing a creative game), and connecting with family and friends (e.g., video-calling a relative) are appropriate. Describing harms such as the physical effects of too much screen time (e.g., tired eyes, feeling grumpy), the emotional effects (e.g., feeling sad or left out by something they see, accidentally seeing something confusing or scary) are also appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe complex or large-scale societal harms. Students do not need to understand issues like the digital divide, the spread of misinformation, or data privacy.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to create a "Benefits and Harms" T-chart on chart paper. Each group brainstorms and records examples from their own experiences (e.g., watching a fun video, playing too long and feeling tired), then draws small icons to represent each. Groups take turns explaining one benefit and one harm to the class, describing how it affects their feelings or well-being. Students demonstrate understanding by sharing personal examples and categorizing them correctly as benefits or harms.

Students work individually or in pairs to review a set of short scenarios about using technology (e.g., "You video chat with your cousin." "You play a game for a long time and feel tired."). Using either physical cards with smiley and frowny faces or a digital drag-and-drop activity, students categorize each scenario as a benefit or a harm. They then explain to a partner or record a short sentence describing why it affects their feelings or well-being. Students demonstrate understanding by correctly identifying benefits and harms and explaining the personal impact of each scenario.

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students collect data about their own experiences with technology, creating a graph to visualize the class's perceived benefits and harms. The class conducts a survey to answer the question "What is the biggest benefit of using classroom tablets?" The survey offers multiple options (e.g., "Learning new things," "Playing games," "Creating art.").

ela.standard: Write narratives in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.
ela.description: Students write a personal narrative about a time they used technology, focusing on describing the benefits or harms they experienced.

science.standard: Make observations of plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.
science.description: Students use pictures of animals from a classroom book and a short educational video and describe one benefit (e.g., learning new facts) and one harm (e.g., feeling scared or confused by images). They demonstrate understanding by explaining how technology affects their learning and feelings compared to observing animals in real life.

other.standard: Identify the benefits and costs of making various personal decisions.
other.description: Students work in pairs to list personal technology choices (e.g., playing a game, watching a video, video chatting with family), and they identify one benefit (e.g., learning something new, having fun, connecting with others) and one cost or harm (e.g., feeling tired, missing playtime, feeling frustrated) for each. They share their lists with the class, demonstrating understanding by explaining how each choice affects their feelings or well-being.

standards.statement: Describe how widely used computing systems may impact an individual's life and community.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to describe both benefits and harms (e.g., effects on safety, privacy, economy, culture) of computing systems in wide use. They should be able to reason about specific scenarios and identify which individuals or communities (e.g., themselves, their parents, children, elderly people, teachers) are impacted by a particular benefit or harm and describe the nature of the impacts.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe the benefits and harms of computing systems or the impacts on communities without first learning about these technologies and communities. Students do not need to memorize a list of technologies and their impacts on specific communities.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to analyze picture cards of widely used technologies (e.g.,video games, video calls, traffic lights, online shopping, screen readers). Groups complete a T-chart identifying one benefit and one harm for each technology and note which group of people is affected (e.g., children, parents, elderly people, teachers). Students demonstrate understanding by explaining how each technology impacts individuals or communities.

From a teacher-created presentation (e.g., digital slideshow), students learn about technology use in their community (e.g., increased screen time, online shopping). For each scenario, students type one benefit and one harm and select who is impacted (e.g., individual, community). Students demonstrate understanding by sharing one completed scenario and explaining the type of impact.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 3 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students discuss the benefits and harms of computing technology and share their ideas in a variety of formats (e.g., round-robin, debate).

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Working in groups, students brainstorm possible solutions to reduce harms of computing technologies while maintaining the benefits (e.g., setting timers for screen use, using parental controls, increasing access to technology).

other.standard: Describe health-promoting behaviors for the dimensions of wellness.
other.description: Students describe how media consumption habits impact their community and discuss how to empower those around them to make intentional decisions that support their overall well-being.

standards.statement: Investigate the impacts of widely used computing systems on natural resources and the environment.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should investigate the environmental effects of widely used computing systems (e.g., artificial intelligence, computers, tablets, monitors). They should designate their effects as harmful or beneficial to Earth's environment and its natural resources. Students can consider large sources of impact (e.g., not disposing of e-waste properly, burning fossil fuels for power, mining of materials, modeling of solutions using technology, conserving energy with "smart" systems) and individual sources of impact (e.g., water and energy usage, frequent device upgrades, recycling/reuse of computing systems and components, information availability about the environment, reduction in paper usage).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to investigate the impacts of computing systems that are not in wide use (e.g., quantum computing). Students do not need specialized equipment or knowledge of science concepts beyond what is grade-level appropriate.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students read age-appropriate articles or watch age-appropriate videos on the impact of AI technologies on the environment and work in small groups to identify and sort the impacts of AI technology into harmful (e.g., water use,  energy use) and beneficial (e.g., climate modeling, "smart" agriculture) categories. Students then brainstorm possible solutions to address the harmful impacts and present their findings in a format of their choice.

Students work in small groups to categorize teacher-provided technology impacts on the environment as harmful, beneficial, or unsure. Each group discusses how each impact should be categorized and why, and the group works together to come to a consensus. Groups then share their categorizations with the class.  As a follow-up, students reflect on how they feel about the impacts and whether they think use of the technology is worth it based on the environmental impacts.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots. For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
math.description: Students interpret graphs or charts that show data about the energy consumption of different devices to determine which devices would have less impact on the environment.

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students solve word problems that involve calculating the total energy costs for their classroom devices for a period of time.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 4 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
