ela.description: Students discuss the impacts of technology on the environment.

ela.standard: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; take notes and categorize information, and provide a list of sources.
ela.description: Students write about the impacts of technology on the environment based on age-appropriate articles or videos.

science.standard: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels are derived from natural resources and their uses affect the environment.
science.description: Students explore how the use of energy and water to power technologies, including generative AI, impacts the environment. Students could identify a harmful effect of tech, such as e-waste, and then brainstorm possible solutions.

science.standard: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth’s resources and environment.
science.description: Students investigate ways that technology can help people preserve and protect Earth's resources and environment.

other.standard: Identify examples of the variety of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) that are used to produce goods and services.
other.description: Students work in pairs to analyze a short scenario about producing a computing device (e.g., a tablet) and list the human capital (e.g., factory workers), physical capital (e.g., machines, tools), and natural resources (e.g., metals, electricity) used in its production. They then explain one environmental benefit and one environmental harm of using that device, demonstrating understanding of how computing technologies rely on resources and impact the environment.

standards.statement: Examine how computing systems impact culture and the ways people live and work.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should examine the cultural impact of existing and emerging computing systems that both help and hinder societal needs. Examples of appropriate topics include the different roles social media plays in our culture and society and how generative AI is changing the way people work.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to identify or reference specific ethical frameworks (e.g., utilitarianism) or sociological concepts (e.g., functionalism). Students do not need to access or use the technologies being discussed (e.g., social media, generative AI).

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students imagine how social media is used differently in different countries (e.g., How does social media change how people share traditions, stay connected, or face challenges?) Students then read informational text to create an opinion piece.

Students examine how online shopping and delivery technologies (e.g., websites, apps, drones, delivery trucks) have changed the way people buy goods. This may include researching specific factors, such as delivery times and carbon emissions, to understand both the benefits and challenges of these technologies.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students examine how computing systems used in online shopping and delivery services impact how people live and work. Using simulated delivery time data (e.g., in fractional days or hours), students create a line plot and use fraction operations to compare shipping options. They analyze how faster delivery systems affect consumer expectations, local businesses, and delivery workers, discussing both benefits (e.g., convenience, efficiency) and trade-offs (e.g., increased packaging waste, pressure on workers).

math.standard: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.
math.description: Students explore packaging by comparing the volume of boxes used for deliveries, connecting to environmental impacts like packaging waste.

ela.standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
ela.description: Students read short informational texts or watch age-appropriate videos about social media use in different regions. In groups, they summarize and discuss key cultural impacts.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
ela.description: Each student writes an opinion piece answering the question "Does social media help more than it hurts society?" using examples from the texts.

science.standard: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth’s resources and environment.
science.description: Students examine how computing technologies (e.g., weather modeling, online maps, energy-monitoring systems) help communities make decisions about natural resources. They discuss how these tools change how people live and work by improving safety, communication, and environmental protection.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students identify a community problem influenced by technology (e.g., remote work, online learning, digital communication) and examine how computing tools help address that need. They analyze how technology changes daily life and work by enabling new solutions while also introducing new challenges.

other.standard: Describe how environmental and cultural characteristics influence population distribution in specific places or regions.
other.description: Students work in small groups to analyze short case scenarios (e.g., people moving to rural areas because remote work and internet access enable them to work from home, cities growing around technology jobs). Each group creates a brief chart identifying how computing technology changes cultural practices and work opportunities. They explain how those changes influence where people choose to live, demonstrating understanding of both population distribution and the cultural impact of technology.

standards.statement: Collaborate to improve the design of a computing system to meet the needs of diverse users.
standards.boundary_includes:
Students should recognize that computing systems need to be designed with accessibility and inclusivity in mind so they can be better used by people with different needs, abilities, and ways of thinking. Examples include providing options for closed captions, adjusting font sizes or colors for readability, providing alternative input devices (like voice control or adaptive keyboards), and including features that support the needs of neurodiverse users. Students should collaborate in teams to propose and refine designs that make a system more inclusive. Students may conduct simple peer testing to evaluate design improvements.
Students are not expected to design hardware from scratch or write complex code for accessibility features. Students do not need to perform professional-level usability testing.

practices.practice: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in teams to evaluate an interactive computing system (e.g., a quiz app mockup, a classroom website, an instructional video interface), identifying barriers related to software design, input methods, and system settings. Teams propose improvements that may involve interface changes (e.g., captions, color contrast adjustments), alternative input options (e.g., keyboard-only navigation, voice control), or compatibility with assistive technologies. After creating a revised mockup or feature plan, teams conduct brief peer testing. To demonstrate understanding, each team submits their revised design and a short rationale that explains how their changes improved accessibility across the computing system.

Students work in pairs to improve the accessibility of a small program or digital activity by considering both software design and system-level features. Each pair selects two accessibility goals (e.g., multiple ways to access information, alternative input methods, reduced cognitive load) and proposes improvements that may include clearer instructions, optional hints, adjustable display settings, compatibility with keyboard-only navigation or voice input, or integration with built-in operating system accessibility tools (e.g., screen readers, text-to-speech). Pairs exchange designs for a brief usability test, gathering feedback on how well the revised system supports different user needs. To demonstrate understanding, students present a before-and-after comparison explaining which system-level and interface changes they made, who benefits from them, and how peer feedback informed refinements.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students collect a small data set about how diverse users experience a computing system (e.g., time to complete a task on different devices, number of errors, how often pages fail to load with weak internet). They summarize the results using measures of center and variability and note any clear patterns or outliers (e.g., one device type consistently takes longer or has more errors). In teams, students use the evidence to propose and justify specific design improvements (e.g., fewer steps, larger text, offline/low-bandwidth mode) that better meet varied user needs.

math.standard: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.
math.description: Students calculate percentages of households with internet access in rural versus urban areas and compare proportions.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: In small groups, students debate which social factor (e.g., income, geography, ability, age) has the greatest impact on computing access, supporting arguments with evidence.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students write an article, blog post, or short report explaining the digital divide in their community, citing data and examples.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students define a design challenge for improving computing access in their school (e.g., loaner laptops, Wi-Fi hotspots) and identify constraints (budget, infrastructure).

science.standard: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.
science.description: Students compare survey or research data on access solutions (e.g., free public Wi-Fi zones, school-issued laptops, community computer labs). They analyze which solution had the greatest positive impact on improving access for underserved groups and propose specific improvements (e.g., extending Wi-Fi range, increasing lab hours, providing devices with accessibility features).

other.standard: Draw on multiple disciplinary lenses to analyze how a specific problem can manifest itself at local, regional, and global levels over time, identifying its characteristics and causes, and the challenges and opportunities faced by those trying to address the problem.
other.description: Students analyze digital access initiatives (e.g., free public Wi-Fi, low-cost broadband programs) and evaluate their effectiveness from different community perspectives.

other.standard: Combine concepts collaboratively to generate innovative ideas for creating art.
other.description: Students use the design thinking process to create a collaborative artwork focused on an awareness campaign about inequitable access to computing systems. The final artwork should combine multiple student ideas into a cohesive awareness campaign that illustrates inequities in access while proposing or showcasing potential solutions.

standards.statement: Examine how access to computing systems can vary based on personal and social factors, such as physical ability, geographic location, socioeconomic status, and age.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should investigate how access to computing systems varies across groups and regions, considering factors like income, physical accessibility, community resources, and infrastructure. For example, students may compare access to broadband internet in urban versus rural areas or explore how adaptive technologies support people with disabilities. Students should analyze examples of digital divides at the personal (home access), the school (device availability), and the community (e.g., libraries, Wi-Fi hotspots) levels. Students may discuss the role of government or nonprofits in expanding access.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to perform statistical analyses of large national datasets, but they may use pre-curated datasets, maps, or local surveys. Students do not need to perform advanced policy evaluation.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in groups to complete the same digital task, but each group is assigned different computing access conditions (e.g., fast internet, slow devices, shared device, limited access time). After completing the task, students compare how their level of access affected efficiency, frustration level, and overall task completion. Students then debrief on fairness and social impacts experienced in their groups.

Students analyze curated datasets or maps showing broadband access by region and create visualizations (e.g., charts, infographics) to highlight patterns of inequity. Students examine which groups or regions have greater or lesser access and discuss contributing factors (e.g., income, infrastructure, geographic location). Students conclude by proposing strategies that could potentially improve access.

math.standard: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.
math.description: Students create visualizations of computing access survey data.

math.standard: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
math.description: Students calculate percentages of households with broadband in different regions.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 8 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students debate solutions to digital divides in schools or communities.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students write a policy brief or an article explaining inequities in computing access.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students propose community-based solutions for expanding computing access.

science.standard: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how increases in human population and per-capita consumption of natural resources impact Earth’s systems.
science.description: Students analyze the environmental impacts of expanding computing infrastructure to underserved areas.

other.standard: Draw on multiple disciplinary lenses to analyze how a specific problem can manifest itself at local, regional, and global levels over time, identifying its characteristics and causes, and the challenges and opportunities faced by those trying to address the problem.
other.description: Students explore case studies of digital access initiatives in different regions.

standards.statement: Evaluate the rationales behind laws and policies governing the design and use of computing systems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to analyze and articulate the reasoning (technical, legal, and social) behind various policies related to the design and use of computing systems. Students should consider the rationale for technical approaches (e.g., responsible design practices, policies requiring two-factor authentication for sensitive data), legal approaches (e.g., COPPA) and social approaches (e.g., social movements, political resistance, personal behavioral change) to shaping the design and use of computing systems. Students should focus on understanding why these policies exist, the problems they aim to solve, and their intended and unintended consequences.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students do not need to read and interpret the text of laws or other legal texts.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students hold a mock hearing. One group represents a tech company (rationale: protecting trade secrets and user safety), and another represents consumers (rationale: reducing electronic waste and saving money). Students must evaluate which rationale is more compelling and propose a compromise policy.

Students use an automated tool to check a website's compliance with accessibility laws. They then research the rationale behind the ADA as it applies to the digital world. They write a reflection on whether "designing for the few" (people with disabilities) actually results in "better design for the many" (curb-cut effect).

ela.standard: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence clearly, concisely, and logically such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, substance, and style are appropriate to purpose, audience, and task.
ela.description: Students conduct a mock legislative hearing or a policy brief presentation where they present their findings on the rationales behind a specific law or policy, using clear and logical arguments supported by evidence from their research.

other.standard: Analyze how people use and challenge local, state, national, and international laws to address a variety of public issues.
other.description: Students compare and contrast the process of creating and enforcing laws for computing systems with the process for other types of laws. They research a specific legal case related to technology and evaluate the court's reasoning based on the principles they have learned.

standards.statement: Investigate how computing systems and infrastructure impact society and the environment, identifying who is affected and why.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should research, analyze, and articulate the societal and environmental impacts of computing systems, including the lifecycle of physical components. This includes, for example, examining energy consumption of data centers, the ethics of electronic waste storage and disposal, the social effects of mobile devices, and the supply chains behind computing technologies. Students should identify which communities are most affected by these impacts and explain why, considering factors such as geography, labor conditions, access to resources, and environmental burden. For example, a student could investigate the supply chain of a mobile device, including its human and environmental costs, and analyze how those costs may disproportionately affect certain workers or communities.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to propose novel technical solutions to these large-scale problems, but rather to analyze and communicate the problems themselves.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students are given "Origin Cards" for various parts of a phone (e.g., Cobalt from the Congo, Glass from Kentucky, Assembly in China, E-waste in Ghana). They map this journey and investigate the specific societal and environmental impacts at each stop, identifying who is affected (e.g., miners, factory workers, local ecosystems).

Students use digital tools (like satellite imagery or environmental reports) to locate a major data center. They investigate its carbon footprint and its energy source (e.g., coal, solar). They then identify who is affected. Perhaps a nearby community gets better infrastructure, but a global community is affected by the resulting CO2 emissions.

ela.standard: Assess the extent to which the reasoning and evidence in a text support the author’s claim or a recommendation for solving a scientific or technical problem.
ela.description: Students read articles or research papers on the societal and environmental impacts of computing and write an analysis assessing the author's claims and the evidence provided.

science.standard: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces impacts of human activities on natural systems.
science.description: Students evaluate a proposed technological solution for reducing the environmental impact of computing (e.g., a new energy-efficient server design, a recycling process for e-waste).

other.standard: Evaluate how economic globalization and the expanding use of scarce resources contribute to conflict and cooperation within and among countries.
other.description: Students can investigate the global supply chain of a computing device, mapping the countries and natural resources involved. They can then research the labor conditions, environmental regulations, and resource-related conflicts in those countries to analyze how economic globalization and the demand for scarce materials create interconnected social and environmental impacts.

standards.statement: Identify computing technologies used in daily life that have changed over time.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should recognize and recall basic visual differences of computing technologies used in school or by their own family members that have changed from older versions. Identifying that the current family phone is smaller and flatter than an older phone a parent or grandparent used or that the family watches movies on a tablet now instead of using a TV are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the internal technological advancements (e.g., faster processors, memory capacity) that caused the changes. Students are not required to know specific historical dates, names of inventors, or the technical functions of the different generations of devices.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students interview a family member or other adult in their lives about an old piece of technology they used in the past (e.g., an old camera, an early phone, a large-screen TV). In a whole-class setting, students use verbal descriptions and drawings to identify the old technology and the modern technology the family uses now to do the same activity. Students would explain one way the old technology was different from the new.

Students work individually or with a partner at a learning center using an app that lets them drag and drop and record. Students are presented with pictures of computing technologies used in schools or at home (e.g., a computer tower vs. a tablet, a home video game console from the 1980s vs. a modern one). Students are asked to identify and drag the "old" picture and the "new" picture of the same kind of technology next to each other and then use the device's recording feature (with teacher support) to record a sentence that identifies a change they see (e.g., "The old one is very big, and the new one is flat.").

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Looking at pictures of various old and new technologies, students  assign them to simple categories (e.g., "things used for talking," "things used for playing"). Then they identify which category has more examples of modern computing technologies used by their family.

ela.standard: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.
ela.description: To strengthen their descriptive communication skills, students identify a computing technology, describing its appearance and comparing it to the older version. The teacher could prompt students to provide additional detail about the differences in size, shape, or color.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.
science.description: To connect a physical change to a technology and a functional change, students identify two versions of a technology (old and new) that solve the same problem (e.g., a landline phone and a cell phone). They then compare the basic strengths and weaknesses (e.g., weakness: a landline is always at home, strength: a cell phone can go with you).

other.standard: Child expresses self in increasingly long, detailed, and sophisticated ways.
other.description: Students sit in a circle and use picture cards of old and new technologies (e.g., a rotary phone and a smartphone, a CD player and a tablet) to describe how people used technology "long ago" and how they use it today. Each student shares a complete sentence explaining the difference (e.g., "Long ago people used ___, and now they use ___."), demonstrating understanding of how computing technologies have changed over time while expressing ideas in longer, more detailed ways.

other.standard: Child shows interest in and curiosity about the world around them.
other.description: After a read-aloud or a short video about how computers have changed over time, students imagine what a computer might look like in the future. They draw a picture of what they envision, which encourages students to see themselves as part of the history of computing.

standards.statement: Compare how an everyday activity changed after a specific computing technology was introduced.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should compare observable differences in how people completed a familiar task before and after a computing technology was introduced. Concrete, everyday examples, such as how people communicate (e.g., writing letters vs. sending text messages) or find information (e.g., using library books vs. searching online) are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the technical details of how technologies work or their historical timelines. Students are not required to analyze societal shifts or economic impacts.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: In two groups, the class finds a local landmark (e.g., the library, the school). One group uses a large paper map, and the other uses an online digital map. The teacher observes which group finds the location first. In a whole-class discussion guided by the teacher, students create a simple Venn diagram on the smartboard comparing the similarities and differences of using paper maps versus digital maps to find locations. Students then individually write or dictate, on paper or using an appropriate app, a simple explanation of how digital maps changed the way people find locations.

Students work in pairs using curated online resources (e.g., videos, interactive sites, ebooks) or physical books provided by the teacher to research how a daily activity (e.g., taking pictures, playing games, reading books, communicating over distance) was changed by a computing technology (e.g., digital cameras, video games, ebooks, email). Student pairs complete a simple "Then and Now" T-chart writing or drawing how people completed the activity before and after the computing technology became popular. Students then share with the class or another student pair their T-chart and one thing that is different (e.g., "Email is faster.") and one thing that is the same (e.g., "You still use words to talk to a friend.").

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section.
ela.description: Students compare a daily activity before and after a computing technology (e.g., playing board games vs. video games). They will then write a short explanatory text describing how daily life changed.

ela.standard: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.
ela.description: Students read or watch a short piece about the invention of a specific computing technology (e.g., the personal computer). They will then compare daily life immediately before and after its adoption, describing the connection between the invention (the cause) and the resulting changes in daily routines (the effect).

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students compare how a task was done before and after a specific computing technology (e.g., calculating sums by hand vs. using a calculator). By observing the difficulties or limitations of the "before" method, students can define the problem that the technology was designed to solve, highlighting the difference in daily life.

science.standard: Analyze data obtained from testing different materials to determine which materials have the properties that are best suited for an intended purpose.
science.description: Students compare the tools used for a task before and after a computing technology (e.g., writing with chalk on a slate vs. typing on a tablet). By discussing or testing the properties (e.g., ease of use, permanence, ability to share) of each "material" (tool), students can explain how the adoption of the new technology changed the daily experience based on the properties of the tools.

other.standard: Describe how human activities affect the cultural and environmental characteristics of places or regions.
other.description: Students compare pictures or descriptions of a place in their community (e.g., the main street, the library) from before widespread computing technology versus after. Then they describe the observable differences, explaining how technology adoption (e.g., fewer bookstores due to online shopping, library computer labs) changed the characteristics of that place.

other.standard: Create a chronological sequence of multiple events.
other.description: Students construct a visual representation that compares daily life before and after a computing technology by creating a simple chronological sequence (e.g., a visual sequence that presents "Before: Families gathering around a radio for news/stories" and "After: Each person using a tablet or computer for news/stories").

standards.statement: Analyze the ways that people from different cultures, backgrounds, and time periods have designed computing technologies to help them solve problems and express themselves.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore how computing technologies have emerged from people's efforts to meet specific needs and express ideas within their geographic, cultural, and historical contexts. An analysis focused on how computing technologies have supported individuals with different abilities throughout history or changed the modes and frequency of communication is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct detailed history on the evolution of computing as a whole. Students are not required to compare complex cultural or societal impacts of technology across time periods.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students imagine how difficult it might be to use a tablet or computer if they could not see and discuss how that might change the way they use technology. The class then brainstorms possible solutions to help someone who is blind or who faces temporary challenges (e.g., using a computer in bright sunlight) use a computer more easily. Students learn about Chieko Asakawa, a computer scientist from Japan who is blind and created a screen reader. As an extension, students could explore accessibility tools on classroom devices (e.g., text-to-speech, voice assistants) and talk about how these features make technology more helpful and inclusive for everyone, in both permanent and situational contexts.

Students learn about creative computing (e.g., digital art, short animations, interactive storytelling) from diverse creators around the world. Students read or watch short videos that profile some of these creators, focusing on how their cultural or personal backgrounds influence their work. Students then use simple creative tools or drawing apps to design a picture or short digital story about themselves, their families, or their ideas and share their creations with the class. Finally, students complete a reflection on how technology helps people express themselves in unique ways.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section.
ela.description: After exploring examples of computing technologies designed in different cultural or historical contexts, students write a short informative text about one technology (e.g., calculator, tablet, communication app). Their writing includes an introduction stating what the technology is, two or three facts about who designed or used it and the problem it helped solve or the idea it helped express and a concluding sentence explaining why it was important in its time or community.

ela.standard: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.
ela.description: Students read or listen to a simple informational text about how different communities and time periods developed communication technologies (e.g., handwritten letters, telephones, email, video chat). In small groups, students sequence picture cards and describe how each technology was designed to solve a communication problem or meet a cultural need, explaining how it changed the way people connected or expressed themselves (e.g., "Telephones let people talk right away instead of waiting for a letter").

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students observe and gather information about a real-world problem that scientists or engineers faced (e.g., studying animals in the dark, measuring temperature in dangerous places, collecting weather data from far away). They then work in pairs to ask questions about the problem and identify how a computing technology (e.g., thermal cameras, digital thermometers, weather satellites) was designed as a tool to address that need. Students explain what the technology observes or measures that humans cannot easily do.

other.standard: Describe how people have tried to improve their communities over time.
other.description: Students examine examples of how people in their local community or other communities have used computing technologies to improve life over time (e.g., traffic lights with computer sensors to keep people safe, library computers for everyone to access information, emergency alert systems to warn about weather), then work in small groups to create drawings or diagrams showing one technology and explain orally or in writing what community problem it helps solve.

standards.statement: Examine how computing innovations have changed the ways people live, work, or communicate over time.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore and explain how computing innovations across different time periods have progressively changed daily life, work, or communication, focusing on concrete, observable changes in human behavior. Examining how finding information, communicating verbally and in writing, enjoying entertainment, shopping, doing tasks at school and work have evolved over time due to computing innovations are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the technical details of how computing innovations work or to create timelines of all computing innovations. Students are not required to examine complex societal impacts of computing innovations.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to create a simple timeline showing the progression of innovations, including computing innovations, in one area of human life (e.g., communication, entertainment, work, learning) across at least three different time periods. Each group selects a focus area and arranges teacher-provided pictures of three or four innovations in chronological order on a poster (e.g., a written communication timeline might show pictures of letters → telegraph → email → smartphone texting). Students write one or two sentences for each stage, identifying the innovation, noting whether it was a computing innovation, and describing what changed at that point based on short descriptions provided by the teacher.

Students work in pairs within an assigned focus area (e.g., how people listen to music, take pictures, find information, watch shows) and use age-appropriate books, articles, videos, and websites to explore how daily activities have evolved over time due to computing innovations. Each pair creates an interactive programming project showing three or more innovations in order from oldest to newest (e.g., record players → CD players → MP3 players → streaming music apps). Their project should include images, approximate time frames (e.g., "long ago," "when our parents were kids," "today"), what each technology did, and how it differed positively and negatively from what came before. Students then share their projects with another pair and discuss what they notice about how things changed over time.

math.standard: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students solve word problems comparing the cost of buying physical encyclopedias in the past versus a yearly internet subscription today, calculating the difference to see how computing has changed access to information. By finding the savings, they mathematically evaluate the economic impact of shifting from physical storage to digital search tools.

ela.standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
ela.description: Students read age-appropriate informational texts about the history of something people do in daily life that has changed due to computing innovations, using sequence words (e.g., first, next, then, finally) to describe the progression of change over time.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: After examining the progression of computing innovations, students write a short text explaining how people's lives changed over time due to computing innovations, using temporal words (e.g., before, after, during) to show the sequence and explaining what was different at each stage.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students examine how access to health information has changed over time (e.g., printed pamphlets, phone hotlines, websites, mobile health apps). They identify observable changes in how people find and use health information and explain how computing innovations (e.g., apps, AI tools) help meet these needs. After discussing remaining challenges (e.g., language barriers, limited internet access), students define a simple design problem to improve access for a specific group, including criteria for success and constraints related to time or materials.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students identify the "problem" of needing to communicate information across long distances and trace how modern digital systems solved this more effectively than manual methods used in the past. They evaluate why older tools were replaced, recognizing that new computing innovations are designed specifically to overcome the limitations of previous designs.

other.standard: Compare life in specific historical time periods to life today.
other.description: Students work in groups to create classroom exhibits, showing the impacts of computing innovations across decades or generations, featuring stories and artifacts from families, local organizations, schools, or the wider community.

other.standard: Generate questions about individuals and groups who have shaped significant historical changes and continuities.
other.description: Students build their understanding that real people made choices and created innovations that have significantly changed society. They generate questions about computing pioneers, innovators, and innovations that changed how people live, work, and communicate.

standards.statement: Investigate the contributions of diverse individuals and communities in the history of computing.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore stories and achievements of individuals and communities whose contributions to computing are often underrepresented or overlooked in mainstream accounts. Students should focus on understanding the concept of diversity or its lack in computing history. Researching and explaining the contributions of women, people of color, and innovators from global communities is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explore the factors that led to historical underrepresentation or exclusion in computing. Students are not required to memorize a comprehensive list of every historical figure.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work individually or in pairs to research an underrepresented person or community in computing history. They create a storyboard, digital poster, computer animation, skit, or diorama illustrating that contribution and why it matters.

Students work as a class to investigate how traditional knowledge systems and cultural practices reflect computational ideas. Students explore how such systems and practices (e.g., weaving patterns, beadwork, Indigenous counting systems) show algorithmic thinking or binary patterns. The class compares these with how modern computers store or process information, emphasizing that computing concepts exist across cultures and time periods. Students show their understanding by creating a drawing, pattern, or short explanation that connects a cultural practice (e.g., weaving, beadwork) to an idea used in computing today.

math.standard: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
math.description: Students solve word problems that calculate the time difference between when an overlooked innovator completed their work and when they finally received credit. This applies multistep subtraction to mathematically quantify the historical delay in acknowledging diverse contributions to the field.

math.standard: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
math.description: Students analyze the geometric patterns in Indigenous weaving or textiles to identify the repeating "rule" (algorithm) used by the artisan. They translate this cultural design into a numerical sequence, connecting the computational thinking of diverse ancestors to the logic used in modern coding loops.

ela.standard: Add audio recordings and visual displays to presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes.
ela.description: Working in pairs or small groups, students research and create an interactive visual display (e.g., poster, diorama) illustrating the contribution(s) of a diverse individual (e.g., Mark E. Dean) or community (e.g., ENIAC programmers) that includes conductive touchpoints that play audio recordings to enhance the presentation.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: Students act as historians to write a biography entry for a computing pioneer who was previously left out of standard textbooks, using clear facts and definitions. This writing task requires them to synthesize research into a permanent record, effectively "debugging" history by adding the missing contributor.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students investigate a specific engineering problem solved by a diverse inventor and compare their unique solution to other methods available at the time. They evaluate how that individual's distinct approach or perspective met the design constraints more effectively than standard solutions.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information.
science.description: Students explore how ancient cultures used drum beats and smoke signals as encoded patterns to send messages over long distances. They connect these early, diverse communication innovations to the binary patterns used in modern computers, recognizing that the concept of "coding" has global, historical roots.

other.standard: Generate questions about individuals and groups who have shaped significant historical changes and continuities.
other.description: Students generate questions about individuals and communities that have changed society with computing innovations. Students then explore texts (e.g., biographies, articles) about these overlooked contributors based on their questions explaining the technical contribution and the historical events happening at that time.

other.standard: Compare life in specific historical time periods to life today.
other.description: Students compare the work experiences of early computing pioneers to the work of computer scientists and engineers today, with specific attention to how opportunities have changed for diverse groups. For example, students investigate the working conditions and opportunities available to computing pioneers like the women computers at NASA in the 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s—who worked in segregated facilities, had limited advancement opportunities, and whose contributions were often unrecognized—to the opportunities and working conditions today at NASA.

standards.statement: Analyze how the inclusion or exclusion of diverse individuals and communities has shaped the design, development, and societal impact of computing technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze historical and contemporary examples of computing innovations, identifying how inclusion or exclusion of certain groups influenced technological progress and access. Analyzing the development of early programming languages or accessibility tools is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct independent historical research or examine complex sociopolitical movements in depth. Students are not required to know specific dates, laws, or named individuals beyond those directly connected to major computing milestones.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to examine historical or contemporary examples of computing innovations (e.g., early computer keyboards, voice-to-text software, closed captioning, screen readers, touchscreen devices). They discuss how the inclusion or exclusion of certain groups (e.g., people with disabilities, non-English speakers, people without access to advanced technology) influenced the design of the technology, who could use it, and how widely it was adopted. In addition, students discuss how inclusive design has increased access and improved technology's impact. Students present or write a persuasive argument defending the importance of including a particular group in the design and development of computing technologies.

Students analyze a current example of an accessibility technology (e.g., voice recognition, screen readers) and discuss how the inclusion of users with different needs shaped its design. They then propose one improvement that would make the technology more usable for a specific group of people and explain how their proposed improvement would impact society.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students try a short task with two versions of a prototype (e.g., small text vs. large text, audio-only vs. captions+audio). They record completion times to the nearest 1/4 minute. They create a line plot and discuss how prototypes change who can access the information and why that matters in computing design.

ela.standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
ela.description: Students use two short teacher-provided sources (one print, one digital) about tools like screen readers, captions, or voice typing to answer "Who does this help and why?" They share how these features show the effect of including overlooked users in computing design.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
ela.description: Students write a proposal for one improvement that would make the technology more usable for a specific group of people. They support their claim with information about how it could help people.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students examine a simple tech product mockup (e.g., login screen, website menu, game controls) and identify a user who might be excluded (e.g., issues with vision, hearing, language, motor skills, limited internet). They write a design problem statement with criteria (must be usable by ___) and constraints (time/cost/materials), linking inclusive design to better computing outcomes.

other.standard: Explain probable causes and effects of events and developments.
other.description: Students work in pairs to analyze how historical practices (such as lack of diversity in workplaces or historical segregation) served as a form of exclusion in technology design. They explain the resulting impact on specific communities, connecting historical social issues to the development and access to modern technology.

standards.statement: Compare the roles of individuals, communities, organizations, and governments in shaping computing technologies across major eras in computing history.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and describe examples of historical and contemporary individuals, communities, organizations, and governments that have influenced the development of computing technologies. Students explain the motivations of these individuals and groups in advancing computing. Students also recognize how these different actors have interacted with one another. Students compare the different roles these groups have played (e.g., designing, funding, regulating, using technologies) and recognize that these actors sometimes work together or influence one another.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to memorize timelines, technologies, or related facts. They are not expected to conduct deep ethical or social analyses. Students are also not expected to evaluate or rank individuals or groups by their relative importance.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students are assigned to a stakeholder group (e.g., an individual programmer, a government organization) and argue from their perspective how and why a significant technology (e.g., the internet, artificial intelligence) should be developed. The "stakeholders" include Ada Lovelace (individual), open-source software developers (community), the Association for Computing Machinery (organization), and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (government). Students have access to a profile of their stakeholder group, the technology's historical development, and major world events occurring during the technology's development.

Students use a digital research tool or interactive timeline to investigate major computing milestones and label each with the type of influence involved (i.e., individual, community, organization, or government). Students will then write brief reflections comparing how these roles changed across computing eras.

math.standard: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.
math.description: Students research and collect quantitative data about a technology (e.g., the number of households with high-speed internet access). Students create a dot plot or histogram to display this data for each major era, then use the visualizations to support a comparative analysis of how the influence of different stakeholder groups (individuals, communities, corporations, and governments) grew or shrank over time.

math.standard: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.
math.description: Students compare the frequency or influence of different contributors across eras using ratios or visual data representations.

ela.standard: Identify aspects of a text that reveal an author’s point of view or purpose (e.g., loaded language, inclusion or avoidance of particular facts).
ela.description: Students analyze different historical information sources about the same computing era, such as the development of artificial intelligence. Students identify each author's point of view and purpose to understand and then compare how the roles and motivations of these different entities shaped the technology's impact.

ela.standard: Write arguments focused on discipline-specific content.
ela.description: Students write evidence-based explanations comparing how different groups shaped computing technologies.

science.standard: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
science.description: Students investigate the history of computing hardware, tracing the environmental impact of e-waste from the personal computer era to today. Students will compare the roles of individual consumers, online repair communities, electronics manufacturers, and government regulations in both creating and attempting to solve this problem over time.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students compare how engineering needs and constraints (e.g., cost, safety, accessibility, scalability) shaped the design of computing systems across eras (e.g., early computers, mainframes, personal computers, cloud systems).

other.standard: Analyze how response to art is influenced by understanding the time and place in which it was created, the available resources, and cultural uses.
other.description: Students analyze examples of digital art from major computing eras and connect the aesthetic and technical qualities of the artwork to the technology available at the time. Students then create a visual timeline that compares how different stakeholder groups directly influenced the development of the underlying technology, which in turn shaped what artists could create and how the art was culturally used and perceived.

standards.statement: Analyze intended and unintended impacts of historical computing technologies on society and the environment.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should distinguish between the intended purpose of a computing technology and its unintended consequences. Students identify and describe clear societal and environmental impacts, such as changes in communication, employment, privacy, e-waste, and energy consumption. They make simple cause-and-effect connections between computing technologies and their outcomes.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct cost-benefit analyses or perform complex calculations to determine environmental impacts. They are also not expected to make detailed predictions about future technologies or develop solutions to the unintended effects they identify.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students will create a visual map as a group, in which they are given a historical technology and use a large poster to visually map out its intended societal impacts alongside its unintended social and environmental impacts.

Students research a specific historic technology using the internet. Students then create a two-column digital infographic that contrasts the intended purpose and societal impacts with its unforeseen impacts, such as e-waste or data privacy issues.

math.standard: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (e.g., 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent.
math.description: Students analyze the environmental impact of smartphone production (e.g., calculating the percentage of rare earth minerals used in a device vs. the total global supply, determining the percentage of e-waste that is properly recycled). Students use these calculations to quantify and compare the intended impacts of the technology against its unintended resource depletion and waste.

math.standard: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions. For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.
math.description: Students analyze a dataset related to the societal or environmental impacts of a historical computing technology (e.g., household internet adoption rates, reported screen time, energy use of data centers). Using random samples (real or simulated) from the dataset, students calculate estimates (e.g., average usage, percentage of households affected) and compare results across multiple samples to observe variation. They use these estimates to draw inferences about the broader population and discuss how the intended purpose of the technology relates to its unintended societal or environmental impacts.

ela.standard: Introduce claim(s), acknowledge alternate or opposing claims, and organize the reasons and evidence logically.
ela.description: Students research a historic technology and then write a structured argumentative essay. Students introduce a claim about its overall societal impact, then acknowledge opposing claims by logically presenting evidence for both its intended and its unintended impacts.

science.standard: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how increases in human population and per-capita consumption of natural resources impact Earth’s systems.
science.description: Students construct an evidence-based argument focused on historic technology with specific focus on the environmental impacts of the technology on Earth's systems. Students research and analyze the intended and unintended impacts of the technology to support their arguments.

science.standard: Construct an argument supported by empirical evidence that changes to physical or biological components of an ecosystem affect populations.
science.description: Students analyze how computing technologies contributed to resource extraction and electronic waste, connecting it to broader environmental impacts.

other.standard: Analyze multiple ways that images influence specific audiences.
other.description: Students analyze propaganda posters, advertisements, and digital art from different eras of computing. Students examine the intended visual messaging and then contrast it with artwork or photography that reveals unintended societal or environmental impacts to analyze how images can shape public perception of technology.

standards.statement: Analyze the historical trajectory of specific computing technologies and how their development is linked to societal and environmental factors.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to investigate a computing technology (e.g., the internet, a social media platform, a specific type of integrated sensor technology) from its inception to its current state, identifying key moments where nontechnical forces directly influenced its design, adoption, or ethical challenges. They should use reliable secondary sources to draw and support their analytical conclusions. For example, high school students could research the rise of mobile computing, analyzing how shifts in economic factors and social trends drove its rapid adoption and evolution.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct or synthesize research on the primary source documents of these technologies, nor are they required to master economic models or complex legal frameworks related to technology regulation.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Referencing a set of historical events (e.g., the Great Depression, World War II, the Space Race, COVID-19) and a set of computing advancements (e.g., mainframes, microchips, satellite communication, video conferencing), students match the advancement to the event and analyze the link (e.g., "Video conferencing tech existed for years, but the social factor of a pandemic turned it into a primary tool for communication.").

Students research the shifts from magnetic tape to floppy disks to CDs to SSDs and, finally, to cloud storage. They create a presentation that analyzes the trajectory. They identify that the shift to cloud storage was an economic choice for businesses (pay-as-you-go) and an environmental challenge (e.g., the massive power use of data centers) compared to the physical manufacturing of disks.

math.standard: Model with mathematics.
math.description: Students use mathematical models to represent historical or societal phenomena (e.g., the adoption of computing technologies over time, economic impacts, environmental costs).

math.standard: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.
math.description: Students analyze data distributions, trends, and associations that can reflect technological diffusion, inequity of access, or economic influence. This supports reasoning about how technological change connects to societal and economic factors.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas, concepts, and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.
ela.description: Students write an analytical research paper examining the historical development of a specific computing technology and explaining how societal and environmental factors influenced its design, adoption, or ethical challenges. Using reliable secondary sources, students organize and synthesize evidence to clearly explain the causal relationships between these nontechnical forces and the technology's evolution.

ela.standard: Determine the central ideas or information of a primary or secondary source; provide an accurate summary that makes clear the relationships among the key details and ideas.
ela.description: Students analyze historical documents (e.g., government policy changes, court cases, company memos, academic papers) to find evidence of the political and economic factors that influenced the trajectory of a chosen technology, thereby integrating historical research skills with CS analysis.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students analyze the history of a technology (e.g., data center energy consumption, the development of e-waste) and then, based on the historical impact, propose and evaluate a revised design or policy solution using the standard's criteria and trade-offs.

standards.statement: Propose modifications to existing policies and legislation that encourage ethical innovation and minimize societal risks associated with technology.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to articulate the rationale behind policies and legislation that guide technological development. This includes explaining how specific laws, like data privacy regulations and rules about algorithmic transparency, are designed to address societal concerns such as discrimination, a loss of privacy, or job displacement. Students should focus on understanding the reason behind technology policy rather than on the process of lawmaking. For example, a student could justify the need for legislation like the European Union's GDPR by explaining how it gives individuals more control over their personal data, thereby minimizing the risk of privacy breaches and misuse.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to draft legal documents, interpret complex legal jargon, or have a deep understanding of the legislative process itself.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students read a summary of a law that allows AI to screen job resumes and review data that shows AI is biased against people from certain ZIP codes. Students propose a modification to the bill (e.g., "An annual bias audit by an independent third party is required.") and explain how this minimizes the societal risk of discrimination.

Students research a current debate topic (e.g., Section 230, which protects websites from being sued for what users post). They must propose a modification that creates a middle ground, protecting free speech while holding platforms accountable for specifically dangerous content, such as viral "challenges" that cause physical harm.

ela.standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
ela.description: When analyzing legislative documents or policy proposals related to technology, students use their ELA skills to break down the text, identify the main arguments, and evaluate the evidence presented. They can assess whether the proposed policies logically address the stated societal risks and whether the claims about technology's impact are supported by evidence.

other.standard: Assess options for individual and collective action to address local, regional, and global problems by engaging in self-reflection, strategy identification, and complex causal reasoning.
other.description: Students examine policies related to AI, data privacy, cybersecurity, or social media regulation. Using civic reasoning skills, they evaluate whether current laws reduce harm and promote ethical innovation. Then, using computational and ethical thinking, they propose realistic policy changes.

other.standard: Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to construct an argument for or against an approach or solution to an economic issue.
other.description: Students analyze the economic trade-offs associated with technology legislation (e.g., a law requiring stricter data privacy may increase the cost of doing business for tech companies, potentially impacting innovation [supply] while also increasing consumer trust and demand for services). This activity helps students understand the complex interplay between government regulation, business, and consumer behavior.

standards.statement: Describe how new technologies create both benefits and risks in personal and family life.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should describe how new technologies (both those they interact with on a daily basis and those they may have learned about in other ways) may not have an exclusively positive or negative impact on their personal or family life. They should consider examples of both benefits and risks. Examples such as video calls with relatives, online learning, AI technologies, or using smart devices at home are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe complex social or economic impacts nor complex new technologies (e.g., quantum computing).

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to sort picture cards of different new technologies (e.g., smartphones, tablets, smart speakers) into "Mostly Helpful," "Mostly Risky," or "Both." Each group shares one example and explains how the same technology can have both benefits (e.g., learning new things) and risks (e.g., spending too much time online).

Students use a simple digital tool to create a "Tech in My Life" presentation, slideshow, or animation. They add pictures or drawings showing one new technology they use at home and describe one positive and one negative effect it can have on their family life (e.g., "We can use tablets or smartphones to watch videos to learn; however, we can also spend too much time viewing a screen that it hurts our eyes).

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students create scaled bar graphs after surveying the class, their families, or other at school on which benefit of technology is most important to them (e.g., games, homework help, talking to family) and which risk they worry about most (e.g., privacy, broken screen, too much screen time). Students then use these bar graphs to describe the benefits and risks of technology and which are more or less important in their lives.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
ela.description: Students write a short paragraph or create a digital slide explaining one new technology they use and describing both a benefit and a risk.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 3 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students discuss in pairs or groups how technologies like tablets or smart speakers can be both helpful and challenging in family life.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Working in small groups, students identify a family need and design a simple technology solution (e.g., a digital chore reminder), listing criteria for success and constraints such as cost or time. Groups explain the technology's benefits and risks to family life, demonstrating how new technologies can both help and create challenges.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans.
science.description: Students examine ways that people are alerted about weather emergencies (e.g., "smart alert" apps, radio, TV) and describe the benefits and risks in current methods and emerging technologies.

other.standard: Explain probable causes and effects of events and developments.
other.description: Students explore a historical "new" technology, such as the first telephone or the first car. They describe how these technologies created benefits (e.g., faster travel, more ways to communicate) and risks (e.g, accidents, less privacy) for families in the past, comparing them to the risks and benefits of technologies today.

standards.statement: Analyze how the limitations of existing technologies can lead to emerging technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to identify a limitation in an older or existing technology (e.g., a weakness, something that doesn't work well, a problem) and logically explain how overcoming that limitation could motivate the creation of a new, emerging technology, focusing on cause-and-effect reasoning in innovation. Analyzing both past (e.g., mainframe computers to laptops, older mobile phones to smartphones) and more current emerging technologies (e.g., auto-complete to generative AI, older model cars to self-driving cars) is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to research the actual motivations for the creation of technologies.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students engage in a teacher-led whole-class discussion on technology for keeping computing devices private. Students generate a list of limitations of using a physical key or a typed password (e.g., forgetting the password, losing the key, someone seeing you type it). Working in pairs, students analyze how these limitations led to emerging biometric technologies (e.g., fingerprint scanners or facial recognition) by identifying a current limitation. It does not have to be in a technology (e.g., not being able to open the door because their arms are full of books). They identify or imagine an emerging computing technology that could overcome the limitation. Students create a poster showing the limitation and how their emerging technology solves it.

The whole class researches one general area of computing (e.g., transportation, communication) to identify technologies that have changed over time. Students will then work individually to analyze the progression from a limitation to an emerging technology for one of the technologies identified by the class (e.g., the limitation of human drivers getting tired and making mistakes, leading to the emerging technology of self-driving cars). Students produce a timeline, flowchart, or other visualization that connects the limitation to the emerging technology and explain the human need being met.

ela.standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
ela.description: Students read articles about the history of the internet, cell phones, or other computing technology and write a short paragraph explaining the limitations that led to the technology.

ela.standard: With some guidance and support from adults, use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of one page in a single sitting.
ela.description: Students gather information about emerging technologies and collaboratively produce digital presentations or written reports, emphasizing the limitations that led to the technology.
