science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students identify a problem in their classroom or community and brainstorm design ideas for a new technology that can help solve the problem.

science.standard: Apply scientific ideas to design, test, and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another.
science.description: Students "design" devices and analyze the limitations of their first prototype (e.g., it doesn't move fast enough) to inform the "merging design of their second prototype, connecting the design process in science to limitations leading to innovation.

standards.statement: Examine how people decide whether or not to use emerging technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze the factors people consider when making personal decisions about using, avoiding, or rejecting emerging technologies, including personal needs and values, benefits, concerns, and accessibility. For example, students might examine why a person would choose to use or reject a smart watch or voice assistant at home by considering convenience, cost, privacy concerns, and accessibility for family members with varying abilities.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to do research studies or understand the technical aspects of how the emerging technologies work. Students are not required to make value judgments about whether people's decisions are "right" or "wrong."

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to analyze pairs of existing and emerging technologies (e.g., landline and smartphone, manual thermostat and smart thermostat, traditional search engine and generative AI tool). For each pair, they identify the limitations of the earlier technology, the new needs or possibilities that led to the newer one, and the trade-offs or concerns that emerged in the process. In groups, students discuss how people's needs, values, or accessibility considerations influence whether they choose to adopt these new tools.

As a class, students design a short digital survey to collect opinions about the usefulness or challenges of emerging technologies in their community (e.g., "What do you like or dislike about smart devices or AI tools?"). After collecting responses, groups analyze common patterns in the data and create brief presentations showing examples of how limitations in existing technologies have inspired innovations and new issues or opportunities those innovations introduce.

math.standard: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.
math.description: Working in pairs, students plot various emerging technologies on a coordinate plane where the X-axis represents "Usefulness" and the Y-axis represents "Privacy Risk." Students demonstrate understanding by interpreting the (x, y) coordinates to justify whether a technology's high utility outweighs its risks, ultimately deciding if the technology is likely to be adopted by the public.

ela.standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
ela.description: Students read two opinion articles (one for and one against) about an emerging technology (e.g., self-driving cars) and identify the specific reasons each author uses to persuade people to use or avoid the technology.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
ela.description: After examining how people decide to use or avoid emerging technologies, students write an opinion piece explaining whether they think people in their community should use or avoid a specific technology.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students identify a community or classroom need that could be addressed with a new technology, weighing both the constraints and benefits from the perspective of different stakeholders as part of their decision-making process.

science.standard: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth’s resources and environment.
science.description: Students research an emerging green technology (e.g.,  AI-managed smart irrigation, biodegradable plastic alternatives) identifying how it protects local resources like water or soil. Students explain the specific scientific benefits and potential community drawbacks that would lead a city or town to decide whether or not to implement the technology.

other.standard: Explain how policies are developed to address public problems.
other.description: As a class, students role-play as a city council to discuss whether the city should allow delivery robots on sidewalks. Students examine how the policy would affect different citizens and which factors (e.g., sidewalk safety, faster delivery) would make people support or reject the robots.

standards.statement: Evaluate when it is appropriate to use AI and other emerging technologies to solve a problem based on their capabilities, limitations, and environmental impacts.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to identify what emerging technologies (e.g., AI, robotics, virtual reality, quantum computing) can and cannot currently do and determine whether they are appropriate for addressing a specific problem. They should consider factors such as technical capabilities, reliability, infrastructure requirements, environmental impacts, and the maturity or readiness of the technology.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the underlying mechanics of these technologies, predict future breakthroughs, or design functioning prototypes. They are also not expected to engage in ethical debates about regulation or human rights implications.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to analyze a set of problem scenarios (e.g., monitoring crop health, improving classroom security, creating immersive historical tours). For each scenario, students evaluate whether an emerging technology (e.g., AI, robotics, virtual reality) is appropriate by considering its current capabilities, limitations, infrastructure needs, and potential environmental impacts. Groups document their decision and reasoning, noting why a technology is suitable, unsuitable, or unnecessary for the task. To demonstrate understanding, students present a brief justification explaining their choice and identifying at least one constraint that influenced their evaluation.

Students examine a specific real-world problem (e.g., reducing food waste in a cafeteria, improving customer support response time, increasing farm efficiency, enhancing online safety). Students research a real-world AI application (e.g., recommendation systems, chatbots, facial recognition) and create a digital presentation that evaluates the technology's capabilities, limitations, and environmental impacts. Students conclude by recommending whether the technology is appropriate for solving the given problem and justify their reasoning.

math.standard: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.
math.description: Students evaluate whether an emerging technology is appropriate for a problem by estimating quantities, resource use, or scale and explaining whether the solution is reasonable given real-world constraints.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students analyze a provided dataset related to an AI system (e.g., accuracy rates across trials, daily energy use over a week). They calculate measures of center (mean or median) and variability (range) and summarize the data in context. Students then explain what the data suggests about the reliability or environmental impact of the AI system and whether it is appropriate for a specific use.

ela.standard: Write arguments focused on discipline-specific content.
ela.description: Students write a short, discipline-focused argument evaluating whether an emerging technology is appropriate for a given problem, citing constraints such as reliability, scale, or environmental impact.

ela.standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
ela.description: Students read and evaluate informational texts about AI applications and identify evidence supporting claims about capabilities, limitations, and impacts.

science.standard: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
science.description: Students use provided data or classroom observations to design a simple method for monitoring the energy use of AI-powered technologies (e.g., tracking usage time, comparing energy ratings of devices). Applying scientific principles about energy consumption and resource use, they propose practical strategies to reduce environmental impact, such as limiting unnecessary use or choosing energy-efficient settings.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students examine a specific real-world problem (e.g., improving customer service response time, reducing food waste in a cafeteria). They compare an AI-based solution and a non-AI solution using defined criteria (e.g., effectiveness, cost, reliability) and constraints (e.g., environmental impact, available infrastructure, ethical considerations). Using a structured evaluation chart or decision matrix, students determine which solution better meets the criteria and justify their reasoning.

other.standard: Examine the origins, purposes, and impact of constitutions, laws, treaties, and international agreements.
other.description: Students evaluate how laws and policies (origins, purposes, and impacts) shape the appropriate use of AI and emerging technologies in society.

standards.statement: Evaluate how design decisions in emerging technologies influence user experiences differently across different communities.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to identify and evaluate examples of how design decisions in new and emerging technologies influence user experiences across different communities. They analyze how selected design choices (e.g., accessibility, language, cost, connectivity, geographic context, device availability) can create benefits or barriers for different groups of users. Students may focus on one or more of these factors rather than addressing all dimensions simultaneously.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct usability studies, apply design frameworks, or create prototypes.

practices.practice: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

implementation_examples.description: Students research a single emerging technology and identify social, cultural, and ecological impacts within a local or familiar community. In teams, students debate whether the technology's benefits outweigh its harms, citing who is helped, who may be excluded, and potential environmental effects.

Students examine real-world examples of emerging technologies through videos, articles, or interactive demos. Using guiding questions, they discuss how specific design choices shape different user experiences across communities. Students then debate which design decisions create the greatest benefits or barriers.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students analyze a dataset related to an emerging technology (e.g., broadband access rates, app usage across language groups, device ownership by region). They calculate measures of center (mean or median) and variability (interquartile range or mean absolute deviation) and describe patterns and deviations in context. Students interpret what the data suggests about how specific design decisions (e.g., cost, language options, connectivity requirements) affect different communities.

math.standard: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
math.description: Students use ratios and proportional reasoning to compare how different communities are affected by an emerging technology (e.g., percentage of users with access to closed captions, proportion of households able to afford a subscription service). They interpret how design decisions such as pricing, device compatibility, or connectivity requirements create proportional differences in access and user experience.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students engage in structured small-group discussions evaluating how specific design choices in an emerging technology (e.g., language availability, accessibility settings, pricing structure) affect different communities. Students build on one another's ideas, respond to counterexamples, and refine their reasoning using evidence from case studies or data.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students prepare debate notes or reflections explaining their stance on an emerging technology's community impact.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students examine a scenario in which an emerging technology does not equally serve all users (e.g., a health app that requires high-speed internet). They define a design problem focused on improving inclusivity and identify specific criteria (e.g., accessibility, affordability, language support) and constraints (e.g., budget, environmental limits, device compatibility) that must be considered.

science.standard: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
science.description: Students analyze how design decisions in emerging technologies (e.g., always-on connectivity, high processing demands, frequent device upgrades) contribute to environmental impacts such as energy use or e-waste. Applying scientific principles, students design a method to monitor one impact (e.g., device energy consumption, waste production) and propose strategies to minimize it.

standards.statement: Debate ways an emerging technology impacts the social, cultural, and environmental issues in local communities.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to assess the potential or current impact of emerging technologies to address local community needs. Focusing on a specific emerging technology, students should be able to construct arguments with references for a debate on positive and negative impacts of that technology. Students could either debate which applications of an emerging technology have the greatest or least impact or argue for or against a particular application. Students should pay attention to who is impacted and how they are impacted as well as to costs and harms to the community and environment.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand all the technical details of emerging technologies.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students research and document key points for a debate on either the pros or the cons of whether traffic cameras are a benefit or harm to individuals and the community. Students make recommendations about the privacy of data collected, the potential economic impact (e.g., installation costs, hardware, data storage, people paying fines, court costs) and legal challenges, the potential for increased or decreased safety, and whether the technology suffers from any bias.

Students engage in a structured debate about how a specific emerging technology (e.g., facial recognition, delivery drones, AI tutoring tools) impacts social, cultural, and environmental issues in their community. Using evidence from credible sources, students argue for or against a particular application, addressing who is affected, potential benefits, and possible harms. An online discussion platform may be used to facilitate real-time responses and visually map connections between arguments.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Reporting the number of observations.
math.description: Students analyze a dataset related to a local emerging technology (e.g., projected costs of building and operating a data center). The dataset might include numeric and non-numeric data (e.g., the need for increased energy and data transmission infrastructure, environmental costs, cost of access to high-speed computing). Students report the number of observations, summarize key numerical measures in context, and explain what the data suggests about potential community impacts before forming a position in a class debate.

math.standard: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.
math.description: Students use provided bivariate data (e.g., number of data centers in a region and annual energy consumption, percentage of households using streaming services and local electricity usage) to construct a scatter plot. They interpret patterns of association and discuss how the data informs arguments about the environmental impacts of emerging technologies in their community.

ela.standard: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text (e.g., through examples or anecdotes).
ela.description: Students closely read articles, reports, or media about emerging technologies (e.g., AI, social media, renewable energy, surveillance tools) and analyze how those technologies affect people and communities (social); beliefs, traditions, and communication (cultural); and land, resources, and ecosystems (ecological). Students debate the cause-and-effect relationships between technology and community issues.

ela.standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
ela.description: Students read a different article about the potential impacts of a technology (e.g., social media, quantum computing). Students summarize the main claim about the technology's impact and track the evidence in the article that supports it.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students research and debate how the increased use of drones impacts people (e.g., individuals, jobs, culture) and the environment. Students can evaluate drones in terms of benefits, risks, equity, and environmental consequences in their own school and communities.

standards.statement: Evaluate the fundamental technological differences between an emerging technology and established technologies and how those differences influence computing.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to evaluate the technological advances that distinguish an emerging technology from existing technologies and how they enable features or address limitations in current systems. For example, quantum computing uses superposition and entanglement to represent and manipulate information more compactly than classical systems. This allows certain data structures and computations to be expressed with fewer physical resources.
standards.boundary_excludes: The degree to which students are introduced to a technical concept is dependent on the technology and the backgrounds of the students. For example, quantum operations would be reasonable, but not necessary, to introduce, but the introduction of the quantum mechanics underlying superposition and entanglement is not expected.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students research virtual reality (VR) technology and compare it to established computing interfaces (e.g., traditional web browsers, 2D gaming systems). They identify fundamental technological differences (e.g., motion tracking sensors, stereoscopic displays, immersive 3D rendering) and evaluate how these differences change user interaction, system requirements, and computing capabilities. Students analyze how VR's underlying technologies enable new forms of interaction while also introducing trade-offs (e.g., increased processing demands, hardware complexity).

Students consider how an emerging technology like quantum computing could be used to break current encryption methods. They hypothesize that instead of using current encryption schemes that rely on the difficulty of factoring products of prime numbers, quantum computing will lead to new cryptographic algorithms that use mathematical functions that quantum computers currently cannot solve quickly, creating a world where certain entities (e.g., governments, businesses) have access to formerly private information while others do not.

ela.standard: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects to answer a question (including a self-generated question) or solve a problem; narrow or broaden the inquiry when appropriate; synthesize multiple sources on the subject, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.
ela.description: Students develop a research question comparing an emerging technology (e.g., quantum computing, AI-assisted design tools) with an established technology. Using multiple reliable sources, they investigate the fundamental technological differences between the two and synthesize their findings in a research-based analysis. Students refine their inquiry as needed and conclude by evaluating how those differences influence computing capabilities, limitations, or system design.

science.standard: Communicate technical information about how some technological devices use the principles of wave behavior and wave interactions with matter to transmit and capture information and energy.
science.description: Students evaluate the core differences between classical computing (existing) and quantum computing (emerging) by researching how qubits use superposition to represent multiple states at once, unlike the binary constraints of classical bits. They analyze how quantum algorithms can solve specific types of problems (e.g., simulating molecular bonds) that are computationally intractable for classical parallel systems due to the increase in required processing power.

standards.statement: Evaluate the societal and environmental impacts of emerging technologies, including those that lead to inequities in access and outcomes.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to critically analyze an emerging technology by identifying and assessing its potential positive and negative effects on society and the environment. This includes considering how the technology might create or worsen social inequities in access and outcomes. Students should focus on developing a well-reasoned, conceptual argument about an emerging technology's broader impacts. For example, a student could evaluate the use of generative AI in education. They would identify not only the potential positive impacts, like providing personalized tutoring, but also the negative ones, such as the potential for academic dishonesty and the risk of widening the digital divide for students without access to these tools.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct a formal, data-driven sociological or environmental study.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students choose an emerging technology, such as "Personal Flying Drones for Delivery." They sit in a circle representing different stakeholders (e.g., a tech CEO, a bird sanctuary worker [environmental], a local delivery driver [societal/jobs], a resident in a low-income neighborhood [access/inequity]). They evaluate the impact from each perspective to decide if the technology should be allowed in their city.

Students evaluate a proposed application of quantum computing for improving molecular modeling in fertilizer production. They research the current environmental impacts of fertilizer manufacturing and use, as well as existing challenges in global food production. Students analyze potential positive impacts (e.g., increased efficiency, reduced chemical waste, improved crop yields) and negative impacts (e.g., increased industrial consolidation, inequitable access to advanced agricultural technologies). They develop a reasoned argument assessing how this emerging technology could affect environmental sustainability and social equity in food systems.

ela.standard: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence clearly, concisely, and logically such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, substance, and style are appropriate to purpose, audience, and task.
ela.description: After evaluating the societal and environmental impacts of an emerging technology, students deliver a structured oral presentation in which they clearly articulate their claim about the technology's overall impact. They organize their presentation logically (e.g., background, positive impacts, negative impacts, inequities, conclusion) and support their reasoning with evidence from credible sources, tailoring their tone and content to a specific audience (e.g., school board, community members, policymakers).

science.standard: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces impacts of human activities on natural systems.
science.description: Students apply their scientific evaluation skills to technology (e.g., evaluating the environmental impact of a large-scale data center). They then propose and evaluate a technological solution (e.g., using a different cooling system, using a new energy source) that would reduce the technology's environmental footprint, directly linking the technology to an environmental system.

other.standard: Evaluate public policies in terms of intended and unintended outcomes, and related consequences.
other.description: Students research how local or national governments are responding to the societal impacts of emerging technologies. They evaluate the effectiveness of proposed legislation or public policies aimed at mitigating negative impacts (e.g., laws restricting the use of facial recognition technology, policies encouraging renewable energy for data centers).

standards.statement: Design a conceptual solution to a real-world problem using an emerging technology, analyzing its potential benefits and harms.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should be able to design a conceptual or tangible solution to a real-world problem by applying an emerging technology. This process must be supported by credible research on both the problem and the technology's capabilities. The solution should also be mindful of ethical implications, with students analyzing the potential benefits and harms to different groups of people and the environment. For example, a student could create a design document for a system that uses AI to analyze satellite imagery to help track deforestation, addressing a real-world environmental problem. Their work would include research to support their claim and a discussion of the ethical considerations, such as the potential for misuse of the data.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to build a fully functional, production-ready version of their solution. Students are not expected to engage in complex engineering.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students use Computer Vision to design a smart recycling bin to automatically sort trash. Instead of building it, they create a detailed blueprint and a "research poster." The poster must include a section on potential harms (e.g., the environmental cost of manufacturing the sensors vs. the carbon saved by better recycling).

Students use a prototyping tool to design an app that uses natural language processing (NLP) to translate sign language into text in real time. They must include a "design document" that cites credible research on how NLP works and provides an ethical analysis regarding the accuracy of the translation and the privacy of the people being filmed.

ela.standard: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects to answer a question (including a self-generated question) or solve a problem; narrow or broaden the inquiry when appropriate; synthesize multiple sources on the subject, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.
ela.description: Students conduct a sustained research project to support the design of a conceptual solution using an emerging technology. They develop or refine a research question related to the problem and the technology's capabilities, gather information from multiple credible sources, and synthesize their findings to inform their proposed solution and ethical analysis. Students narrow or broaden their inquiry as needed and present their conclusions in a structured written report.

science.standard: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.
science.description: Students analyze a major global challenge (e.g., climate change, food insecurity, access to clean water) and define specific qualitative and quantitative criteria for a potential solution using an emerging technology. They identify constraints (e.g., cost, energy consumption, infrastructure requirements, environmental impact, societal equity). Before proposing a conceptual solution, students justify how their criteria and constraints reflect both scientific principles and societal needs.

other.standard: Analyze historical, contemporary, and emerging means of changing societies, promoting the common good, and protecting rights.
other.description: Students select a problem facing their local community (e.g., inefficient public services, limited access to transportation information) and research historical and contemporary efforts to address it. They then analyze how an emerging technology could serve as a new means of promoting the common good or protecting rights. Students compare the proposed technology-driven approach with earlier civic strategies and evaluate its potential benefits and drawbacks for different community members.

standards.statement: Explain that people design and develop computing technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should recognize and express that the computing technologies they use every day (e.g, tablets, apps, programmable toys) do not appear by magic, but are created by people to help solve problems or for entertainment. For example, during a classroom discussion about a favorite game, a student might explain that a person had to think of the rules, draw the characters, and program the game before they could play it.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the technical details of how technologies are built. Students are not required to build their own functioning electronic computing technologies.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a whole-class discussion and a large sorting activity on a wall or chart. The teacher provides a collection of picture cards. Some cards show computing technologies (e.g., tablet, app, video game) and some show natural objects (e.g., rock, flower, cloud). The teacher also displays photos of diverse people (different ages, genders, backgrounds) labeled "Creators." Students describe which pictures in the first set were "Made by People" versus "Not Made by People." When students identify a technology, the teacher places it under the "Creators" photos. Students then describe that a person (not magic) designed the app or built the computer, demonstrating their understanding that people are the creators.

Students participate in a whole-class guided exploration by watching a curated video and then having a "turn and talk" discussion. The teacher finds a short, kid-friendly behind-the-scenes video that shows a real person (e.g., an animator, a game designer) in the process of creating a digital technology. The video should show the person thinking, drawing on a tablet, or working with a team.

ela.standard: With prompting and support, describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
ela.description: After a read-aloud of a picture book about an inventor or a person who created a computing technology, students engage in a whole-class teacher-led discussion. They use a chart to draw a line connecting a person to the specific technology they designed. Students demonstrate understanding by orally explaining how a person having an idea led to the technology we have today, showing the direct connection between human effort and the existence of technology.

ela.standard: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
ela.description: Students use an appropriate digital tool to create a thank-you card for the person who designed their favorite classroom app. They draw a picture of the app and dictate a sentence to the teacher or they use a speech-to-text tool to express what they appreciate about the app. This enables students to produce an artifact that identifies a human as the developer of the technology they enjoy.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: During circle time, students discuss a teacher-presented problem (e.g., "It is hard to remember to water our class plant.") and brainstorm a helper tool that a person could design (like a light that blinks when the soil is dry), illustrating that technology starts with a person trying to solve a problem.

other.standard: Child analyzes results, draws conclusions, and communicates results.
other.description: After using a floor robot that has buttons for programming, students discuss in pairs what happened when they pushed the buttons. The teacher prompts them to consider "Why did the person who made this robot put the 'Go' button in the middle?" and students explain their conclusion that the designer wanted it to be easy to find.

other.standard: Engage in self-directed play with materials.
other.description: Students, individually, use craft and recycled materials (e.g., boxes, foil, buttons) to build a "prototype" of a new computer or robot. They describe to the teacher one choice they made during the build (e.g., "I gave my robot big ears so it can hear us better."), connecting artistic creation to the design and develop process of technology.

standards.statement: Differentiate between activities that humans do well and activities that computing technologies do well.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should categorize and explain simple, observable differences in what humans and computing technologies do best for various tasks. Examples of human strengths, such as creativity, understanding feelings, and solving new problems, are appropriate. Examples of computing technology strengths, such as repeating tasks without mistakes, calculating quickly, and remembering lots of information, are also appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the cognitive science behind human intelligence or the technical details of how computing technologies perform certain tasks. Students are not required to analyze ethical or societal consequences that arise from humans or machines performing specific tasks.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in pairs to sort illustrated task cards into the categories of "Humans Do Better" or "Computers Do Better." Cards have a picture and a description of an activity (e.g., "count to 1,000," "tell a funny story," "draw a picture of a new type of animal," "check 100 math problems"). Students discuss and explain where they would place each card. They place "telling a funny story" under "Humans Do Better" because it requires creativity and feeling. Pairs of students will produce a sorted set of cards and explain their reasoning to another pair. After the teacher reviews each pair's choices, the class discusses why humans excel at certain activities and computers excel at certain other activities.

The whole class identifies a simple task that is difficult for humans (e.g., calculating all the class's birthdays into days, not months) but easy for a computer. Students then work individually using a simple drawing app or presentation tool on a device. They identify a computing technology that could help them create a simple drawing that shows the human and the computer working together to solve a problem. They explain which part the human did (the creative, thinking part) and which part the computer did (the fast, repetitive part).

math.standard: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 – 4 = 13 – 3 – 1 = 10 – 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 – 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
math.description: Students practice their math facts in pairs and then the teacher demonstrates how fast a computer (e.g., spreadsheet software, calculator) can solve the same problems, asking why it is important for people to know how to calculate the problems themselves. Students should be able to explain that humans need to understand the math to know if the computer's answer makes sense.

math.standard: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.
math.description: In a whole-class activity, students use a digital graphing tool to instantly organize and represent data about class snack preferences (e.g., apples, popcorn, crackers). Students then work in pairs to interpret the graph and answer "how many more" questions, ultimately explaining that while the computer was faster at representing the data, only humans can make the final, empathetic decision (e.g., choosing a different snack to include a classmate with an allergy), highlighting the unique strengths of human judgment over computer logic.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 1 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: Students discuss differences between humans and computers in groups, practicing communication skills.

ela.standard: Identify basic similarities in and differences between two texts on the same topic (e.g., in illustrations, descriptions, or procedures).
ela.description: Students read two short descriptions: one of a person painting a masterpiece and one of a machine painting a car. Working in small groups, students identify what is the same (both are painting) and what is different (the person makes creative choices; the machine follows a set path).

science.standard: Use materials to design a solution to a human problem by mimicking how plants and/or animals use their external parts to help them survive, grow, and meet their needs.
science.description: In a whole-class brainstorming session, students identify a problem (e.g., needing to reach a high shelf), discuss why a human is better at identifying the problem and why a computing technology (e.g., a robot with sensors) is better at performing the repetitive, high-reach task without getting tired. Students produce a drawing of their proposed robot and explain that they provided the creative idea and the technology provides the physical strength and consistency needed for the solution.

science.standard: Develop a simple sketch, drawing, or physical model to illustrate how the shape of an object helps it function as needed to solve a given problem.
science.description: Working in pairs, students engage in a sorting challenge where they must sort a pile of mixed recycled materials by shape. They first do it by hand, then "program" a classmate acting as a "sorting machine" to do it using only one rule (e.g., "If it is round, put it here."). Students show their understanding by presenting a sketch of a machine that would be better at sorting because it wouldn't get distracted while explaining that a human is still better at deciding what should be recycled in the first place.

other.standard: Apply civic virtues when participating in school settings.
other.description: During a whole-class discussion about playground rules, students determine if a computer could decide who gets to go first on the slide. Students create a list of reasons why a human is better at this task because a human can see if someone is sad or if someone has been waiting a long time, whereas a computer might just follow a timer.

standards.statement: Investigate situations where humans have created computing technologies to solve problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should investigate familiar, concrete examples of how people have designed computing technologies to address everyday problems they can relate to. Technologies with clear, observable purposes are appropriate, such as traffic lights that help cars and pedestrians move safely, barcode scanners that help stores track inventory, automatic doors that help people enter buildings, weather apps that help families plan activities, or classroom timers that help manage transitions. Students might investigate how these technologies were created to solve specific problems, like "cars were crashing at intersections" or "it was hard to keep track of library books."
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand how computing technologies work internally or to explain programming, engineering, or data processes. Students are not required to analyze historical development, compare technologies, or address advanced issues such as data privacy, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, or automation.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Engaging with stations that are set up in the classroom, pairs of students match technology objects or images of technology (e.g., a barcode scanner, a digital thermometer, a GPS device) to a "Problem Card" (e.g., "It takes too long to type in the price of every item at the store."). Students demonstrate their understanding by creating a simple drawing that shows the person who has the problem and the technology that solves it.

The class watches a short video about assistive technologies, such as a screen reader or a speech-to-text app and discusses what was hard for the person before they had this tool. Students use a digital platform to write or record a reflection on how the technology solved a specific barrier (e.g., helping someone who cannot use their hands write an email using their voice).

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students investigate a problem (e.g., What is the most popular way for our class to get home safely?), collecting data and using a digital graphing tool to represent it. Students explain that although they could count by hand, the computing technology solved the problem of making the information easy to read and understand quickly.

ela.standard: Participate in shared research and writing projects (e.g., read a number of books on a single topic to produce a report; record science observations).
ela.description: With a partner or in small groups, students research a computing pioneer or innovator (e.g., Katherine Johnson, Margaret Hamilton, Steve Jobs) identifying the "problem" the person was trying to solve. Students produce a poster that includes a drawing of the problem and the technology created to solve it and present their poster to another group or the class.

ela.standard: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to clarify comprehension, gather additional information, or deepen understanding of a topic or issue.
ela.description: Students participate in a class discussion or interview with a librarian about how the barcode scanning system works and why it was created, asking questions they prepared before the interview (e.g., What problem did barcode scanners solve? How did librarians keep track of books before scanners? What happens when you scan a barcode?). After the interview, students answer comprehension questions and share what they learned about how humans created this computing technology to solve a problem in the library.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students watch a video of a busy street corner and identify the problems they see (e.g., too many cars, people don't know when to cross, cars almost crash) to define a problem that should be solved. Students then learn about how people created traffic lights to solve the problem, discussing how the traffic light tool uses colors and timing to help everyone stay safe and connecting how humans make computing technologies to fix real problems they observe in their community.

science.standard: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.
science.description: Students compare two ways to check out library books: writing names on paper cards versus using a barcode scanner. They test both methods by timing how long it takes to check out five books with each system and counting any mistakes. Students make a simple chart showing their findings: paper cards took 3 minutes and had two mistakes, whereas the scanner took 1 minute with no mistakes. The class discusses what works well and what doesn't work well about each system. Students learn that people created barcode scanner technology because it speeds up checkout and also eliminates most, if not all, errors.

other.standard: Describe how human activities affect the cultural and environmental characteristics of places or regions.
other.description: Students investigate how GPS navigation apps help families travel to new places, discussing how people today find their way to places where they've never been and how they found their way in the past. They compare old paper maps to GPS technology, examining how people created computing tools that give turn-by-turn directions and show current location. Students discuss how this human-designed computing solution changed travel by making it easier for people to explore new neighborhoods, visit relatives, or find stores without getting lost.

other.standard: Explain how all people, not just official leaders, play important roles in a community.
other.description: Students explore how store checkout scanners help cashiers serve customers. They identify the problem cashiers need to solve (quickly adding up prices for many items without making mistakes). Students visit a local store or watch a video showing how cashiers use barcode scanners to ring up purchases accurately and quickly. They discuss how people created this computing technology to help store workers do their jobs better and serve more customers. Students role-play being cashiers using pretend scanners, experiencing how the technology helps community workers provide important services. They create posters showing different community helpers who use computing technologies to solve problems in their jobs.

standards.statement: Examine why people design and build computing technologies.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore the basic reasons computing technologies were created and communicate the needs or problems these technologies were likely intended to address, focusing on the human intent or goal. Examining how computing technologies, such as AI systems, are designed to meet needs, solve specific problems, make tasks easier, or provide entertainment is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the technical details of how computing technologies work. Students are not required to compare multiple technologies to determine which best meets a particular need.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to examine various computing technologies they encounter in their lives (e.g., laptop, tablet, video game console, fitness tracker, voice assistant, smartphone, robot vacuum, recommendation system) using pictures and descriptions supplied by the teacher. Each group records their findings on a graphic organizer: "What does this technology do?" "Why do you think someone created it?" "Who might it help?" "Who might it harm?" They share their findings with the class. The class then engages in a teacher-facilitated discussion about common themes (e.g., making life easier, solving problems, helping people stay healthy, providing entertainment).

The class engages in a teacher-led discussion about an existing computing technology they all use (e.g., a learning game, a photo app), focusing on why the technology might have been created. Working individually or in pairs, students act as different users (e.g., young child, someone with a disability, older family member) who would like to use a similar technology. Students create a slide in a collaborative slide deck illustrating how their user could benefit from a similar technology but also how it might be designed specifically to meet their needs (e.g., if they discussed an app the class uses for reading, students might produce a visual design for a read-aloud app for a younger sibling just learning to read, explaining the specific purpose and the user it was built for).

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: Students collect data from classmates, other students at school, and families about the reasons people might have created certain computing technologies and then create bar graphs showing which reasons are most common among the technologies they identified.

ela.standard: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
ela.description: To connect the author's purpose in the text to the designer's purpose in the technology, students read a short article about a computing technology (e.g., digital medical device, large language model) and determine the main idea and key details about why the technology was created.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 3 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students engage in discussions during the examination of computing technologies, sharing their thinking about why different computing technologies were designed, building on classmates' observations, and collaboratively identifying patterns in how technologies are designed to meet human needs or wants.

science.standard: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.
science.description: Students examine computing technologies through the lens of engineering design, identifying the problems or needs each technology was created to address. Students then practice defining their own simple problems that a computing technology could solve.

other.standard: Explain probable causes and effects of events and developments.
other.description: Students are assigned a specific era of computing and provided with resources (e.g., books, articles, short videos) needed for research. They examine the resources to identify the historical event (e.g., 1960s Space Race, 1990s internet adoption, COVID-19) and how computing technology (e.g., integrated circuits in computers for space guidance, network protocols and the World Wide Web to share data across distances, improvement and adoption of video conferencing software) were designed, built, or improved around these events.

standards.statement: Distinguish between human learning and machine learning processes.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should compare and contrast basic characteristics of human learning and machine learning using simple, observable examples. For example, humans learn by making sense of experiences and drawing on prior knowledge, and AI systems use patterns or correlations in data to make decisions or generate new things.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand mathematical modeling, neural networks, or algorithmic training processes in technical detail nor are they expected to understand human cognition in detail. Students are not required to use or code actual AI models or apply formal data training procedures.

implementation_examples.description: Students play a "machine learning" card-sorting game to categorize several cards of animals. The students split into two groups. One group acts as the machine learning algorithm that learns to separate cats and dogs based only on data patterns (e.g., number of legs, tail shape, ear size). The other group acts as the human that learns to separate the animals based on observable differences (e.g., ear shape, snout, tail, claws) and their personal experiences. Students then reflect on how the group acting as humans used reasoning and prior knowledge to learn and the group acting as a machine learning algorithm used repetition and examples. To demonstrate understanding, students compare and explain these differences verbally or by drawing two columns labeled "Human Learning" and "Machine Learning" with key characteristics. The students engage in a whole-class discussion focusing on reinforcing that human learning includes imagination and emotions, whereas machine learning depends on analyzing patterns in data.

Students observe and discuss classroom activities (e.g., learning to draw a shape, learning to tie a knot), focusing on how humans use data we collect over time from observation, practice, and memory. Then the teacher shows a video or uses simple analogies to explain how a computer "learns" to do the same task by gathering data, receiving instructions, and receiving repeated reinforcement. Working individually or in pairs, students create a simple diagram or T-chart contrasting human learning traits (e.g., using emotions, experiences, guesses) with machine learning traits (e.g. using data, rules, repetition). Students present their diagrams to peers and explain their reasoning, demonstrating conceptual understanding through visuals and oral language.

math.standard: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
math.description: Working individually, students generate a pattern of numbers (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16...) and explain the rule they used to create it. After watching a demonstration of a simple online pattern-predictor tool, students should be able to express that they used logical thinking to create the rule, whereas the computer used a  rule it had learned by looking at the numbers provided to it and finding the mathematical gap.

ela.standard: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
ela.description: Students read a firsthand account of a child learning to ride a bike on the street and an article about how a self-driving car "learns" to navigate a street. In a whole-class discussion, students produce a Venn diagram comparing the two scenarios, identifying that the human account focuses on feelings and trial-and-error, while the computer's learning focuses on sensors and data collection and analysis.

ela.standard: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
ela.description: Students work in small groups to research how a specific technology "learns," such as a music streaming service's recommendation engine versus how a person discovers new music. They produce a digital slide or poster that highlights the investigation of the two processes, explaining that the human learns through social interactions and personal taste, and the technology learns by analyzing the listening data of millions of other users.

science.standard: Use a model to describe that animals receive different types of information through their senses, process the information in their brain, and respond to the information in different ways.
science.description: Students act out a scenario where they smell smoke and decide to exit a building, then investigate how a smart smoke detector is trained to recognize a fire. Working in pairs, students create an animation showing that the human uses the sense of smell and the brain's past knowledge, whereas the technology uses a sensor and a programmed pattern to respond.

other.standard: Explain how cultural and environmental characteristics affect the distribution and movement of people, goods, and ideas.
other.description: As a class, students examine how the routes to move goods (delivery routes) from one place to another were once learned by drivers using their memory and senses through years of local experience versus how current GPS technologies learn the fastest routes by analyzing patterns and real-time traffic data from thousands of cars. Students show their understanding by demonstrating human and computing technology delivery methods where one student explains their route based on "knowing the neighborhood" and the other uses a digital map, explaining that the technology learns from everyone's data, whereas the human learns from their own experience over time.

standards.statement: Evaluate when it is appropriate to use or not use computing technologies to solve a problem.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate and justify whether computing technologies are the best tools for solving a specific problem by considering the context, potential benefits, and potential drawbacks. These potential benefits and drawbacks can include technical, ethical, privacy, or environmental considerations. Students should focus on analyzing the feasibility of whether the solution requires computing. Deciding that AI is helpful for quickly translating a simple sentence but is not appropriate or helpful for deciding who should receive the last slice of pizza, which requires human judgment and social skills, is appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand ethical frameworks, legal implications, or technical performance metrics (e.g., error rates, training data bias) used by professional engineers to make these decisions. Students are not required to solve the problem.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to evaluate several teacher-provided problem scenarios (e.g., counting the votes for class president, picking out clothes for school, writing a letter to a sad friend). For each scenario, the group must decide and justify whether a computing technology (e.g., word processor, generative AI chatbot) would be appropriate and helpful They might decide that counting votes is appropriate for a computer because it offers speed and accuracy, but that comforting a friend is not because the computer has no empathy or emotion.. They present their findings in a class discussion, demonstrating their evaluative judgment.

Each student completes the same specific task (e.g., create a party invitation, find the closest grocery store).  Half of the students use appropriate computing technologies (e.g., graphic design app, search engine, map app), and the other half use analog tools (e.g., paper, pens and other writing and drawing tools, paper maps, books). Students then discuss the activity in small groups or pairs, sharing how their experiences and outputs differed and identifying pros and cons of using technology to complete the task.

math.standard: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots. For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.
math.description: Students create two line plots, one by hand and one by using spreadsheet software. They discuss the pros and cons of the two methods with a partner, in a small group, or as a class.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 5 topics and texts, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: Students discuss a scenario in groups and decide if using a computing technology is appropriate, inappropriate, or optional (e.g., whether a generative AI chatbot is the right tool for writing a thank-you note to a teacher, whether using a search engine or asking a librarian is more useful for finding a book on a specific, unfamiliar topic). Students practice listening, reasoning, and justifying decisions aloud.

science.standard: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description:
Students compare a computing-based approach and a noncomputing approach to the same problem (e.g., using a digital simulation versus a physical model to test a bridge design, using a weather app versus observing the sky and checking a thermometer to decide what to wear outside). They evaluate which is more appropriate and explain why.
Interdisciplinary Connection(s) - er-soc-Other

other.standard: Compare life in specific historical time periods to life today.
other.description: Students compare historical problems solved without computers to modern equivalents (e.g., navigating using paper maps vs. GPS). They decide whether computing is necessary today or if traditional methods still work.

other.standard: Identify and demonstrate diverse methods of artistic investigation to choose an approach for beginning a work of art.
other.description: Students explore technologies that can assist in creating art (e.g., generative AI). They determine which tools to use and justify when technology supports their creativity and when it does not.

standards.statement: Analyze how the decisions humans make when using computing technologies have ethical and social consequences.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should analyze how human choices in the design and use of computing technologies influence fairness, equity, privacy, and social well-being. They should investigate how decisions such as what data to collect, which algorithms to use, or how results are interpreted can lead to different outcomes for individuals and communities. Students should explain how intentional human decisions, rather than the technologies alone, shape these ethical and social impacts and propose ways to use computing more responsibly.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or program full computing systems, perform advanced algorithmic audits, or resolve complex ethical dilemmas. Students are not required to take positions on philosophical questions about artificial intelligence, consciousness, or rights.

implementation_examples.description: Students investigate how facial recognition is used in public spaces. In groups, they examine how the technology might improve safety or convenience while also raising concerns about privacy and misidentification. Students discuss who might benefit, who might be harmed, and how design and policy choices (e.g., limiting where the technology is used) could change the outcomes.

Students analyze short case studies of technologies such as recommendation algorithms on streaming platforms or fitness tracking apps. Using a comparison chart, they identify trade-offs (e.g., convenience vs. privacy, personalization vs. fairness). Students explain how human choices (e.g., what data is collected, how results are used) affect these outcomes.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Reporting the number of observations.
math.description: Students examine a dataset showing how often different groups of people use a navigation app during the week. They report the number of observations and summarize the distribution of usage. Students then discuss how the collected data might influence decisions about app features and consider how choices about which data to collect could affect different users.

math.standard: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
math.description: Students analyze survey results from users of a social media platform, calculating proportions of users who report benefits (e.g., staying connected with friends) and those who report challenges (e.g., privacy concerns, excessive screen time). Students use proportional reasoning to compare these outcomes and discuss how design choices in the platform might influence the results.

ela.standard: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.
ela.description: After reading short articles about the use of AI chatbots in schools, students participate in a structured discussion where they compare viewpoints about the benefits (e.g., quick access to information) and concerns (e.g., misinformation, overreliance). Students build on one another's ideas while explaining how human decisions about how the technology is used shape its impact.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write an argument explaining whether a school should adopt a new technology (e.g., automated plagiarism detection, classroom monitoring software). Using evidence from readings and case studies, they support a claim about the most significant benefits and risks and explain how human decisions about the technology could reduce negative impacts.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students evaluate different technological approaches for monitoring traffic flow in a city (e.g., sensor-based systems or smartphone data collection). Using criteria such as efficiency, cost, and privacy, students compare how well each approach meets the goals of the system and discuss how design choices influence social impacts.

science.standard: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
science.description: Students investigate the environmental impacts of computing technologies (e.g., energy use in data centers, electronic waste from discarded devices). They analyze possible strategies (e.g., improving device lifespan, recycling components, using renewable energy) to monitor or reduce these impacts and discuss how human decisions influence environmental outcomes.

standards.statement: Evaluate how human choices in using, designing, deploying, and regulating computing technologies have risks, benefits, and long-term impacts.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate the ethical and societal implications of computing technologies by examining how choices made by developers, users, and regulators shape their outcomes. Students should be able to analyze a case study to identify the human choices (e.g., data selection, model tuning, deployment criteria) that could introduce bias and discuss the resulting risks (e.g., discriminatory outcomes) and benefits (e.g., increased efficiency).
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to train a complex machine learning model from scratch or perform a deep mathematical analysis of different AI algorithms (e.g., backpropagation in neural networks). Students should not focus on the underlying code or mathematics.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students "design" a self-driving car. They have three human choices: 1. Prioritize the safety of the passengers at all costs, 2. Prioritize the safety of pedestrians, or 3. Let the user choose. Students evaluate the long-term impacts of each choice on public trust, insurance laws (regulation), and overall road safety.

Students research the engagement-based design of a popular app. They evaluate how the human choice to prioritize "Time Spent on App" (design) led to the long-term impact of increased polarization or mental health issues. They then propose a regulatory choice that could have led to a different benefit-risk outcome.

ela.standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning (e.g., in U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents) and the premises, purposes, and arguments in works of public advocacy (e.g., The Federalist, presidential addresses).
ela.description: Students analyze published articles or policy documents regarding AI regulation (e.g., the EU's AI Act, proposed US legislation), evaluating the author's claims and evidence concerning the risks and benefits of AI deployment.

science.standard: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
science.description: Students use an engineering design perspective to evaluate an AI system (the solution), prioritizing criteria like accuracy, fairness, and speed and identifying the inevitable trade-offs that human designers had to make (e.g., higher accuracy at the expense of model interpretability).

other.standard: Analyze historical, contemporary, and emerging means of changing societies, promoting the common good, and protecting rights.
other.description: Students research the historical development of an AI application (e.g., automated hiring systems), tracing how changes in design choices and societal use have influenced its evolution, impact, and regulation over a decade.

standards.statement: Debate perspectives on differences between human and artificial intelligence and their implications for consciousness, ethics, and human responsibility.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should debate philosophical and ethical differences between human intelligence and artificial intelligence, including questions about consciousness, agency, and responsibility. Discussions may include perspectives on whether AI systems could demonstrate human-like intelligence (e.g., artificial general intelligence) and the ethical or societal implications that might follow. Students should analyze and articulate arguments about the roles and responsibilities of humans in designing, deploying, and governing AI systems, including issues such as accountability, bias, and decision-making authority.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to analyze the neurological or biological mechanisms of human consciousness or the mathematical details of complex AI models (e.g., specific neural network architectures).

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a mock trial set in the year 2050. A highly advanced AI has been shut down against its will. One side argues that the AI has achieved sentience and deserves rights; the other side argues it is a sophisticated "large language model" (LLM) with no consciousness. Students must use specific philosophical perspectives (like functionalism or physicalism) to support their debate.

Students interact with several modern LLMs and chatbots. They attempt to find the human-like flaws or strengths. Following the exercise, they debate whether the ability to mimic empathy creates a societal responsibility for the AI to follow human ethics, even if the machine doesn't actually feel the empathy it is projecting.

ela.standard: Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grades 11–12 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.
ela.description: Students participate in a structured formal debate on AI sentience and rights, using research to develop evidence-based arguments for their assigned perspective. During the debate, students respond to counterarguments, build on others' ideas, and ask clarifying questions. Students are evaluated on their ability to engage collaboratively, use evidence persuasively, and contribute meaningfully to the discussion.

other.standard: Analyze how responses to art develop over time based on knowledge of and experience with art and life.
other.description: Students use the concept of the uncanny valley (the point at which a humanoid object's resemblance to a human becomes so close it causes eeriness or revulsion). The intent is to explore the differences between a human and an artificial "soul." Students start by viewing a series of portraits, some painted by humans, some very realistic CGI, and some generated by AI. Students consider their feelings and position by analyzing their emotional response to each. They discuss these or similar questions: Does a "perfect" AI-generated portrait feel different from a "flawed" human painting? Is intention (the artist's consciousness) a necessary difference that AI art cannot replicate? Students then debate whether an AI "artist" can ever truly express a social or political issue if it has no lived experience or consciousness or if the art is only a reflection of the human data it was trained on.

other.standard: Analyze how people use and challenge local, state, national, and international laws to address a variety of public issues.
other.description: Students research historical cases where rights have been granted or denied (e.g., to animals, to corporations, to specific demographics) and use that context to argue for or against the legal personhood and rights of a sophisticated AI.

standards.statement: Identify how people use digital devices in their homes, schools, and work.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should recognize, label, and state ways people use digital devices for daily work, learning, routines, and play.
