Examples such as using a digital thermometer to check temperature before going outside or parents checking work emails on a phone are appropriate. Students should participate in classroom discussions and activities where digital devices are used for communicating, learning, or helping with a task. Examples such as using manipulatives, role-play, or simple digital tools are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to name all device types or explain technical details. Students are not required to operate digital devices independently or use advanced features of digital devices.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a whole-class activity where the teacher gathers students' ideas of how people use digital devices. They share which device is used and what it is used to do. As a class, students sort the examples into home, school and work. Students draw a picture of one digital device they saw and describe its purpose with a simple sentence. They share their examples and explain their drawings to the class.

Students engage in a role-playing activity in groups where they act out scenarios involving digital devices in daily work. One student might pretend to be a parent checking emails on a phone for their job, another might play a cashier using a computer to scan pretend groceries, and another could act as a nurse using a tablet to record patient information. The remaining group members identify the device the child was using and what they used the device to do.

math.standard: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.
math.description: Students use an app to practice counting and discuss how using an app on a school device to reinforce number sense is similar to how people can use digital devices to complete school work.

math.standard: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
math.description: Students work in pairs using a tablet to sort shapes to classify objects. In a class discussion, students identify the tablet as a digital device they used to sort the shapes.

ela.standard: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about kindergarten topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
ela.description: Students identify and explain digital device use in daily life in a whole-class discussion.

ela.standard: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose informative/explanatory texts in which they name what they are writing about and supply some information about the topic.
ela.description: Students participate in creating a whole-class chart by drawing and writing about how people use devices at home, school, and work.

science.standard: Use tools and materials provided to design and build a structure that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on Earth’s surface.
science.description: Students use a digital thermometer to record and discuss classroom temperatures.

other.standard: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making.
other.description: In a class discussion circle, students share examples of digital tool scarcity and possible responses (e.g., taking turns to use the one computer at home, choosing a different center if the technology center is full, prioritizing which show to watch when screen time is limited).

other.standard: Child writes for a variety of purposes using increasingly sophisticated marks.
other.description: Students draw and caption a picture of one device they saw someone in their family use at home. During circle time, they share their drawing, expressing what it shows in a full sentence (e.g., "My dad used a laptop to do his work at the table.")

standards.statement: Describe how computing is used by people in their life at home, school, and community.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should identify and describe simple, familiar examples of how people use computing devices every day at home, school, or in the community. Examples such as a teacher using a tablet to read a story, a parent using a phone to call family, or a sibling using a computer to do school work are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to describe the internal parts of computers or the complex inner workings of the computing systems technology. Students are not required to use the computing devices themselves or to know specific technical terms.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students individually brainstorm and draw a simple timeline of their day or week, adding pictures or words to show items in which computing is used (e.g., alarm clock, smart speaker, map app, tablet learning app, grocery store scanner, TV remote). The class then discusses how these devices help people in their daily lives. If some students have limited access to technology, the teacher may choose to complete the activity as a class instead of individually.

Each student draws or writes about a person they know (e.g., family member, teacher, friend) who uses a computing device and describes what that person uses it for (e.g., "My dad uses a computer to pay bills." "My teacher uses a smartboard to show videos." "My mom uses her phone to get directions when we're going somewhere."). These examples can be displayed on a wall to illustrate the range of ways people use computing.

math.standard: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.
math.description: Working in groups and counting uses of computers, phones, and other computing devices, students collect information about how people around them use technology. They create visual representations of the data collected (e.g., tally chart, pictograph) and ask questions about the data (e.g., "How many people use phones?" "How many more people use phones compared to computers?").

ela.standard: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
ela.description: With teacher guidance, students work individually to recall and draw or write about one specific time they saw someone in their life use computing (e.g., a parent using a phone to find directions, a teacher using a computer to take attendance, a store worker using a scanner), then share their example with a partner.  Together they answer the question "How does computing help people do their work or activities at home, school, or in the community?"

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they name a topic, supply some facts about the topic, and provide some sense of closure.
ela.description: The whole class goes on a teacher-led walk through the school building to find adults using technology (e.g., librarian scanning books, secretary answering a digital phone, cafeteria worker using a touch-screen register). Students then work individually to write a two-sentence report of what they observed, naming a person they saw, the device used, and the purpose.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students identify a "problem" in their classroom (e.g., It's hard to hear the teacher over the air conditioning) and investigate if there is a computing technology that could solve it (e.g., a microphone system). Students share a story or drawing of how that specific technology helps solve the problem so the teacher can do their job more effectively.

science.standard: Use observations of the sun, moon, and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted.
science.description: Working in small groups, students use a weather app or weather website to see the sunrise and sunset times for the week and compare them to their own window observations. Students express that meteorologists use computers at work to predict the patterns in weather for families at home, demonstrating how computing technology helps people plan their daily lives around the natural world.

other.standard: Explain how all people, not just official leaders, play important roles in a community.
other.description: During a unit on community helpers, the teacher invites a guest speaker (e.g., firefighter, nurse). Students work in pairs to brainstorm three questions about how that professional uses technology to help people. They show their understanding by drawing a picture of themselves in a possible future career using technology to help the community.

standards.statement: Investigate how personal interests connect to computing in different industries and careers.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore and describe, in simple terms, how their passions and hobbies connect to computing. They should also investigate how computing is used in different jobs and industries that relate to those interests. For example, a student who loves drawing could learn how artists create digital illustrations or a student who enjoys sports could explore how coaches use computers to track scores and performance.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand technical details about how computing systems work, specific job qualifications, or the exact tools used in various careers. Students are not required to conduct in-depth career research or simulate real-world industry work.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: A diverse range of community members present at career day to explain how they use computers in their jobs. Afterward, students select one example of how computing supports someone's work and write about how they could prepare for that career. If a diverse range of careers is not represented in the community, teachers can share videos of professionals discussing how they use computing in similar ways.

Students choose something they love to do (e.g., reading, cooking, inventing, playing soccer, helping others). They then identify a related career and learn how that career uses computing. Students draw or write about how someone in that career might use computers in their work (e.g., a student who loves baking could write about how a baker uses computers to design cake decorations, a student who enjoys being outdoors could draw a picture of a park ranger using a tablet to record animal sightings).

math.standard: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put- together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
math.description: Students gather data on the class's personal interests (e.g., how many like sports, art, science). They draw a bar graph to represent this data and use it to select industries to research, connecting the personal interests of the class to career exploration.

ela.standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
ela.description: Students read a text about someone working in a particular industry or career that includes an illustration or text about their use of computing. Students then answer questions about who uses computing, what they are using, when they are using it, why they use it, and how they use it.

ela.standard: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
ela.description: Students explore how computing tools support writing-related careers (e.g., authors, journalists, bloggers, technical writers). With guidance and support, students use digital tools to draft, revise, and publish a short piece of writing collaboratively. After publishing, students discuss how the computing tools they used (e.g., word processors, spell check, shared documents) help writers in different industries and how developing these skills connects to future career opportunities.

science.standard: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.
science.description: Students interested in inventing and creating tools investigate a career and think about these questions: What problem does this job solve? How could a new or improved computing tool help this person do their job better?

other.standard: Recognize that you have many life roles (e.g., personal, leisure, community, learner, family, and work roles).
other.description: Students investigate and consider their current role as a learner, their personal passions and leisure choices, and their potential future work roles in the context of computing. Working individually, they share their findings in a short report or discussion.

other.standard: Media and technology skills to enhance learning.
other.description: Students investigate how computing is used in industries and careers related to their interests and use media and technology skills (e.g., create a video) to showcase how they might use computing in a future career.

standards.statement: Explain how people in different industries use computing technologies and skills to accomplish their work.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should describe how people in different fields (e.g., healthcare, transportation, entertainment) use computers and basic computing skills (e.g., finding information, storing data, communicating, creating media) to do their jobs. Examples such as a bus driver following GPS routes, an animator creating cartoons using digital tools, or a shop owner tracking inventory on a laptop are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand how the identified technologies work or to demonstrate the referenced computing skills. Students are not required to research industries or careers in depth or understand training requirements.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description:
Stations representing different industries (e.g., healthcare, transportation, entertainment, education, retail, and public safety) are set up in the classroom. Photos of workers using computing tools are displayed at each station. For example, at the public safety station, there could be photos such as:
• A firefighter checking a tablet inside a fire truck to view a digital map or GPS and find the fastest route to a fire or emergency.
• A police officer typing on a laptop in a patrol car to write a report or look up traffic laws.
• A paramedic using a tablet to enter patient information so the hospital knows what to expect when the ambulance arrives.
• A meteorologist viewing a weather radar map on a large screen to monitor storms or track severe weather.
Students rotate through the stations and discuss which computing tools are shown in the photos. They complete a sentence about each station (e.g., "In [industry], people use [tool] to [job task].").

Students view a demonstration of how one familiar computing-based innovation (e.g., navigation feature, school communication system) solves a real work problem. As a class, students identify the different roles involved (e.g., designing how people use it, programming how it works, testing it, keeping information updated) and describe the type of computing tools or skills each role uses. Students then complete a simple digital drag-and-drop map that shows how the roles connect and collaborate to meet the needs of different users, and they share a brief explanation of how the technology supports work in that industry. students then explore the map and determine the various skills and tools that individuals use to connect to the other people on their team using the map.

math.standard: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
math.description: As a class, students collect data on items that are "sold" in a classroom store and, with teacher guidance, use a digital spreadsheet or graphing tool to create a bar graph of the items sold. Students explain how a real store manager would use this computing skill to decide which toys to buy more of for their shop.

ela.standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
ela.description: Working in pairs, students read a text about how an industry (e.g., animation) has changed over the years (e.g., from hand-drawing to computer coding). Students create a sequence chart showing the evolution of the industry (e.g., first artists drew every frame, then programmers created algorithms to move characters, now animators use CS skills to create 3D worlds), explaining the cause (e.g., invention of new computing technologies) and effect (e.g., faster creation, more realistic movies) of the change in the industry.

ela.standard: Introduce a topic and group related information together; include illustrations when useful to aiding comprehension.
ela.description: Students read one or more nonfiction books about an industry. In groups, students make a poster that includes an illustration with a title (e.g., "Computers help [job] do [task] using which [tool or skill].").

science.standard: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard.
science.description: In small groups, students use a digital weather simulator or interactive map to test design solutions for a hurricane scenario (e.g., a physical sea wall vs. a computer-based early warning app). Students produce a written claim explaining that the early warning app has merit because of its use by professionals in meteorology and because emergency management can use the real-time data analysis and automated communication to reduce the impact of weather-related hazards.

other.standard: Explain probable causes and effects of events and developments.
other.description: In pairs or small groups, students create posters using "then and now" cards to compare historical work methods with modern ones in industries like banking or the postal service. Students explain that although the cause was a need for efficiency, the effect was a shift toward specialized CS skills (e.g., using automation, shifting to digital data management) to accomplish tasks that were once done manually.

other.standard: Long- and short-term academic, career and social/emotional goals.
other.description: Students set long-term career goals and then investigate the computing skills needed for that career, explaining the short-term goals they would need to work on to gain those skills.

standards.statement: Investigate how the workforce adopts new computing technologies and continues to update their computing skills.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should examine and analyze how people in a variety of careers have learned and updated computing skills to adapt to changes in their work. Examples such as doctors learning to use digital records, teachers adopting video conferencing tools to teach remotely, farmers using GPS technology to plant and cultivate crops more precisely, or programmers applying AI tools to shorten development and debugging time are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct formal research or interviews with the workforce. Students are not required to demonstrate the computing skills or use the tools used by the workforce.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups of three to four to explore teacher-provided scenario cards describing professionals who learned new computing skills. Each card presents a different professional (e.g., a librarian, a graphic designer, a programmer, a nurse) and describes the computing skill they learned, why they needed to learn it, and how it helped them in their work. Groups read their scenarios and discuss these questions: What did this person learn? Why did they need to learn it? "How does this show adaptability?" They then create a poster or chart showing their findings. Each group presents its work to the class, and together the class compiles a list of reasons professionals need to continue learning throughout their careers.

Students work individually to interview an adult in their community (e.g., family member, neighbor, school staff) using a shared set of four to five class-developed questions about how computing tools and skills in their job have changed over time. Students take notes during the interview and compare at least one past and one current computing technology used in that profession, including why new skills were required. Each student creates a short presentation (slides, poster, digital tool) explaining how learning new computing skills changed the person's work. Students present to the class and contribute to a discussion identifying common reasons workers continue updating their computing skills.

math.standard: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.
math.description: Students analyze a dataset showing the percentage of workers in a specific field (e.g., healthcare, education, agriculture) adopting a new computing technology over time. They create a linear model to represent the trend and interpret the slope as the rate of technology adoption and the intercept as the estimated starting level of adoption. Students explain what these values suggest about how quickly workers in that field are updating their computing skills.

math.standard: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.
math.description: Students examine data representing the adoption of a new computing technology in the workforce (e.g., AI tools, electronic medical records, video conferencing platforms). They compare linear and exponential models to determine which best represents the adoption pattern and then justify their choice. Students explain how different rates of change reflect how quickly workers update skills and how computing technologies spread over time.

ela.standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
ela.description: Students read informational articles or biographical texts about professionals who adapted to technological changes in their fields, then explain the cause-and-effect relationship between changing job demands and the need to learn new computing skills.

ela.standard: Report on a topic or text, tell a story, or recount an experience in an organized manner, using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace.
ela.description: Students present the results of interviewing a community member about how computing and technology have changed their work over time to their classmates.

other.standard: Compare the benefits and costs of individual choices.
other.description: Students discuss the benefits (e.g., staying employed, helping more people, working more efficiently) and costs (e.g., time, effort, possible frustration) of professionals choosing to learn new computing skills, developing economic thinking about career decisions.

standards.statement: Examine how professionals collaborate while using computing technologies to solve problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should focus on describing ways different professionals (e.g., scientists, doctors, artists, engineers) work together on a task using common digital tools for communication and sharing information. Real-life scenarios, like doctors sharing digital X-rays to diagnose a patient or architects using shared design software to plan a building, are appropriate.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to understand the technical details of how the network or collaborative software functions. Students are not required to engage in complex collaborative projects or to use professional tools.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups as professional architect teams using paper and pencils to simulate collaborative design. Their task is to design a new playground. First, each student individually draws one part of the playground on a small sheet of paper without talking. Then, the group tries to assemble the individual pieces into a coherent plan, discussing the challenges of not having a shared view. Finally, they receive a large sheet of paper, their "shared digital workspace," where they can all draw and revise the plan together. Students demonstrate understanding by reflecting on the two processes, writing or discussing how the shared workspace (representing a computing technology) made it easier for their team of professionals to collaborate and solve the design problem compared to working separately.

Students work in pairs or small groups using a collaborative online document or slide presentation tool. The task is to co-write a short story or presentation on a chosen topic. Each student takes on a specific role (e.g., writer, illustrator, editor) and uses the tool's features (e.g., simultaneous editing, comments, chat) to collaborate on the final product. Students then demonstrate understanding by presenting their final story and reflecting on the process. They describe specific ways the computing technology helped them collaborate effectively as a team of professionals to solve the problem of creating a shared digital product.

math.standard: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.
math.description: Working in small teams, students use a shared slide deck to design a shipping container that meets given volume requirements by proposing dimensions and calculating volume using multiplication and addition. Each team presents their final container design and explains how the shared digital workspace supported real-time collaboration and problem solving, connecting professional computing practices to mathematical reasoning about volume.

math.standard: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.
math.description: Working in teams as professionals (e.g., city planners, scientists), students each plot assigned coordinate points related to a shared problem using a collaborative digital graphing tool. Teams interpret the completed coordinate plane to identify patterns, explain the meaning of points in context, and describe how the shared computational tool supports professional collaboration and problem solving.

ela.standard: With some guidance and support from adults, use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of two pages in a single sitting.
ela.description: Working in collaborative writing teams, students use a shared online document to plan, draft, revise, and publish a digital resource, modeling how professionals use computing technologies to work together. Teams produce a final published document and explain how digital tools such as commenting and revision history supported their collaboration and writing process.

ela.standard: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
ela.description: Working in writing groups, students draft an opinion piece in a shared document and use commenting tools to provide peer feedback focused on strengthening claims, reasons, and organization. Students submit a revised opinion piece and explain how collaborative digital tools supported editing and revision.

science.standard: Measure and graph quantities to provide evidence that regardless of the type of change that occurs when heating, cooling, or mixing substances, the total weight of matter is conserved.
science.description: Working in research teams, students conduct assigned experiments (e.g., mixing baking soda and vinegar, melting ice) and use a shared spreadsheet to record and compare weight measurements before and after the change. Teams collaboratively analyze the data and create a digital graph, modeling how professionals use computing tools to work together and using the results to show that matter is conserved.

science.standard: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth’s resources and environment.
science.description: Working in investigative groups, students research how different communities use science to protect environmental resources using shared online research tools and reliable digital sources. Groups collaborate in a shared presentation platform to synthesize their findings into a multimedia report, modeling how professionals use computing technologies to work together and communicate solutions.

other.standard: Create and use a chronological sequence of related events to compare developments that happened at the same time.
other.description: Working in small groups, students research different topics from the same historical period and use a shared digital timeline tool to create chronological sequences of key events with dates and descriptions. Groups compare their timelines side by side and annotate connections between concurrent events, modeling how professionals collaborate using computing technologies to analyze developments happening at the same time.

other.standard: Describes the perspective of others during a variety of activities.
other.description: Working in groups as sports analysts, students use a collaborative video annotation tool to analyze a recorded physical activity from the perspectives of a player, coach, and opposing team member. Students demonstrate understanding by adding comments and marked plays to the video, modeling how professionals use computing technologies to collaboratively evaluate performance and viewpoints.

standards.statement: Analyze how workers in different careers use computational thinking to solve real-world problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should investigate and describe examples of computational thinking across a range of professions. Students should be able to connect computational thinking concepts such as abstraction, decomposition, and pattern recognition to specific job functions, identifying parallels between how they think when coding and how professionals think when solving domain-specific problems.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to explore specialized programming frameworks or conduct domain-specific simulations that require advanced mathematics, physics, or proprietary software.

implementation_examples.description: Students work in small groups to create a Career Computational Thinking Map. Each group receives cards with different careers and short job descriptions, then sorts them by computational thinking concepts such as abstraction, decomposition, and pattern recognition. After sorting, students choose one career and design a poster showing how that professional uses computational thinking to solve a real-world problem (e.g., an architect decomposing a building design into structural components). Groups present their posters to explain the concepts and parallels to coding practices.

Students use a collaborative digital tool to share research on how professionals apply computational thinking. Each student completes a template with sections for career name, real-world problem, computational thinking concepts, and a simple flowchart or pseudocode of a process (e.g., a logistics manager creating an algorithm for delivery routes). Students upload their completed templates to a shared gallery and review peers' work, commenting on similarities across careers.

math.standard: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
math.description: Students analyze how an environmental engineer uses data models to predict flooding by examining a simplified rainfall dataset and calculating measures of center. They create a graph and explain how pattern recognition in computational thinking supports mathematical predictions.

math.standard: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.
math.description: Students model how a game designer uses algorithms to balance gameplay by writing simple equations for scoring systems. They present their equations and explain how decomposition and abstraction help designers adjust difficulty levels.

ela.standard: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
ela.description: Students write an article explaining how a social media manager uses pattern recognition to understand audience engagement. They include examples of metrics e.g., likes and shares) and connect these patterns to computational thinking concepts.

ela.standard: Come to discussions prepared, having read or researched material under study; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
ela.description: Students participate in a debate on whether computational thinking is essential in nontechnical careers such as healthcare or law. They cite researched examples and explain how abstraction and decomposition apply to these fields.

science.standard: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
science.description: Students explore how an environmental engineer decomposes a flooding problem into variables (e.g., rainfall, soil type). They create a simple predictive model and explain how abstraction and decomposition guide the process.

science.standard: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
science.description: Students investigate how environmental engineers use computational thinking to reduce water pollution. They design a simple plan that decomposes the problem into steps (identifying sources, predicting runoff patterns) and use pattern recognition to propose strategies for minimizing contamination.

other.standard: Analyze the purposes, implementation, and consequences of public policies in multiple settings.
other.description: Students research how policymakers use computational thinking to model economic impacts of legislation. They present findings in a short report connecting abstraction and algorithms to policy analysis.

other.standard: Demonstrate persistence in developing skills with various materials, methods, and approaches in creating works of art or design.
other.description: Students analyze how graphic designers use decomposition and abstraction when creating layered digital art. They create a sketch showing how design elements are broken down and recombined to form a cohesive piece.

standards.statement: Evaluate how automation in technology can create or replace jobs and change how people work.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should explore how automation technologies (e.g., robotics, artificial intelligence, machine learning) have changed or are changing the nature of work across industries and analyze the social and economic trade-offs of automation. Examples where automation improves efficiency, accuracy, and safety as well as cases where it disrupts or replaces jobs are appropriate. Students should also consider how automation affects job tasks and skill requirements, raises ethical and human-centered questions, and prompts workers and industries to adapt through upskilling, reskilling, or new roles.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to design or program automated systems, conduct in-depth economic analyses, or engage in labor-market forecasting.

practices.practice: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

implementation_examples.description: Students conduct interviews with older family members, neighbors, or community members (either in person or via a class virtual call) to learn how automation has changed their work over time. Each student prepares a short list of questions about tasks that were once manual and how technology has altered those tasks or job roles. After the interviews, students create a summary highlighting examples of automation, its benefits, and its challenges and share insights in a class discussion connecting these changes to computational thinking concepts like abstraction and decomposition.

In teacher-supervised teams (or as a class), students work with a simple AI chatbot or voice assistant to simulate an Automation Advisor. They design a scenario in which a company is considering automating a specific job (e.g., warehouse sorting, customer service). Students interact with the AI to gather ideas about what tasks could be automated, then create a short video or infographic showing the proposed automation plan, its efficiency gains, and potential social impacts.

math.standard: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.
math.description: Students analyze a dataset showing job changes in manufacturing before and after automation in a specific field. They calculate percentages of jobs lost and gained and explain how these numbers reflect automation's impact on employment trends.

math.standard: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.
math.description: Students compare productivity rates before and after introducing automated systems in a factory. They compute ratios of output per hour and discuss how these changes illustrate automation's effect on efficiency and labor needs.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
ela.description: Students write a persuasive essay arguing whether automation creates more opportunities than it eliminates. They use examples from specific industries (e.g., retail, transportation) to support their position on how automation changes work.

ela.standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
ela.description: Students read two nonfiction articles about automation and the future of work, one emphasizing efficiency and job creation and the other highlighting job loss and ethical concerns. They compare the texts to identify conflicting claims and interpretations, then write a short analysis explaining how these differences influence public perception of automation's impact on employment.

science.standard: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.
science.description: Students compare two approaches to automating agricultural tasks (e.g., robotic harvesters vs. drone monitoring) and evaluate which solution better balances efficiency and job preservation. They present their reasoning based on real-world impacts.

science.standard: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.
science.description: Students analyze how self-driving technology affects transportation safety and employment. They create a short report weighing benefits like reduced accidents against drawbacks such as job displacement for drivers.

other.standard: Analyze the role of innovation and entrepreneurship in a market economy.
other.description: Students play a simulation game (e.g., Cookie Tycoon) where they manage a virtual business and decide whether to invest in automation (e.g., automated ovens, robotic packaging) to increase production. After gameplay, students analyze how automation changed their workforce needs, efficiency, and profits and reflect on how automation creates or replaces jobs and changes how people work.

other.standard: Demonstrate awareness of practices, issues, and ethics of appropriation, fair use, copyright, open source, and creative commons as they apply to creating works of art and design.
other.description: Students use AI-assisted design tools (e.g., Canva AI, Adobe Firefly) to create a sketch or mockup that illustrates which design tasks remain human-driven and which are automated. After completing their design, they write a short reflection on the ethical implications of using AI in creative work, including considerations of originality and copyright as well as its impact on artists' careers, available work, and the nature of creative tasks.

standards.statement: Analyze how diverse teams of people use computational thinking and technologies to solve problems.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should understand the real-world application of computer science, including how CS is used at work, the kinds of challenges that practitioners face, and how practitioners contribute to a more inclusive field. A concrete example of this is having students analyze a podcast or video series featuring computer science professionals from diverse backgrounds and then identifying how they use their skills and have navigated workplace barriers.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to conduct formal, academic research on these topics or to interview professionals themselves, but rather to analyze existing, publicly available narratives. Students are not required to solve complex social problems, but rather to understand and articulate the issues and solutions presented in the narratives.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students watch or read the narrative of the NASA "human computers" (Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan, and Mary Jackson). They analyze how their unique perspectives and mastery of algorithms and decomposition enabled them, despite the societal barriers they faced, to solve the problem of orbital mechanics that others couldn't..

Students research a modern, diverse team (e.g., the group at Google that developed Real Tone, an effort to make camera algorithms more equitable for different skin tones). They analyze the narrative to see how having photographers, engineers, and colorists from diverse backgrounds led to a change in the software's abstraction of "skin color."

math.standard: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.
math.description: Students analyze a professional narrative (e.g., that of a data scientist, public health analyst, engineer) describing how a team used data to solve a problem. Students examine a related dataset and construct or review a linear model representing the team's findings. They interpret the slope and intercept in context (e.g., rate of change in cases, growth in users, cost over time) and explain how collaborative use of computational tools supported the team's conclusions.

math.standard: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.
math.description: Students analyze a professional narrative describing how a team used computational tools to solve a real-world problem (e.g., estimating server energy use, calculating data storage needs, modeling production costs). Students solve a related multistep problem using appropriate units (e.g., kilowatt-hours, gigabytes, dollars per hour), demonstrating how units help structure reasoning and ensure accurate conclusions. They reflect on how teams use careful quantitative reasoning and computational tools to break complex problems into manageable steps.

science.standard: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.
science.description: Students analyze a professional narrative describing how environmental scientists, engineers, and community stakeholders collaborated to address water quality challenges. Students identify the criteria (e.g., water purity levels, cost, accessibility) and constraints (e.g., available materials, local infrastructure, environmental conditions) considered by the team, and examine how computational tools (e.g., models of water flow or filtration rates) supported this analysis. They explain how the inclusion of diverse perspectives influenced how the problem was defined, which criteria were prioritized, and how trade-offs were evaluated.

standards.statement: Connect computing knowledge and skills acquired to students' personal goals and career aspirations.
standards.boundary_includes: Students should evaluate how their personal interests and career aspirations connect to computing knowledge and skills. This involves critically reflecting on their own strengths and passions and researching how these can be applied in various computing-related fields.
standards.boundary_excludes: Students are not expected to make a final career choice or to pursue an internship or work-based learning experience. Students are not expected to make a final commitment to a specific career path.

practices.practice: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

implementation_examples.description: Students participate in a brainstorming session where they identify their passion (e.g., fashion, medicine, music). They then use a Venn diagram to find the overlap where computing knowledge (e.g., 3D modeling for fashion, database management for medicine) makes their goal more achievable or innovative.

Students create a digital Career Roadmap. They identify one specific skill they've learned (e.g., "designing a user interface") and write a pitch for how that skill would make them a better candidate for their dream job (e.g., "As a physical therapist, I would be able to design better app-based recovery plans for my patients.").

math.standard: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.
math.description: Students research a computing-related career aligned with their personal interests (e.g., game design, cybersecurity, data science) and analyze publicly available data such as projected job growth or salary over time. Using a linear model, students interpret the slope as the rate of change (e.g., salary growth per year, increase in job openings) and the intercept as the estimated starting value. Students explain how these quantitative trends might inform their career decision-making.

math.standard: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.
math.description: Students identify a personal goal related to a computing field (e.g., launching a small app, pursuing a certification, saving for college). They define two related quantities (e.g., hours of practice and skill level, time and savings, number of projects completed and portfolio strength) and write a function that models the relationship between them. Students explain how this mathematical model represents their progress and reflects how computing skills develop over time toward a career aspiration.

ela.standard: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
ela.description: Students write a personal narrative or argumentative essay about how their personal interests align with a particular computing career.
